speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
subsubtopic: PRAIRIE DROUGHT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour on behalf of more than 2,000 farmers in southwestern Manitoba, most of them residing in my constituency of Brandon-Souris, to present a petition to the House of Commons noting that the crops in southwestern Manitoba were actually worse in 1989 than they were in 1988, the year in which the drought assistance program was available.
My petitioners very appropriately call for assistance either from the provincial or federal levels of government or preferably jointly, and they note that if this assistance is not forthcoming many farmers in our area will not survive. This, in turn, will have a very drastic impact of the whole of southwestern Manitoba.
In closing, I would like to add my very strong personal words of support to this very appropriate petition.

Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 36,1 am today tabling a petition from Lebel-sur-Quevillon, Quebec, further to the recommendations of the task force on tax benefits for northern and isolated areas.
Lebel-sur-Quevillon is undoubtedly an isolated community and for that reason, the signers of this petition consider the Brunelle recommendation to be discriminatory, unfair and inappropriate to the purpose of the northern tax benefit plan. It does not encourage settlement of the North and resource development there.

subsubtopic: POST SECONDARY EDUCATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the duty to present to this House 10 new petitions signed by students from Ottawa University who simply point out that overcrowded lecture halls, deteriorating laboratory equipment, a lack of library resources, the student-teacher ratio, the elimination of some cur-riculums as well as deteriorating buildings and facilities are a typical feature of Canada's postsecondary education system today.
Mr. Speaker, these students put forward a number of other arguments. On this basis, these citizens call upon Parliament and government to commit to holding a top level federal-provincial conference in order to establish the financial responsibilities of both levels of governe-ment with respect to postsecondary education and to put an end to the shameful neglect higher education has been subjected to in Canada.

subsubtopic: GOODS AND SERVICES TAX
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I also have a petition signed by Canadians who are strongly opposed to the goods and services tax proposed by the Conservative government. Thgy say that this tax is totally unfair and unjustified; that it will impose an extra burden on poor and lower income families; that it will raise inflation; that it will create serious difficulties for small business. Therefore, they humbly ask Parliament to reject this proposal to impose a 7 per cent goods and services tax on Canadians.

subsubtopic: GOODS AND SERVICES TAX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present several petitions from areas throughout the Algoma riding, including communities in Blind River and Elliot Lake, Espanola, Mindemoya, Tehkum-mah, and a number of other communities throughout the Manitoulin district of northern Ontario, in which they call on the government to withdraw the goods and services tax, even though it has been reduced from 9 per cent to 7 per cent. They point out that this will be very hard on senior citizens. It will increase the cost of goods and services in northern Ontario. It will be especially onerous to the tourist industry.
I hope the government will take these humble petitions from my constituents into account in its policy with regard to this tax.

subsubtopic: NORTHERN TAX BENEFITS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a number of petitions related to the northern tax benefit. They have different wordings, and I will be giving information to the House on the issue.
The first petition is from a number of people in the communities of Thompson, Pikwitonei, Snow Lake, Cross Lake, Ilford, York Landing, Norway House, Puka-tawagan and Princess Harbour. In this particular petition they call upon the federal government to reject the recommendations of the task force on northern and isolated areas. They believe that we should develop a fair and equitable tax benefit program which recognizes the financial needs of people in northern and isolated areas.
I also have a petition strictly from the people of Thompson, Manitoba, expressing their concern with the situation that Thompson and Wabowden and Paint Lake have been left out of the northern tax benefit, even though they are definitely northern communities. They have been prescribed, as have communities in other northern areas like northern Alberta, northern Quebec, northern B.C.. They believe that the federal government has not paid attention to the northemess of their communities and that it is time these communities receive the full northern tax benefit as their neighbouring communities do.
In addition to that, after the task force on northern benefits made its report, we have another 772 names from The Pas, Flin Flon, Cranberry Portage, Cormorant, Moose Lake and Gillam. The people in these communities say that the task force on tax benefits for northern and isolated areas, released Friday, October 27, fails to address the realities of the north, the high cost of living and working in these areas-the whole cost of isolation. They call upon Parliament to reject the recommendations of the report and to develop a fair and equitable tax benefit program which recognizes the financial needs of people in northern and isolated areas.
In addition to that, Mr. Speaker, there are people from The Pas, Manitoba who also set out a petition rejecting the task force on tax benefits for northern and isolated
March 13, 1990

areas. They again talk about the need for real tax benefits for people living in northern and isolated areas.
They call upon Parliament to reject the proposal of the task force and call upon the government to act in this area.
I wish Tory Conservative MPs would get up with their petitions on this issue and express their concern and outrage with what the task force on isolated areas has recommended, which is basically denying thousands of communities in northern Canada from receiving this benefit.
I have another petition from The Pas. I will not bore the Speaker by reading it, but it is along the same lines. The petitioners point out that the federal government task force is ignoring the north and it is time that we had action from the government to reinstate the full tax benefit for people in northern Canada.
I do not want to go through all my petitions today, but I do want to indicate that certainly in northern Manitoba there is a drastic reaction to the federal government and the task force proposals. I would expect the Parliamentary Secretary for the Government House Leader to get up with his petitions on the northern tax benefit as well.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-NON-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in moving closure, the Government of Canada has just moved closure on 1,090,000 Canadians who are now collecting unemployment insurance benefits that average $215.88 a week. The government has just moved closure on perhaps the poorest group of people in Canada, who cannot make ends meet, and this government, supported by these Tory members here today, has just approved of a bill that not only will increase the qualifying periods but will decrease the period of time that these people can collect unemployment insurance.
Just imagine, $215.88 a week, Canadian average, and the big bully Government of Canada is going ahead with this bill and moving closure in this Chamber. The government claims that it is going to streamline the unemployment insurance scheme and it is going to increase the training component. On the one hand, the government is out of touch and on the other hand it is out of mind.
The government, in moving closure, is saying that people throughout Canada will need to be living in an area of less than 15 per cent unemployment in order to maintain the repeater provision of 10 weeks to qualify for unemployment insurance. The present law is for 11.5 per cent unemployment. This means that now, with the drawing of all these lines, it will depend upon which side of the line you live on. That is what will determine whether you will collect unemployment insurance or not.
Just imagine the discrimination involved in that. The majority of the people who live in rural areas, in the case of Newfoundland and Labrador, do not work where they live. If they work as a group, either on the ocean, in a mine or in the forest, when they go to register for unemployment insurance the question that will be asked is "Where do you live?" because where they live will determine whether they collect unemployment insurance.
Prior to this bill, 11.5 per cent was the cut-off point. Now, under this Tory government, it is 15 per cent and that is going to mean three different rates in the province of Newfoundland and Labrador.
Then the government says it is going to increase the money for training. What a silly proposal this government brought in in 1984. Since 1984 this group of Tories approved training programs that say that if you are an unemployed logger living in a logging community and there is a job-creation project in your community which has to do with cutting wood, you cannot go to work on it because you are already trained to cut wood. If you are laying a pipe under the ground that is a part of the water system in your community, as dozens of communities are

March 13, 1990
Government Orders
in Newfoundland, you put in a part of the water system and you apply next year for this so-called training program of the federal government. The government says: "Oh, no. They have already been trained as ditch diggers. You can't go to work two years in a row training to be a ditch digger, so your project does not qualify anymore."
In various places in Newfoundland and Labrador we have communities with half a waterline under the ground. Just imagine half a waterline under the ground. The pipe is half in in the community. It was put there prior to this government coming to office. I can name the communities for you, Mr. Speaker. The pipe is half under the ground in Whale's Gulch, Valleypond and Hillgrade.
This government came into office and said: "Every single job creation program funded by the federal government of Canada from this moment on has to be a training program. We can't train you again to dig a ditch so therefore you can't have any more money to put in your waterline." Shame on the Government of Canada for making a decision like that. Shame on the Minister of Employment and Immigration who stands in the Chamber and says: "We want more money to put into a program."
The government says to these communities which have part of a waterline underground: "If you want to build a building, you can build a building." The communities want to finish their waterlines, but they cannot do that. The Government of Canada says: "No. That waterline is half done under the ground. You already trained the workforce in the area to dig the ditches. Therefore we will now give you money to train them to be carpenters but you are not allowed to hire any carpenters."
Just imagine the upheaval in that particular community. Imagine the group of working people in that community for whom, under this new legislation, whether they will qualify or not for unemployment insurance depends upon which side of the line they live on. If they do not qualify, a fellow will say that he now needs 16, meaning
16 weeks. If he does not have enough for the 16 then he will have to go on a 26, which is a training program. If he does qualify, he will go on a 25. That is the Government of Canada today: If you need an extra two or three, you can go on a 26, and if you qualify, you can go on a 25.
When the Government of Canada came into power in 1984, under a Tory principle it said to every community in rural Canada that was developing its water system: "You can't get any more money for that, but we'll give you money to waste. We'll give you money to do anything else, but you can't do it two years in a row." That is the training program the government promised in 1984. It promised that under its training component it was going to give unemployment insurance to everybody who was in a registered school of instruction for a vocation. In other words, everybody who was in a post-secondary institution who qualified for unemployment insurance under the Tory plan in 1984 was going to be able to collect unemployment insurance.
What do we see today? Today we see one of the most discriminatory systems of payment for training ever in effect in the country. Two individuals sit in a vocational school. They worked together and both are laid off. One is receiving unemployment insurance and the other does not qualify. A full 50 per cent of those people who applied for unemployment insurance under a promise of this government in 1984 do not qualify for that unemployment insurance.
The Government of Canada now comes along and says: "Now we have got a new system. It is now going to depend on what side of the line you live on," because it is now 15 per cent unemployment in effect and not 11.5 per cent.

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-NON-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 11, 1989,1 rose in this House to introduce this government's labour force development strategy.
I rise now, almost one year later, to underline the continued commitment of this government, and of the people of Canada, to that strategy. I will not reiterate the extensive procedural views expressed by the government House leader yesterday, but I would urge all members to review his very clear statement outlining how the other place has transgressed all of its traditional constitutional powers with this message.
Liberal senators claim that they cannot pass Bill C-21 which the House sent them. They claim they have serious reservations about what the government proposes to do in the fields of training and unemployment insurance. What is it that we want to do as a government which so unsettles them? We want to improve the social benefits available through UI.
We want to ensure that unemployment insurance provides incentives for claimants to work. We want to adjust the financing of the programs so that those who benefit also pay a fair share and we want to increase the training available to Canadian workers. Those are our goals. What are their goals? Their goal is political theatrics.
[Translation\
The Liberal senators will say to whoever wants to listen that the government drafted this bill in the conviction that the unemployed are lazy and should be punished. Nothing could be further from the truth. This bill is based on the assumption that people really want to
Government Orders
work and that they must acquire new skills to play a worthwhile role in a fast-changing economy.

Bill C-21 is based on the assumption that the strategy of throwing money at the unemployed denies them the chance to break out of a cycle of UI dependence that has gone on in this country through generations of Liberal governments. In a climate characterized by the sorts of political games which Liberal senators seem to favour, it is difficult to see their amendments as sincere attempts to improve this bill. Indeed, most of their recommendations are not even new.
However, the government has reviewed the message offered by the Senate and as stated by the leader of the government in this House, and we can support the intent of some of the recommendations. Identification of literacy as a training need, more detail in our development plan, more explicit protection for the system of benefits for self-employed fishermen are all amendments that we can support.
However, I think that hon. members will agree with me that many of the recommendations of the Liberal senators represent an assault on the taxpayer and an assault on the rights of this elected House. By their own admission, Liberal senators suggest that the most significant recommendations are those related to the funding of UI by the federal government.
Recommendations 7 and 9 would cost taxpayers at least $1.5 billion each and every year. Is this not an assault on the rights of the House? Of course it is. And I should not have to remind members that we simply do not have that kind of money as a government and as taxpayers and as the people of Canada. It is an affront to the rights of this House to have appointed senators attempt to dictate spending to us. Senators have no right to force us to raise taxes or increase the deficit.

While we must improve the skills of Canadian workers in order to compete effectively with other countries, we must also continue to put our financial house in order. The Liberal senators, however, want us to finance a major part of regular unemployment insurance benefits and the majority of benefits paid to self-employed fishermen, realizing all the while that this will only increase the deficit.

March 13, 1990
Government Orders

Now perhaps that understanding is lost on Liberal senators who only remember how to spend other people's money. It is not lost on this government that has proposed many improvements to UI within a context of fiscal reality. That is the reason we are asking employers and workers to fund the insurance system from which they benefit. It is not the unemployed who pay, it is the employed and their employers, and it is the latter who pay the lion's share.
I must also reject the scare stories spread by the Liberals that we are privatizing UI, whatever that may mean. The federal government will continue to play a key role in managing this vital program. As we consult with employers and workers on UI policies we will ensure that UI continues to reflect the legitimate needs of workers and employees, but we will also seek their input into the solutions. In short, recommendations from Liberal senators on these topics are completely unacceptable.
Let me now turn to the issue of increasing penalties for workers who quit jobs without just cause. Liberal senators have directly contradicted a basic aspect of this bill with their recommendation on this issue. Senators seem to have decided that anybody who quits a job probably had no choice. Let me quote Senator Norbert Theriault on this issue. He said:
Those are personal decisions and decisions that would only be
made with good reason.
But that is not why previous Liberal governments felt it necessary to impose harsher penalties on those who quit without good reason. It was a Liberal government that initiated this principle. However, members of this House understand that while some workers do have good reason to quit, others do not. That was the purpose for improving the just cause provisions in Bill C-21.
Strengthening the law to ensure that people who quit jobs without just cause cannot as quickly get unemployment insurance was a change which this House approved. That change alone will save $450 million per year, money which could be put to better use within the UI system.
But Liberal senators seem to believe that spending $1.1 billion a year in benefits to people who are fired for misconduct or who quit their jobs without just cause is an
appropriate use of UI funds. I may point out that we are almost the only country in the world that would tolerate such a thing.
The impact of this incentive and the general tightening of entrance requirements and benefit duration was best summarized by a witness before the Senate committee, Mr. Patrick Grady of Global Economics. He estimated that passage of Bill C-21 would result in reduction of the unemployment rate by up to 1 per cent. Now, is the other side not interested in lower unemployment rates in this country?
The next group of recommendations from the Senate that I want to discuss does three things. First, it rejects the decision made by this House to invest UI funds in developmental uses for people. Second, it rejects the decision of this House to recognize the difference between counselling decisions and financial or legal decisions. Third, it restricts our ability to be innovative within the UI program. Some senators think that everything that has been done in the past should be frozen there forever.
None of these recommendations is acceptable and I will explain why. A critical component of the Labour Force Development Strategy is the counselling of UI claimants that takes place in Canada Employment Centres. Employment counsellors work with claimants as partners to determine the best approach to meet individual employment needs. It is counselling that helps people find jobs, as I would point out to some of the shouting voices over there, who are not even prepared to listen.
Among the tools claimants and counsellors will use in this process are the developmental programs such as training and relocation and entrepreneurship that this bill would allow; training, relocation and entrepreneurship being things the other side is against. These are designed to use UI funds to give people a break, to give them the skills and opportunities to break out of the UI cycle. We believe that a small investment now is better for the individual and will save years of future UI costs.
The costs of training courses, the ability to capitalize benefits and the ability to help claimants move to areas of greater employment opportunities are all aspects of an active employment policy. That does not necessarily mean moving to another province. It does mean moving
March 13, 1990

within one's own region when there are opportunities available.
Our original decision to pay for support costs like these from the UI account was based on the understanding that these are costs that represent a short run cost and a long term saving to the UI account, and are a far greater benefit to the individual UI claimant. For that reason, we cannot accept the recommendations which would eliminate many of these investments from the UI account.

As far as the second question is concerned, the decisions made at the time of counselling are not legal ones. Counselling is a complex process which consists in helping a claimant make the right decisions about his future.
Referral to a training course is a major decision which costs taxpayers thousands of dollars. It is not like a routine purchase at the corner store.
The House showed it understood this when it agreed to simplify the Unempoyment Insurance Act and establish clearly that claimants cannot appeal decisions relating to training or other developmental uses.
This House also realizes that an arbitration board cannot possibly assess, during a 30-minute hearing, all the complexities involved in many hours of counselling, trial runs and reflection on the part of the claimant and the counsellor with whom he or she works.

The third flaw in this group of recommendations is the desire of Liberal senators to restrict our ability to develop new approaches in aiding the unemployed.
The UI Act is quite precise in its definitions and 50 years of jurisprudence have made that even more exact. However, if we want to encourage innovative and active programming, a basic belief in this bill, then we need some latitude for special cases, and that is what the senators want to restrict.
Let me give an example. Under the current law a claimant who loses her job and decides to start a business to use her skills would be cut off UI automatically. This bill gives us the flexibility that we need to implement new uses for UI funds which our trading partners are
Government Orders
finding so successful now and which is happening in other imaginative systems around the world.

The last group of recommendations should give all members of this House cause for concern. This is a very important matter.
Need I remind hon. members that in recent years, the Liberal senators have constantly sought ways to obstruct the work of the elected House. This message is a brazen attempt to increase their powers.
The Liberal senators want the power to impose changes in regulations and plans on the elected government. The Liberal senators sent us a series of recommendations that in effect would allow them to turn down the proposed amendments to the regulations on fishermen's benefits. They also worded their message in such a way that, with some clever parliamentary manoeuvring, they would be able to reject the government's plan to use unemployment insurance funds for training purposes.
This House cannot accept amendments that would give non-elected senators the power constantly to obstruct the wishes of the elected House.

The more pernicious action can be found inherent in recommendations 7 and 9 of the Liberals in the Senate. Members will know the parliamentary rule that the Senate may not increase taxes or expenditures, but the recommendation from the Senate seeks to do indirectly what it cannot do directly. Liberal Senators have decided that they have the right to stop the elected government from controlling the deficit by controlling government spending. Liberal Senators have decided that they can say and that they have the right to say that the government must continue every program, every legal obligation it has ever had but, if taxes have to go up to pay for it, it is not their problem.
Let me quote Senator Theriault again: "If the GST has to be 10 per cent then they must tell the people it has to be 10 per cent. They should not destroy a fundamental program."
This House must tell Senator Theriault and his unelected colleagues that the government, democratically elected, is accountable to the Canadian people and nobody knows that better than we do. It is accountable for the taxes it levies and for the programs it administers

Government Orders
and that government elected must have the ability to control its spending.
Let us be clear on one thing. Real leadership implies accountability, and accountability is what is at issue here. Canadians know the economic reality facing this government and this country. They have no patience for political games. Even The Toronto Star, my neighbourhood newspaper, recognizes the tactics of the senators for what they are. It stated: "To hog tie the government with billion dollar amendments that would wreak havoc on its deficit fighting strategy is little more than political grandstanding and obstructionism."

Unlike the Liberal senators, this government has made real decisions. It has chosen to consolidate the safety net that unemployment insurance provides and to improve the system, in recognition of the fact that Canada must do what all industrialized countries are doing.
I may remind hon. members that during all this time we have spent considering the bill, our economic partners have spent billions of dollars to increase the skills of their workers. If we accept this message, Canada will surely fall behind even more, compared with its competitors.

Let me conclude by reminding the House that 50 years ago unemployment insurance was developed to provide income to workers who had lost their jobs. The bill which is again before us continues that role. UI will still be there to provide income to workers who lose their jobs, but we wanted to do much, much more.
This government is well aware of the important challenges facing Canada in the international economy and facing the future of Canadian workers. It knows that a well trained workforce is a critical part of meeting that challenge and providing stability and security for Canadian workers.
We believe that the principles behind the proposed changes to unemployment insurance are sound. The changes themselves are moderate ones. I firmly believe that this House should reply to the message from the
Senate by saying that if it agrees that UI should become a more effective program which provides better benefits to parents and older workers, which increases incentives to work, which responds to the fiscal realities of today and which, above all, helps train and retrain Canadian workers to provide them with a better future, then pass the original bill which this House sent to you and let this government make those improvements now, nearly one year after we began this exercise.
I urge all hon. members to vote in favour of this motion by the government House leader.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-NON-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to discuss the amendments proposed here by the other place to Bill C-21, an act to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act.
During the 1988 election campaign the Conservatives promised Canadians that the unemployment insurance system was a sacred trust and that there were absolutely no plans to change it. Scarcely six months later the Minister of Employment and Immigration confessed that yes the government would be making major changes to the system. Indeed the changes proposed were so major as to alter the face of the system altogether and divert it from its original purpose.
When Canadians appeared before the committee they pointed out the numerous flaws of the proposed new system. They tried to explain to the government how devastating the changes would be to unemployed workers all across the country, and they conveyed the sense of betrayal that Canadians felt knowing that the government had broken yet another promise but also that the government was not listening.
We have before us today the amendments proposed by members in the other place, changes that recognize the government's stated intention of deficit reduction but which also recognize the needs and the dignity of unemployed Canadians. Many of those Canadians who have special needs reside in Atlantic Canada, and it is on behalf of those people in particular that I speak today.
My colleagues and I have risen in this House countless times to voice the concerns of Atlantic Canadians, and I will do so once again because I hope that by dogged persistence we can finally make the government under-
March 13, 1990

stand what it proposes to do to these people as nothing else seems to be working.
Times have never been easy on Canada's Atlantic coast. The region has always depended on an overwhelmingly seasonal resource based economy. For instance, the economy of my province of Prince Edward Island is dependent upon fishing, farming and tourism. Because our economy is seasonal unemployment insurance is an integral part of that economy. We do not like it but that is the way it is.
For example, in 1988 Prince Edward Island received over $138 million in unemployment insurance benefits. That is approximately $1,076 for every man, woman and child in that province. Compare that to the $422 per capita on the average in Canada.
Approximately one out of every five Islanders in the labour force relied on UI benefits at some point during the year. As a matter of fact, the UI program contributes more money to the provincial economy than many of our industries. That gives some idea of the vital role that unemployment insurance plays in the lives of Islanders and indeed of all Atlantic Canadians. That is why, when the government announced its intention to stop its contribution to the fund as of January 1990, Atlantic Canada went into shock. That is why such a decision can be viewed only as yet another step in the federal government's gradual abandonment of Atlantic Canada. By cutting out some $2 billion from the program and by diverting remaining funds to vague "training programs", the government is removing a major pillar of the regional economy.
Members of the other place realized the devastation that the passage of this legislation as is would wreak. That is why they proposed in their report that the government continue to ensure regionally extended benefits. One-half of the value of those weeks of benefits paid when the regional unemployment rate is over 6 per cent would continue to be funded from general revenues, and not from the UI account which will consist of employer and employee contributions only. In this way the government will not be able to avoid its responsibility for high regional unemployment.
Bill C-21 proposes to divert funds intended for income maintenance to training programs. This is a praiseworthy
Government Orders
goal; no one would deny that. However Canadians want to see some substance behind those lofty words. They want proof that the government has devoted a great deal of thought to what achieving this goal really means. They want to see that the government understands how the Canadian economy is developing before they trust it to divert these funds for developmental uses.
What kind of economy is emerging in Canada? Last month the Economic Council of Canada released a study entitled "Good Jobs, Bad Jobs: Employment in the Service Economy". This respected organization concluded that Canada will experience a continued trend toward service industry jobs. The services which have the most potential to stimulate regional economies are called "dynamic services" that include transportation infrastructures, telecommunication systems, municipal infrastructures, financial services and business consulting services. These are the areas which will see the greatest job creation and the most growth.
However the council concludes that these dynamic services are overwhelmingly located in the large centres such as Toronto, Vancouver and Calgaiy. Perhaps jobs are being created every day in Canada. We know they are. but what the government does not like to admit when reeling off impressive statistics is that these jobs are located in just a very few centres.
For example, in Prince Edward Island unemployment has continued to soar. We currently have a rate of 16.2 per cent, the same as our neighbouring province of Newfoundland. We want to know: Where are the jobs that the Prime Minister loves to boast about?
The council goes on to state in its report that it expects that the good, well paying jobs will continue to be concentrated in large cities, a trend which will widen regional disparities.
Job creation tends toward the high skill, high paying jobs which we have already stated are concentrated in large cities. The low skill, low paying jobs, if we get them, these are the ones that the regions have. Are Atlantic Canadians supposed to be happy with the crumbs from central Canada's table? That is the message from a government which gears its fiscal policy toward the overheated economy of southern Ontario at the expense of the rest of the country.

March 13, 1990
Government Orders
Since the government has not yet proven itself capable of developing and managing a realistic, effective, full employment strategy, it will be understood why unemployed Canadians are skeptical and nervous when the government sings the praises of training.
Another sign that the government seems to have forgotten how the Atlantic Canada works is the changes it would make to the entrance requirements and the duration of benefits. Once again the seasonal economy dictates that it is almost impossible for many Atlantic Canadians to find full-time year-round work. This government's ministers should spend some time on the east coast, and then they would find out that it is virtually impossible to fish in the wintertime, to grow crops in the wintertime, and that the tourists cannot enjoy our beaches at that time of year. We did not plan it that way, but it is that way nonetheless.
As a result, many workers barely scrape together the number of weeks of insurable earnings they need to qualify for the benefits. When they have qualified they need all of the weeks of benefits they can get to see them through. This money does not go toward vacations in Florida or fancy cars, as the government's blame the victim mentality would suggest. No, no. Instead, this money goes to pay the rent, to buy food, to buy clothing, and to educate their family.
Almost as important is the vital role that UI benefits play in local economies. When central industries such as fishing, farming and tourism shut down for a great part of the year, individual workers are not the only ones who face lean times. Local businesses and service industries need the stimulation that the UI benefits provide in order to survive, much less thrive. If these businesses falter not only do the owners and managers and their families suffer; so do the people whose employment depends directly or indirectly on these industries.
I am saying all of this in an effort to make the government realize what an integral, essential role UI funds play in every aspect of Atlantic Canadian life. UI moneys are a vital link in our economy simply because of the nature of that economy. If that link weakens or disappears the whole chain will weaken or even disintegrate.
The government's proposed new structure for eligibility and benefit duration provides damning evidence that the government fails to understand the facts I have just outlined or, even worse and hopefully not true, it just
does not care. The proposed changes make little or no sense.
Under Bill C-21 the maximum duration of benefits would be reduced in most instances, except in cases where claimants have acquired a very large number of weeks work and reside in an area of very high unemployment. What are the chances of that combination? Virtually none. This totally unrealistic picture of the economy is further reflected in the relationship between benefit duration and regional unemployment rates which the government would impose. Three weeks of benefits would be paid for each percentage point interval of unemployment between 6 per cent and 8 per cent. This would increase to four weeks for each point interval between 8 per cent and 12 per cent. It would decrease to two weeks for each point interval between 12 per cent and 16 per cent.
What it boils down to-and I really wonder if the people who designed this new system bothered to test their model at all-is that the region of St. John's, Newfoundland with an unemployment rate of 12.4 per cent will lose up to 11 weeks of benefits, while the region of Toronto with a rate below 4 per cent will lose a maximum of three weeks. This makes absolutely no sense, and that is the bottom line.
The government must follow the recommendation of the other place and moderate these changes. As well benefits in regions with veiy high unemployment, which means most of the Atlantic region, must not be reduced.
One group of Atlantic Canadians who are especially concerned about the government's confusing plans are the fishermen. I should not have to remind any member of the House of the severe crisis that industry is already in. We need only think of Canso, Lockeport, Gaultois, Grand Bank, and Trepassey to call up images of the trauma afflicting the people who depend on the fishery for their livelihoods and for the life-blood of their communities.
Now more than ever fishermen and their families need the support of the unemployment insurance program. In 1956 the Unemployment Insurance Act was amended to extend coverage to self-employed fishermen. In fact fishermen's premiums are paid directly into the Consolidated Revenue Fund and not into the unemployment insurance fund. This means that they are not actually protected by the program. Rather, the government is
March 13, 1990

responsible for making up the difference between the premiums paid and the benefits collected.
Every unemployed person in Canada is fearing the loss of the UI support system, but no one has more reason to be worried than the fishermen. Bill C-21 would place the full cost of fishermen's benefits on the UI fund. By withdrawing its contribution to this fund, the government is placing the future of the fishermen's benefit at great risk. The government has promised that these benefits are safe. Well we all know how the government keeps its promises. If it truly wants to reassure the fishermen of Atlantic Canada, the government will not balk at taking concrete steps to protect the benefits as recommended by the amendments here today.
For that matter, if this government's true goal is positive reform of unemployment insurance, it will not balk at any of the amendments proposed here today. They are moderate, sensible and sensitive to both the government's professed goal of deficit reduction and to the needs and the dignity of unemployed Canadians.
It is for this reason that I fully support these amendments and I urge the government to support them as well.
I move:
That the House continue to sit through the lunch hour for the
purpose of continuing consideration of the motion now before the
House.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Dorothy Dobbie (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-NON-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today in support of the motion by our hon. House leader. The amendments to Bill C-21 contained in the message from the other place with very few exceptions are fundamentally in conflict with the intention of the government's bill.
It is the duty of the government to review old legislation and programs and revise others to make them current and responsive to the needs of the times. To do anything less would be to abrogate or ignore our responsibilities and the trust placed in us through the democratic process.
When in November 1988 Canadians cast a ballot, they cast a very decisive ballot in favour of the Progressive Conservative Party. This was not a timid or a tentative vote. The voters gave the Prime Minister's Tories a definite majority, and that majority decision carried with it a compelling message: exercise the franchise that you have been given and exercise it with leadership to get this country's economy back in order. Every member of this government caucus has taken that message to heart. We have all pledged to pursue the action asked for by Canadians when they so resoundingly endorsed a second Conservative majority.
No one in this House has been more conscientious in following that dictate than the hon. Minister of Employment and Immigration. She was one of the very first off the mark last April 11, 1989 with new legislation designed to improve the unemployment insurance system vastly and to make it more responsive and better serve the needs of Canadians in the 1990s.
Bill C-21 is responsive to regional disparities while it reflects the need to make the system more self-sufficient. Bill C-21 recognizes that life in the 1990s will require new skills as our use of technology gains momentum. Bill C-21 also responds to the fact that there are changing roles in family life where both spouses play an active role in raising the children as well as in earning a living.
All these measures and many others were carefully devised by a caring and a conscientious minister who was anxious, as I said before, to respond to today's needs in today's society. We cannot continue with old programs

March 13, 1990
simply because they are in place and expect them to be responsive to the needs of people in the 1990s. She worked swiftly and acted decisively in the interests of Canadians who were vulnerable to the changing employment patterns.
On November 6, 1989 this House passed Bill C-21, and it did so in plenty of time for its benefits to begin flowing during the depths of winter when traditionally those benefits are needed the most.
What happened? Did the unemployed receive their benefits when they needed them most in the depths of winter when things were tough? I wish I could say that was true, but sadly I must report that the answer is no and it seems that the answer is no because some Liberal members in the other place decided to make a mockery of the democratic process and delay the bill to embarrass, harass and intimidate this government.
At any rate this is certainly the perception and regrettably the facts surrounding the circumstances testify to the idea that that perception is indeed true.
We were told by the people in the other place that they were setting up a special committee to hear from Canadians who had not testified before the government's legislative committee. Apparently these are going to be brand new people with brand new ideas, but what happened? We learned that the special committee consulted 54 witnesses whose views had already been made known to the House legislative committee.
What was the point of that? Why go through the exercise, not to mention the expense of hearing all those witnesses? Why do this if the Senate was really committed and really interested in hearing this testimony and hoping to find something of value in it? It was on the record already and they could simply have gone through the records. Added to this the 54 people in question were well-known opponents of the government's bill. They certainly were not experts on unemployment insurance management and they were not experts on the topic of re-employment strategy, so what was the point?
As the minister pointed out when she met the committee a short time later, the records show that these efforts did not identify a single issue of any substance in the bill.

subsubtopic: NATIONAL GALLERY OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the recent decision by the National Gallery of Canada to spend $1.8 million-nearly two-thirds of the Gallery's $3 million annual acquisition budget-to purchase a canvas by an American painter has left Canadian artists somewhat disenchanted and greatly discouraged. Canadian people in general are wondering.
With everything that has traditionally drawn Canada together, such as VIA Rail, the CBC, and language tolerance, being under great strain, would it not have been an appropriate time for an institution of national cultural expression to have promoted the works of Canadian artists? Would the government give Canadians some assurance that it will intercede in this ill-timed purchase and stop payment on the $1.8 million cheque, if that is necessary?

A few days ago, Mr. Speaker, a major event occurred in the area of professional sports which resulted in Quebecers being separated, temporarily I hope, from a great Canadian, a great Quebecer and a great star.
Mr. Peter Stastny, this highly skillful hockey player, has dominated his sport for nearly 10 years and has been recognized as one of the greatest in the world.
Today, on behalf of the people of the Greater Quebec City area, I wish to thank this exemplary athlete for the
March 13, 1990

great times we had because of him. I also wish to emphasize his qualities as a dedicated man and a good citizen who spent much time and energy representing several charitable organizations.
As soon as he arrived in this country, he made up his mind that he would learn French and English, both languages he now speaks fluently. Mr. Stastny realized what a great many politicians and former politicians are unwilling or fail to understand, namely, Quebec's special identity within Canada.
I salute this remarkable citizen and wish him, on behalf of the people of Quebec and the rest of Canada, many more years of tremendous success.

Mr. Speaker, today a new president takes office in the Republic of Haiti, the fifth in four years. Not only must we wish her well, we must urge and support her in any efforts to bring democratic elections and government to a country whose government has been at best anarchic for the past four years.
Last week, as a private citizen, I visited Haiti. It is a beautiful country populated by warm and hospitable people. It is a country that shows what absence of effective government can mean: inadequate services and infrastructure, roads in a state of utter disrepair, high prices, under-utilized though relatively abundant resources, and excessive dependence on imports.
Canadians have natural cultural and democratic ties with the people of Haiti. Today, our Haitian friends very much need our help and our support.
Canada must send a clear sign that it is prepared to support the development of democratic government in Haiti and to support and encourage it tangibly with an indication of our willingness to restore bilateral agreement aid as soon as the new government demonstrates its commitment to democracy through tangible action.

Mr. Speaker, the recent budget chose as one of its
targets our Canadian veterans. The government has cut $35 million to a group of Canadians who have already paid their dues.
As a result of the budget thousands of our veterans will pay more than $3,000 each for lodging. This is a result of the government's update of board and lodging charges for veterans in long-term care.
Cuts to the Veterans Independence Program mean that thousands of veterans who are still living at home will lose assistance for heavy housecleaning.
It is ironic that when Canada needed the service of brave and courageous Canadians our veterans were there. Now, when our veterans need the services of the Canadian government, it turns around and cuts assistance to them.
Remembrance Day is the day that we pay respect to those who died in battle and for those who will always bear the scars of wartime. We wear the poppy as a symbol of remembrance, respect and endless thanks for our veterans. Given the recent cuts to our veterans the Minister of Finance does not deserve the right to wear a poppy on Remembrance Day when he so quickly forgets what it really means.

Mr. Speaker, this past Sunday marked an historic occasion in Chile as an elected civilian government headed by President Patricio Aylwin took over power from the military dictatorship of General Augusto Pinochet. The Pinochet government came to power in 1973 as a result of a violent coup overthrowing and murdering President Salvador Allende. For the past 16 years the Chilean people have been subjected to the murder, torture and jailing of thousands of Chileans at the hands of the dictatorship.
With this change in government the brutality and abuses of the Pinochet regime are hopefully at an end. Already we see the fruits of liberalization as President Aylwin has granted pardon to prisoners of conscience and pledged to dismantle the repressive elements of Pinochet's rule.
Events in Chile also further the trend towards democracy in Latin America, a trend that will not be complete, however, until we can be assured that the military men

March 13, 1990
of these new democracies are truly under civilian control.
I am sure all Canadians join together in congratulating the Aylwin government upon assuming power. We must lend it our support as it works to stabilize the democratic process and to control the military still led by General Pinochet.
This can be done, in part, by contributing to the new social solidarity fund established by the government, designed to support the poorest in Chile and provide essential health, education and housing needs. The Canadian government should consider such a contribution.

Mr. Speaker, all three parties and most Canadians agree that the federal manufacturers' sales tax is a bad tax that has to go.
Indeed, some two years ago the all-party Commons finance committee recommended a multi-stage sales tax to be imposed on the broadest possible base. Yet today those in opposition are falling all over each other in their lust to be seen as the party most against the GST.
Canadians want more than criticism. They want choices. Canadians are asking: Where do the opposition parties stand? What alternatives do they have?
The Liberals want to study the matter some more. Forty years of study is not enough for them. In opposition, just as in government, they cannot take a decision.
Procrastination is not an alternative. Keeping the old FMST is not good enough. It is time to go forward with the GST as the only practicable, workable sales tax reform for Canada.

Mr. Speaker, in 1984, the Mulroney government collected about $8 billion from Canadians with the manufacturers' sales tax. In 1991, if the goods and services tax replaces the manufacturers' sales tax, the government will collect not $8 billion, not $18 billion, but $23 billion on this tax
alone-three times the amount collected in 1984 when this Tory government came to power.
The GST is the largest tax grab in Canadian history. The people of Canada realize this. Seventy-one per cent of Canadians are opposed to the GST, and still this government insists on implementing this unfair regressive tax. When will this government listen?
The Liberal party will not turn its back on the people of Canada. The Liberal party wants the voices of Canadians to be heard. This week throughout the country Canadians can dial 1-900-720-6052 to register their opposition to the goods and services tax.
The people of Canada will not sit idly by while the over consumption of this government shrinks the pocket books of all Canadians. Canadians from east to west will dial 1-900-720-6052 and register their "No" vote for the goods and services tax.
Scrap the tax. Dial 1-900-720-6052.

For many people, Mr. Speaker, Mrs. Geraldine Doucet is the kind of person who is always involved in a great number of activities such as the Jerry Lewis Telethon as well as the Cystic Fibrosis Foundation and Canadian Cancer Society fund raising campaigns.
Because of her participation in Quebec's entertainment industry and her involvement in various voluntary organizations such as Big Brothers and Big Sisters, she was recently appointed president of the Quebec Canada Day Committee.
Mr. Speaker, I know that Mrs. Doucet has all the necessary qualities and a solid experience of community involvement, and which in my opinion make her the ideal choice. I extend my congratulations to Mrs. Doucet and I wish her well.

Mr. Speaker, the Deputy Prime Minister and the Premier of Saskatchewan today announced that Saskatchewan farmers who participated in crop insurance will receive an additional $58 million in mid-April. The payment is the result of the multi-year disaster benefit program. The
March 13, 1990

program provides cash to areas of Saskatchewan that have suffered two consecutive crop failures. This is an important part of the farm safety net program that will provide money to farmers when they need it most.
Over 12,000 farmers will receive an average of close to $5,000 each. This is an important first step in ensuring that Saskatchewan farmers can get this year's crop in the ground.
On behalf of our members of Parliament and farm related business in Saskatchewan, I congratulate our Deputy Prime Minister and the Premier of Saskatchewan for concluding the details of this much needed program.

Mr. Speaker, the arrogance of the Mulroney government is absolutely astounding. While it is telling Canadians they must do their part to fight the deficit, this government is spending $111 million to sell a regressive, merciless tax on a population that does not want it. This tax, after 31 other increases, is the largest tax grab in the history of Canada.
The Liberal party is giving Canadians a chance to be counted in the fight against the GST. This is anti-GST week. Canadians can register their disapproval by picking up the phone and calling 1-900-720-6052. That registers their "No" vote to the GST.
Yesterday, the finance committee chairman stated that this electronic petition means nothing. That is yet another example of this government's arrogance. Every Canadian voice should be heard
For my colleague over here who wants to know the number so that he can also call, it is 1-900-720-6052 to say "No" to the GST.

Mr. Speaker, on March 3, 1990, the defence ministry of the Republic of South Korea announced that a joint Korea-United States team of engineers had discovered a fourth infiltration tunnel constructed by the North Koreans to serve as a potential means of mounting a surprise military invasion of the south by passing underneath the demilitarized zone.
Unlike the other three tunnels found in the western and central areas of the front line in 1974,1975 and 1978, the recently discovered tunnel is located in the mountainous eastern portion of the demilitarized zone, 105 kilometres northeast of Seoul.
It was regrettable to hear of this particular discovery because of the current global detente between east and west. Tension on the Korean Peninsula can only be heightened by such clear indications of unabated aggression and militance on the part of the North Koreans.

Mr. Speaker, as the Royal Commission on Electoral Reform and Party Financing will be discovering during its cross country hearings, the issue of third party expenditures during an election period must be confronted.
This clause in the Canada Elections Act is not enforced today because of an Alberta Court of Queen's Bench ruling in 1984. Yet a similar Quebec ruling went in the exact opposite direction as that of the Alberta case.
The former Chief Electoral Officer of Canada has urged the commission to deal with what he refers to as the phenomenon of advertising by special interest groups. Although there was relatively little involvement by single issue groups in the 1984 campaign, their impact and activity in the 1988 campaign was extensive and profound. As much as $4 million is thought to have been spent promoting free trade. This amount is two-thirds of what a federal party can spend on all expenses during that same campaign period.

March 13, 1990
Oral Questions
While the legitimate political process of the political parties is regulated by the Canada Elections Act, well-funded advocacy groups are free to promote and oppose candidates and registered parties without restriction or limitation.
The House of Commons should demand that the government refer the present Section 70.1 of the Canada Elections Act to the Supreme Court of Canada for a ruling as to its force and effect under the Charter.

Mr. Speaker, Canadians shopping around for a position to take on any issue can enter the Liberal party supermarket. There you can find every position taken on every issue. All you have to do is shop around.
On free trade, walk down one aisle and you will find the member for Winnipeg South saying he will rip up the free trade deal if the Liberals come to power. Walk down another aisle and you hear the member for Etobicoke North saying the trade deal is not such a bad deal after all.
Are you looking for a position on the GST? The Liberal party supermarket is offering all sorts of positions. Some members stand up in the supermarket and tell Canadians that they have a position on the GST. If you call a certain number they will give a scrap-the-tax position.
The Liberal party caters to all customers. Jean Chretien in one aisle says he is not sure what he would do about the GST. Walk down another aisle and you will find leadership hopeful, Tom Wappel, saying that he would keep the GST.
Telemarketing has become a booming business in this country. All Canadians should do their shopping on the GST by phone. They should call the Leader of the Opposition, known as Herbie the Grocer, at 613-996-5084, to find out what positions on the GST the Liberal party is offering today.
At the Liberal party supermarket the motto is: We aim to please. We never say no to anyone.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister. Yesterday, as we all know, he received the Weizmann Award in the Science and Humanities.
Hear, hear!

I want to ask the Prime Minister if he will demonstrate today that the award in question and the applause he just received is justified by moving immediately to double R and D spending in Canada, as he promised before he was elected but which he has not achieved in spite of being in office for five years. Will he keep his promise?
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, the leaders of the Israeli Government who were there last evening, and all the distinguished leaders of the Jewish community in Canada who were present, expressed absolute astonishment at the action of the opposition for not recognizing, which they all recognized, the tremendous work being done by the Government of Canada to advance the cause of science.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I do not know why the opposition members are all so offended by the fact that I was given this award. Mr. Pearson was given the award, as were Margaret Thatcher, Jacques Chirac and Danny Kaye.
You're a song and dance man, too.

In point of fact, total federal spending on science and technology, including research and development, will be about $5.1 billion this year, compared to $4.1 billion when we came into office in 1984.
There has been an increase of some 20 per cent since this government was sworn in. About 90 per cent of all the government funded research and development that is done in the Province of Ontario is paid by the federal government. There is, as well, the fact that Canada has the most attractive R and D incentives-as brought

March 13, 1990

forward by the Minister of Finance-with the exception of Australia.
That is why we are going to continue to make very substantial progress in leading in world-class ventures in the field of science and technology.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is not clear whether the Prime Minister got the award for emulating Mike Pearson or Danny Kaye.
Oh, Oh!

Yesterday, Gerhardt Hertz-berg, a world famous Canadian scientist who received the Nobel Prize after he heard the Prime Minister had received the Weizmann Award said:
I don't think the Prime Minister could expect to get an award for
his contribution to science and technology in Canada.
Sweden, The Netherlands, the United States, West Germany; all
these countries spend just about twice as much as Canada does on
research and development.
That is what Mr. Hertzberg says. I think he knows as much about research and development in Canada as does anybody else in this country.
Why will the Prime Minister not live up to his promise to ensure that Canada spends at least 2.5 per cent of its economy on research and development? Why will he not keep a promise that he himself said was necessary for the future competitiveness of this country? It is time the Prime Minister kept his promise.

Mr. Speaker, I am not going to quarrel with the remarks of my hon. friend. He would be happy to know that the President of the Weizmann Institute, one of the leading nuclear physicists in the entire world who heads up one of the finest and most outstanding research centres in the world, said last night that as Prime Minister of Canada he could think of no one more deserving of this particular award than your humble servant.
Oh, oh!
I know it breaks the hearts of the Grits to see a Conservative receive international recognition, but that is just starting.

Hear, hear!
Oral Questions

I had the honour of creating the National Advisory Board on Science and Technology which I have the pleasure of chairing, the first Prime Minister in Canada to do this.
I had the honour of establishing the Canada Scholarships Program, with $80 million over five years which will provide 10,000 young Canadians with full scholarships in science and technology.
I had the pleasure of bringing forward the Centres of Excellence program which puts $240 million into establishing 14 new Centres of Excellence at Canadian universities across the country.
We have increased research and development very substantially since 1984. The problem is that the Liberals were so disgraceful in their neglect of science and technology that the Leader of the Opposition should never rise in his seat again.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is obvious why the Prime Minister is seeking international recognition. He knows that outside Canada they do not take public opinion polls showing how badly his government and himself are doing in this country.

My question is directed to the Minister of Finance. All of the GST that corporations pay is refunded. Therefore a corporation that buys a sofa for an executive or calls in a plumber does not pay any GST at all. Yet a single parent, a senior citizen, or an unemployed person in Canada has to pay a 7 per cent GST. I want to know why the Minister of Finance thinks that is fair. Why is he taking $5 billion to $6 billion away from the corporations in taxation and putting it on the backs of the consumer?

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member's party is the first to stand up and say they want a visible tax. The hon. member is saying now to tax businesses on the things that they buy for their businesses, to bury that in the price of the tax and then apply another tax on top of that and another tax on top of that. That is precisely what the GST is designed to avoid.
When we say it is a 7 per cent tax, it is not an 8, 9, 10, 11, or 12 per cent tax. It is a 7 per cent tax. All the tax is credited out of the system so there is no hidden tax and there is no tax on tax. It is 7 per cent. That is what the consumer pays. It is very visible and up front, unlike the approach that the hon. member would like to follow.
March 13, 1990
Mr. Speaker, what the minister is saying then is that visibility can be an excuse to gouge the consumer.
Oh, oh!

The consumer has to pay the GST for the most expensive furniture an executive could have but for a place for a family to sit they have to pay 7 per cent GST. I want to know why the minister thinks that is fair. Why is he gouging the consumer to supplement the increased profits of the corporations?

Mr. Speaker, what my friend opposite is saying is hide it and then gouge the consumer. That is the approach the Liberal party would follow. Let me take my colleague through the basis on which this tax is levied one more time. I will do it slowly for him.
The taxes levied today in the federal sales tax are paid by every consumer in this country. However, the consumer has absolutely no idea how much sales tax is in the price of a pad, in the price of a pen, in the price of food, but it is in the price of everything that we buy today.
With the GST we are recognizing that a consumption tax is paid by the consumer. We believe that the consumption tax paid by the consumer should be paid up front and be very visible. That is why all tax on business inputs on the costs of production is credited out so that the consumer only pays 7 per cent and not some multiple of 7 per cent which is the case under the existing tax.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to rise again to complete the remarks that I began before the break.
When we broke for lunch I was pointing out that, as the minister pointed out when she met with the committee, the records show that the efforts of the members from the other place who interviewed some 54 representatives of various groups and organizations, who had already made representations to the House committee, did not identify one single new issue of substance.
It is very difficult to understand why they went through this exercise in the first place. I would have to say that we can only conclude from this that there was a determined and premeditated plan to delay the bill so as to frustrate the government. I cannot think of any other explanation.
This House passed the bill on November 6, 1989. The Senate special committee then waited a whole three weeks, 21 days, before even bothering to convene its first meeting. Another 10 weeks passed before the report was presented in mid-February. That is more than three months after the bill was passed by the duly elected representatives of this House. Another 10 weeks delay, and for what?
The bill was tabled in the House in April 1989 by the hon. minister. That is almost a full year ago. Surely it is unacceptable to the people of Canada to have the government that they chose with such a resounding majority so frustrated. What possible excuse can there be for these constant delays of government business by a non-elected body? I think it is unforgivable.
Canadians have been led to understand that the venerable upper House was put in place and charged with, among other things, the weighty responsibility to provide some kind of a safety valve in the event that some harmful or pernicious legislation somehow slipped passed the hon. members of this House. In the past, senators were chosen for a whole number of reasons. They were chosen for their wisdom, they were chosen for their experience and they were chosen for their ability to accept the great burden of trust that was placed on them.

The senators were put in place to ensure that there was a safety valve. But senators were not to view themselves as legislators. They were never appointed to act as legislators. That duty is vested in the elected members of this House alone. We are the ones who make the legislation.

speechtext:
My hon. friend asks what is wrong with that. My hon. friend surely would agree with me that no Parliament would ever seriously consider giving such a new power to the Senate. To do something like that would be to deny the responsibility, the authority, the trust that was vested in us as elected members of this House by the Canadian people.
My hon. friend surely does not want to deny his responsibilities as an elected member of this House any more than do any of the government members. I cannot believe that Parliament would ever seriously consider giving the Senate such a new power.
I am not going to go into detail on every single recommended amendment, but there are one or two more that Canadians really should be aware of so they can get a clear understanding of just exactly what is going on here.
In one amendment the Liberal senators would reverse a decision of this House, a decision taken here in this House by the elected members of the people. This decision was that unemployment insurance costs would be paid for by those who stand to benefit. Surely that is a sensible thing. Those who stand to benefit are the workers and their employers. But the senators would have these premiums reduced and let the shortfall come out of general revenues, the taxpayers' pockets, which would contribute more to the deficit.
If we were to accept the entire range of amendments that have been proposed, it would raise our deficit by $1.6 billion. What are the senators thinking of? Do they not know how hard it is to raise $1.6 billion? If the senators have forgotten about this, I can say that the people of Canada have not. They know how tough it is to raise $1.6 billion. To accept these irresponsible changes would be to put a burden on everyday working people which is unfair, unwarranted and certainly irresponsible, as I said.
Another of the amendments would cut back on the basic principles behind this bill by relaxing penalties for people who quit their jobs without just cause or for those who are fired for misconduct. The Liberal senators want to change this decision. They would like to send a signal to people that it is all right to quit their jobs, it is all right to live off the public purse.
The people of Canada are not saying that to us. They are saying that they do not want welfare, they want work and they do not want people living off the system when they can work. If people voluntarily quit their jobs or get fired for cause, I think most people would agree that it is quite right that they be penalized in some way.
In view of these facts we really must ask ourselves why these constant delays and threats of delays are happening and what they are all about. Why was Bill C-21 held up for three months by the Senate? Was it because the senators had concerns for the welfare of Canadians? Was it because the House has acted without due consideration of the bill or with a lack of responsibility? Indeed, was it to protect the interests of democracy, perhaps?

March 13, 1990
Government Orders
Sadly, the evidence does not bear this out. It does not support any of these contentions.
Instead, unfortunately, the evidence leads inevitably to the only conclusion to which I can possibly come, and that is that some Liberals in the Senate have abandoned their trust and their responsibility in the pursuit of political points and inappropriate power. I do not want to believe this and I know that Canadians do not want to believe this either, but each time a bill is frivolously delayed, each time legislation is blocked, the conviction must grow stronger that political power games are being played, and by people who do not have an elected mandate over the fate of Canadians.
This must not happen. If it is happening, it has to stop. It cannot continue. We live in a democracy and we should live by the democratic rules. That means that the laws are made by the elected members of this Parliament and not by those who are appointed.
I do not hesitate to make clear the government's attitude toward any political posturing on behalf of some members of the other place. I also do not hesitate to commend those members who have exercised their trust in a responsible and reliable manner, and many have. In fact, there are some suggestions by the Senate that do demand praise and affirmative response. The minister has listened to the wiser counsel and the more reasonable recommendations with interest and with a commendable quick willingness to respond to those suggestions that improve upon the spirit of her bill. I think that that is most commendable.
For example, the Senate has made certain suggestions regarding literacy and we are pleased to recognize and accept these suggestions regarding this very important provision. I know that the minister would want me to acknowledge and commend the senators who suggested this improvement to her bill.
Even though we resist the effort of some Liberal members to subject the government to inordinate strictures regarding the annual plan showing how unemployment insurance funds will be spent in training and developing worker skills, we do recognize fairness and we have proposed a compromise which responds to this.
Finally, we also recognize and share the concerns of the Canadian fishery and the government is willing to amend the act to better protect fishermen. By the way, it must be noted that the benefits for fishermen were never, never touched by Bill C-21.
However, these accommodations have nothing at all to do with tactics that smack of intimidation or power plays by certain members of the upper House. These accommodations, rather, speak of the reasonable and fair attitude of the government and its commitment to do the right thing. We urge the Liberal senators to take the same fair view on behalf of Canadians and we believe that most would like to do so if given the opportunity to follow the dictates of their conscience.
It is a fact that the Liberals do have a majority in the Senate, but they must learn to resist the temptation to abuse the power that this gives them and to respect the trust that we have vested in their office. Canadians must not have their democratic prerogatives so comtemptu-ously ignored. The Senate must pass Bill C-21 with only the three amendments to which the minister has agreed.

Canadians' interest at heart. She pointed out two achievements which the government hopes to accomplish. One was to improve social benefits and the second was to give incentives to encourage work.

The very next year, when the Tories took power under Premier Devine, they had a deficit budget and they have had one ever since. The whole effect that this government has had on Saskatchewan is extraordinary. In Saskatchewan this year farm incomes are expected to drop by 101 per cent. insurance benefits that these people should have a right to receive.

At a time like this, this government brings in a bill that is going to cut $1.3 billion from unemployment insurance, at a time when people in Saskatchewan and various regions of the country need that program desperately and have a right to receive it.

rotten. It is not good to put a sugar coating over a bill that is simply rotten. This is the game the government is playing.
