speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, unemployment is a very serious problem to which our government devotes a great deal of attention. Obviously, the best solution to the unemployment problem is job creation, and on this score, our government has no lesson to learn from anyone. Mr. Speaker, since 1984, our government has created over 1.5 million jobs. The

March 13, 1990
Government Orders
Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) in his recent Budget Speech said:
The economy has expanded for seven consecutive years.
Employment has grown strongly. After-tax incomes have risen.
Economic opportunities have been increased. Poverty has been
reduced by the best kind of social policy-more jobs.
Upgrading the labour force is thus part of job creation and that is precisely the purpose of Bill C-21.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, Bill C-21 involves a labour force development strategy, a dynamic strategy compared to the present unemployment insurance plan.
Bill C-21 seeks to encourage the private sector to provide workers with more and better training. Bill C-21 will also permit use of the Unemployment Insurance Fund to create new job opportunities; it will make unemployment insurance more proactive. That is an innovative feature, Mr. Speaker, that will give workers new opportunities.
Of course, the Liberal senators have been repeating for months that Bill C-21 will lead to the destruction of the unemployment insurance system. Do not believe a word of it. It is the worst kind of fear-mongering and the Liberal senators should stop spreading such falsehoods once and for all.
Contrary to what the Liberal senators are saying, Bill C-21 contains measures that substantially improve the present legislation. I may add that these improvements are most welcome if we are to provide solutions adapted to the reality of a changing economy in the 90s.
Under the present legislation, the UI system is merely a set of passive measures that come into play after the fact. Under the present legislation we react, while the new measures in Bill C-21 will enable us to act. That is what the Liberal senators will not see and will not say.
We must adapt the UI system to new circumstances, and that is exactly what Bill C-21 does. I think this is a very important point, because the provisions of the present legislation fail to consider the real needs of Canadian families at the beginning of the 90s.
Changing values in our society have led to new attitudes. Today, bringing up children is a task shared by both parents. Both parents play an increasingly active role in the lives of their children. If the bill is passed, this fact will be reflected in the UI system. The bill also contains more generous provisions for special benefits, making them more readily accessible to claimants than is the case under the existing legislation.
By making parental benefits available to both the father and the mother, to both natural and adoptive parents, the government reflects in its new legislation the changes that are taking place in Canadian families. Today, women who have given birth are entitled to benefits for a maximum of 15 weeks, and only during the first part of their benefit period. The fathers are not entitled to any benefits at all. That is the kind of situation Bill C-21 seeks to remedy, and that is what the Liberal senators are rejecting.
Another important change in this bill that will make the UI system more equitable concerns workers who are 65 and over. Many of these workers want to keep on working and deserve to have the same rights as younger workers. Bill C-21 extends income protection to workers 65 and over. However, the bill is more than just a few changes in a number of unemployment insurance rules. It allows the government to implement its Labour Force Development Strategy. This strategy is a major government initiative that will make Canada increasingly competitive on world markets.
Obviously, Mr. Speaker, an active of income protection program is more than just distributing cheques to people who have lost their jobs. An active income protection program offers workers a chance to acquire new skills and explore new ways of finding better jobs and keeping those jobs. In this perspective, the government will work with the private sector to help employers offer workers more and better training. We want to align the level of training in the private sector with the levels existing among our main trading partners.
The government will spend more on human resource planning and training new entrants, which will involve the apprenticeship programs, the Industrial Adjustment Service and the Community Futures Program.
March 13, 1990

With the additional funds, the government will be able to work together with employers, workers and communities to help them adapt to changes in the workplace and to increasingly competitive world markets.
Thanks to the Labour Force Development Strategy, there will be more money to train those receiving unemployment insurance benefits. They will be able to acquire the skills they need to find better and more stable employment.
The Labour Force Development Strategy will also give us a chance to try new and innovative approaches in responding to the needs of Canadian workers, by providing financial assistance to unemployment insurance claimants so that they can establish their own businesses or move to areas where there are more jobs. Bill C-21 will have a positive impact on workers, communities and the entire country.
Contrary to what is being said by the Liberal senators, the government is firmly resolved to do what is necessary to ensure that Canadians have all the skills they need to adapt and become part of a changing economy. Thanks to Bill C-21, we will certainly be in a better position to meet their needs.

Thanks to the proposed changes, the UI system will be able to respond to the vaiying employment needs of communities across Canada. Mr. Speaker, I would now like to comment on the role of the Senate in the legislative process involving Bill C-21. It has always been said that the Senate's role consisted in providing "sober second thought" on legislation. Recently, however, it has become the scene of political manoeuvring, with certain people using their position to wreck bills passed by democratically elected members of Parliament.

groups or individuals who had already appeared before the legislative committee.

Mr. Speaker, once again we are debating Bill C-21, which is the government's bill to cut back on the unemployment insurance program.
This bill will make it more difficult for Canadian employees to qualify for unemployment insurance. This bill will shorten the benefit period for which they will qualify if they are collecting unemployment insurance. This bill will terminate the government's contribution to the unemployment insurance fund, which last year was $2.5 billion.
For many years the unemployment insurance program fund has been contributed to by three sources: employees when they are working contribute to the fund, employers contribute to the fund, and the government contributed to the fund. Last year its contribution was $2.5 billion.
However, through Bill C-21 the government is terminating its contribution to the fund. That means that from now on, once this bill passes, only workers and employers will maintain the fund, which means that the contributions that they must make will increase but they are going to receive less in benefits. It is going to be more difficult to qualify, and they are going to get a shorter benefit period.
As a result of this bill, 155,000 Canadians will lose their benefits altogether, that is 155,000 Canadians who would have received benefits under the law as it stands now will no longer get benefits, and 775,000 Canadians will have their benefits reduced as a result of this bill.
In effect, what we are discussing here today are amendments that have been proposed to the bill by the Senate. I want to make it absolutely clear that if we were talking about amendments that were conceived in the minds of the senators, that were bom on the floor of the Senate, then I would have some concern about them because as has been stated by Conservative members in this House the Senate is not an elected body.
The amendments we are dealing with today from the Senate were not conceived in the Senate. The amendments that the Senate is proposing to the House are amendments that have come forward from trade unions in Canada, from churches, from social action groups, from legal aid clinics, and so on. The only thing is that the Senate's amendments do not go as far as our amendments. They are a little milder than our amendments, but they are based on the same principles. Those amendments that the Senate is proposing have a wide consensus in this country and, in proposing the amendments, the Senate better represents the feelings in the country than the government does.

It did not make it part of its platform that it was going to cut back on the unemployment insurance system. when people were laid off they had no income whatsoever. There was no unemployment insurance. All there was were soup kitchens, bread lines and voluntary relief. What that meant was not only did families and individuals suffer as a result of unemployment-they could not feed their children, they could not buy their clothing, they could not pay their rents-but the whole community suffered. What started off as one plant closing, soon snowballed into damage to the entire community. With unemployment insurance, not only can the unemployed person pay his rent, buy his groceries, and pay for the essentials of life, but he keeps the community going.

country, it is the welfare system. It is a social assistance system.

In addressing the bill government members have said that the purpose of the bill is to take away the disincentives in the unemployment insurance system so that Canadians will work rather than rely on the dole. In many parts of Canada, not the big cities such as Montreal, Toronto, Vancouver or Calgary, many places are one-industry towns based on resources. If it is a town based on tourism where tourism stops in the winter such as an ocean resort located in Prince Edward Island and the beaches are closed, there is no work.

out that the Senate of Canada has been given absolutely no mandate to act in that way.

democratic system. That is exactly what we are witnessing now. We are therefore compelled today to take up the time of the House to debate once more a bill which we have already debated.

speakeroldname: Mr. Raymond Skelly (North Island-Powell River) moved:
subsubtopic: LABELLING REGULATIONS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should establish labelling regulations that would require the labelling of farm-reared salmon and steelhead prior to marketing, and regulations that would require labelling in restaurant menus, to permit consumers to select between wild stock and farm-reared salmon and steelhead in the market-place.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have an opportunity to rise in the House to debate this motion this afternoon. It is a motion which I think is extremely important not only to Canadians but to anyone purchasing and consuming farm-reared salmon.
The rationale behind this is that a consumer should have the right to information and to informed choices about the type of food that is consumed. Another aspect of the rationale is that there is considerable reaction to the farm rearing of salmon and to the specific methods in which salmon have been reared, particularly on the coast of British Columbia.
By our requiring the labelling of these fish as to whether it is farm-reared salmon or wild stocks, it will allow the consumer to make a political choice. They can make a statement about their approval of government regulation and how the product that they are to consume is going to be available in the market-place. The bottom line is that I think every member of this House has an obligation to ensure that the consumer has the right to obtain the information about food which they are consuming. Without proper labelling that cannot happen and it basically deprives consumers of their rights.
The first issue is the quality of the product. There is a great deal of concern. In my own area and wherever I travel, people like to eat seafood products, particularly salmon and steelhead. Yet people are concerned in many quarters about the quality of farm-reared salmon.
Disease is a major concern. On the coast of British Columbia, salmon are raised in a very warm area in the Gulf of Georgia, in areas such as the Sechelt Inlet, where tidal exchange is very low and where the opportunity to cleanse the area and remove waste and detrimental chemicals which develop in it is very low.
Another concern about quality is the way net pens and farm-rearing operations are put in place. The large accumulation of waste beneath the pens is a matter of serious concern to people who live in the area, as well as people who consume the product. Net pens held in the same area in a very low tidal exchange accumulate large amounts of food and excrement from the fish held in captivity, as well as wastes from the rearing operation under those pens, and there is a great deal of concern that it can affect the quality of fish, both by removal of oxygen and by encouraging the growth of other organisms in the area.
Another concern as far as quality is concerned in the net pen method of rearing is that very large populations of fish are held, within a very close, confined area, constantly moving, and constantly under stress. That stress leads to greater disease and deterioration of the fish and anyone who has looked into a salmon net pen can obviously see the kind of reaction that is occurring with those fish. There is discoloration and various levels of activity in the fish. Generally there is an appearance of a deteriorated quality of fish in many of those areas because of the close, confining nature of net pens and the high stress levels.
Fish farmers are struggling basically with two major diseases; the kidney disease and vibriosis, which are fairly rampant in some quarters and cause a great deal of concern for fish farmers. In addition to the basic diseases that occur in the rearing environment, there is a concern about diseased eggs coming into the country, particularly with the Atlantic salmon that have been brought into areas on the west coast.
There is strong concern that eventually those diseased eggs from Atlantic salmon drawn out of Norway and Scotland will be transmitted to wild stocks and that the wild stocks will be decimated by the transmittal of those diseases. There is serious concern about both diseases in
March 13, 1990

Private Members' Business
the fish that are developed in the rearing environment and diseases that are brought into Canada via the eggs that are used in the Atlantic salmon from Norway, Scotland and the east coast.
The next matter in terms of quality is the use of antibiotics in the treatment of common diseases in fish. The antibiotics placed in the food are basically broadcast into the populations of all farm reared salmon. The most prominent antibiotics are oxytetracycline of which about five tonnes is used annually and is growing every year as more and more fish farms come on, and sulfamerazine which, again, is a great concern among people who are consuming that. There are indications that the oxytetracycline can last up to 100 days in the stock and there is no guarantee that the fish from the last point of kill to the table is going to be free of antibiotics in the flesh.
Consumers have a right to know. There are people with allergies to antibiotics and if the farm-reared fish are being treated for diseases with antibiotics, they should have the right to know that they are eating farm-reared fish and they run the risk of being exposed to these antibiotics.
Another concern about the use of these antibiotics is that as the food drops to the water bottom it is eaten by the creatures that live there and it seems that antibiotic resistance disease strains are developing. These disease strains, whether they are eaten by wild stocks in the area, or are transmitted from the farm fish to the bottom life and into the wild stocks, combined with the antibiotics, result in the decimation of the wild stocks.
The next element of quality is the chemicals that are used in and around the rearing operations where the farmers are concerned about the build-up in the nets of seaweed and barnacles and other foulants in those nets. They treat those nets with chemicals in order to remove the fouling agent. What we have had in the tributyltin issue is a very dangerous, cancer causing chemical that can be transmitted into the flesh of the fish. Luckily that one has been identified and removed, but there is still a great deal of concern about anti-fouling chemicals that are still being used in the net.
Government regulation of this industry is viewed as being hopelessly inadequate. People at the policy level of the department are assigned second and third priority levels for policy formulation. If they finish their first area of responsibility and their second area of responsibility, they can then move into giving serious time to aquaculture.
The government does not provide the agencies with the resources to do an extensive study of the regulation, particularly when it gets down to the field level for such things as imposing regulations on the development of fish farms. Three years ago there were about 70 fish farms on the coast of British Columbia. By the end of 1989 there were 210 fish farms on the coast of British Columbia with 200 more licences under application and review. The growth of this has been like a gold rush operation and the government, instead of attempting to provide some direction through regulation, policy and enforcement-

The former Minister of Health stands up in the House and asks what have I got against gold rushes. Of course, nothing. But ultimately when the finished product runs the risk of poisoning you, the more there is, the greater the concern in the population.
I know his concern will result in the minister and the government pressing on for this motion which simply gives rights to consumers by requiring a label for farm fish in a restaurant or in any other area where it is to be consumed so that consumers could have the right to make an informed choice about the type of product they eat and the quality. I am certain that the former Minister of Health in this Parliament would be one of the leading spokespersons to advocate that.
At any rate, we were talking about basically the quality of farm-reared fish. We have discussed the problem of disease, antibiotics, the effect of stress on close confinement, the build-up of detritus under these pens that contaminate the bottom life with antibiotics and poisonous chemicals, which can then be transmitted to the population of reared fish as well as wild stocks.
The issue of quality is a serious one. As we move away from the rearing environment to looking at the quality of fish itself, there are a number of schools of thought.

March 13, 1990
Private Members' Business
Some say any fish is a good fish. But there are people who are very concerned that the quality of farm-reared fish may in fact be substantially less due to no examination of the product. There is no attempt to impose quality control by government regulation. There is no attempt to systematically check it for content of antibiotics or diseases. The government must look at that seriously if farm-reared product is going to enjoy the same credibility in the market-place as wild stocks.
There has to be an initiative by the Government of Canada and the Government of British Columbia or other provincial governments in terms of a partnership arrangement where these kinds of standards can be developed and the testing facilities can be brought to bear in a way that will give the consumer confidence.
Another serious concern is with what the industry refers to as morts, and the possibility that a fish dying in the pen can end up in the production process. This has been documented on a number of occasions, where individuals who have been less than scrupulous in the business have wound up putting through dead fish into the production process.
Again, it may only happen very rarely but it gives the entire industry a black eye. Ultimately there is no guarantee that that will not happen. There is no indication of how broadly based it is.
Perhaps an indication of the extensiveness of this problem of dead fish being removed from the pen due to disease and the stress in the environment in which they are reared is the landfill site on the Sechelt Peninsula. It has had a constant struggle with the volume of dead fish being loaded into their landfill site. At various times they have risen up in arms against the producer saying that they are going to have to deal with it themselves because the site will not handle the volume of dead fish that is going in there.
The possibility that some percentage of those dead fish are not going into a landfill site when they are removed from the rearing pens but go into the production process and wind up on somebody's plate becomes quite frightening. This raises the whole problem of control through a credible inspection process so that type of thing does not happen.
The rationale behind this proposal is that quality is of primary importance. People should have an opportunity to make an informed choice about what goes on their plates and into their bodies. There is enough skepticism in the business about the quality that people would like
to know in order to make the choice. If that product were labelled, it would put a market-place constraint on the industry so that they would attempt to upgrade all the members in it and the entire process, to assure the customer they were getting the finest product available.
The second point in the rationale was the opportunity of a consumer to make a political choice in the marketplace. The government in power believes in the sanctity of the market-place to choose the nature of production and consumption. Why does the government not give the market-place the opportunity to determine the quality and the nature of production and consumption of aquaculture or farm-reared fish?
The mechanism might be simply by labelling farm-reared fish. It would allow people to choose between wild stock and the farm-reared fish. If people have confidence in the industry and they see developing quality controls, they would then begin to choose farm-reared fish, or at least give it equal billing with wild stock. In the absence of that, certainly they are not able to choose in an informed way and the rights of the consumer are being violated as are, to some degree, the rights of the fishing industry.
There is the political aspect of the choices. The way in which this industiy has developed has raised serious questions with the people who live along the coast of British Columbia and certainly those who consume the fish in other areas.
The first one is the abuse of the rights of upland owners. On the Sechelt Peninsula we have seen situations where people who live along the beachfront woke up one morning to find a fish farm right smack in front of their homes and their upland operations, denying them basic access to the ocean and affecting the basic quality of the property they paid good money and high taxes for over the years.
In many cases, this is not even the dilemma of the fish farmer. The fish farmer simply took an opportunity provided by lack of government regulation to drop his fish farm right smack in front of an upland owner's operation. People along the coast of British Columbia are absolutely incensed at where fish farms have been located or proposed on prime recreational land. They were talking about Tree Island off of Denman Island, Sechelt Inlet or Wood Bay. The upland owner's rights have been violated. If we label farm-reared fish, the consumer would be able to make a political choice, by
March 13, 1990

saying "I do not approve of this, and I will not buy the product".
I see that there is a minute left. The gold rush mentality of the government is to refuse to regulate in a rational way the development of these fish farms. It has taken a great deal of trial and error and still has a long way to go. The government's unwillingness to provide decent, fair and equitable regulation to this industry to protect consumers and protect upland owners could certainly be compensated for if the consumer could make a choice and say: "I would prefer not to eat that fish because I am uncertain of its quality and because I do not like the way that industry is operating".

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to be able to talk on this subject with the hon. member's introduction of the situation. I only wonder whether it is a desire to limit the labelling of the fish or whether it is an attack on the aquaculture industry. I think that we need to recognize, when we are talking about this industry, that it is not just a new industry but one that has been around in the world for a long time. There are fish farms in the Orient and in Scandinavian countries and recently, in the last few years they have been coming into Canada and now spreading to the east coast of Canada. Aquaculture has become a very significant factor in our Canadian economy.
I think it is regrettable that we have to discuss this whole matter in such a negative manner. I am sure that the hon. member for North Island-Powell River has a lot more in mind than this simple request to establish labelling regulations for farm-reared salmon and steel-head prior to marketing.
The motion also states that the regulations should be established to require labelling in restaurant menus to permit consumers to select between wild stock and farm-reared salmon and steelhead in the market-place. I am sure that he has been in many small restaurants throughout Canada and recognizes that they just cannot afford to carry two types of salmon and a couple of types of trout or steelhead to give the customers choices. Rather, they are going to select the one which they feel
Private Members' Business
is the best quality. Labelling menus will have no value and no effect whatsoever on this.
There is just no rationale at this stage for the government to introduce regulations of this type. We believe that the fewer regulations that governments impose upon industry and business the better off it is. If they are necessary, fine, but to establish regulations just for the sake of having a regulation and more red tape is of no value to the industry, to the public or to the government.
Of course, why should we request that the aquacultu-rists have labels while not traditional fishermen? If the member is concerned about quality, we need to recognize that all of the fish that are produced for the market are inspected. They all go through the same inspection process. They are graded according to quality and size. Certainly any diseased product is not allowed on the fresh market. I believe that in many cases the farm-reared fish have some advantages in quality.
Also, we need to recognize that many of the species that are sold on the market, such as shrimps, can be of mixed stock. They can be of wild stock, or they can be of cultured stock, this has never presented a problem anywhere that we are aware of in Canada.
I would suggest that the motion to label the cultured salmon and steelhead is really out of touch with reality. If the hon. member felt it was that important, why would he limit it to steelhead and to salmon. We have other trout, for example, that are raised commercially. We have oysters, for example, that can be raised by farmers, as well as the wild stock. If we were going to consider labelling the salmon and steelhead then we should, of course, do it to all fish products.
Again, why force the aquaculturists to label their products when we do not make the same request of the traditional producers? For example, the difference between a seine caught fish that has been in the bottom of the seine net for some time or a gill-net fish compared to the trawl caught fish off the west coast is probably more significant than the difference between a freshly harvested salmon from the fish farm.
We also recognize that the time between when it is caught and brought in to the processing plant is very significant in the quality of the fish as well as how long it has been in the freezer. We can talk about the quality of

March 13, 1990
Private Members' Business
fish and how it deteriorates after being in the freezer over a long period of time.
The fact is that labelling would not help the consumer because the label indicating whether it is a farm fish or a wild stock fish will not accompany the product to the table in the restaurant. My understanding is that the federal government cannot require restaurants to establish this type of labelling on the products.
We did talk about the choice of fish and even now in many fish stores there is a choice of farm fish or wild stock fish. We already have the opportunity, in many instances, to choose what type of fish we buy.
Since the health and safety of fish and fish products are insured by the government's excellent inspection system, the consumers of Canadian-bought fish can be confident that any fish product they do buy is of high quality. The industry itself has a quality assurance program and maintains standards of excellence. It would be a disaster for them to have a bad product put on the market in their formative years.
Speakers have mentioned the fact that large quantities of these fish have been put in landfill sites. This would indicate that they are maintaining that quality and not marketing fish of inferior quality.
The aquaculture industry in Canada is a rapidly growing dynamic industry. It has been adding millions of dollars to the Canadian economy each year and is providing thousands of jobs for Canadians. It has been suggested that the total annual production from the aquaculture industry will soon exceed $100 million, and much of that in British Columbia from where the proponent comes. Aquaculture is becoming a more and more important component of Canadian fisheries.
When we consider some of the significant problems that many of our fishing communities are facing, we see that aquaculture development could soon become a very interesting avenue to enhance our fisheries and to provide employment in these areas which, during the winter months, have very severe unemployment problems. With the wild stocks declining as a result of any number of causes, aquaculture can certainly provide an alternative for the economic activity and for the job creation which we require.
It has been shown that it is only with a great deal of difficulty that we can increase those wild stocks, yet
there is an increasing demand for the salmon and the trout that we produce. Therefore, I believe that the aquaculture industry does have a real place in the market and it has a significant potential for further development if it is allowed to develop. We do not want to put any unnecessary obstacles in its way.
The Food and Agricultural Organization estimates that the world aquaculture production will more than double its present level of 10.2 million tonnes by the year 2000. That is a tremendous source of food in this world that is rapidly running out of food. The aquaculture share of the total world supply for fish, crustaceans, molluscs and marine plants wall increase from about 15 per cent in this year to about 25 per cent in the next 10 years. I think that is a very significant increase providing valuable protein to our world's diet. In many countries fish are the only source of protein available.
As Canada is a major exporter of fish products, with something like 80 per cent of all our fish being exported from British Columbia, we must develop the aquaculture sector and not impose further unnecessary regulations upon it. We must pursue already existing programs to support this young and healthy industry.
I believe that the best control is a free market in which, if you have a superior quality product, you can advertise it, whether it is the troll-caught salmon off the west coast or the fresh farm-raised salmon that you are going to have for Christmas dinner. I believe that these are the types of things that are going to create a healthy industry. We must not saddle it with unnecessary regulations. Therefore I cannot support the motion as presented at this time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as associate fisheries critic, I should like to take this opportunity to support the motion presented by the hon. member for North Island-Powell River. As the House is aware, the Liberal Party founded the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. In our present ranks we have five former ministers of the department, the first of which was the right hon. member for Vancouver Quadra. The main right that the Liberal Party strives to uphold in these matters is the right of the consumer to make an informed choice.
We believe that this issue deserves to be studied to determine what benefits can be derived from separate labelling for the consumer.
March 13, 1990

My support for the motion stems from the fact that there are many things in the aquaculture industry of which we are unsure. This pertains to all parts of the industry, not the least being salmon farming. The following are some of the reasons we in this party endorse further study.
We believe that the consumer should have a choice between two types of salmon. Wild salmon and domestic salmon are different as surely as geese both wild and domestic are different. A consumer has the right to know what the product really is and what effect it will have on him or her.
Regulating the aquaculture industry has also been inconsistent throughout the country. The rules vary from province to province, ranging from stringent to lax standards and regulation enforcement. Perhaps it would be in all consumers best interests that labelling be as precise as possible, given that standards vary widely within the aquaculture industry itself.
The use in antibiotics in the salmon farming industry is another reason for supporting the further study of different labelling. In 1987 it was reported that British Columbia salmon farmers lost between 20 per cent and 60 per cent of their stock to bacterial kidney disease. Antibiotics were used to treat the disease which scientists say is caused by overcrowding in the pens. In Europe scientists have discovered that antibiotics can remain in fish flesh for up to 100 days. No studies have been conducted to determine what effect aquacultural antibiotics can have on humans. Regulations for the use of antibiotics have also been spotty at the best of times. This is probably due to the fact that their use is primarily experimental. Furthermore, the impact of antibiotic treatment of disease is poorly documented and the results are questionable.
If indeed these antibiotics remain in the fish, they could easily pass on to the consumer. The non-farmed salmon are drug free. Proper labelling may be important to those people who have reactions to these drugs. It was with this in mind that the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Oceans concluded in its report of July 1988 the following recommendations:
Recommendation 6(A), to conduct research in support of regulatory requirements regarding residues in aqua-
Private Members' Business
cultural products, with the objective of assessing the potential effect on human health and that of the marine organisms.
Recommendation 15, that the federal government in co-operation with all industrial sectors involved in producing salmonid species for the consumer markets develop labelling standards.
Concerns have also been raised regarding the fish excrements which accumulate in and around the fish pens. Further study should be given to the potential effect this could have on the health and quality of the fish. Wild salmon migrate to different areas during then-life span and therefore this is not a factor in their health. It is known, however, that diseases are present in fish excrements, but it is not known if these diseases can be transmitted from it. Clearly this issue needs more study.
With respect to nutrition it has been shown that the fat content of farmed salmon is higher than non-farm salmon, while the nutritional value of non-farm salmon is slightly higher. Consumers who are diet conscious will certainly appreciate a distinction between the two types.
To conclude, Mr. Speaker, as I have clearly demonstrated, many areas need further research to ensure the protection of all Canadian consumers. Furthermore, we believe that all Canadians have the right to make an informed choice. Consequently I support the motion that further study into the labelling of salmon is required.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise today to deal with the motion moved by the hon. member for North Island-Powell River (Mr. Skelly), and I hope that my comments will reassure Canadian consumers about the close watch the Department of Fisheries and Oceans is keeping on the fish farm industry, as well as the industry's responsibility and the quality of its products.
Mr. Speaker, the federal government has jurisdiction over coastal fishing, certain in-shore fishing, public harbours as well as off-shore and in-shore navigation. These powers, defined in the Constitution, are the responsibility of the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. This is the only federal department whose activities deal mainly with our waters and their resources.

March 13, 1990
Private Members' Business

Through its ongoing programs the Department of Fisheries and Oceans provides support to the aquacul-tural industry in a number of areas. For example, the science sector of Fisheries and Oceans conducts research and experimental development, undertakes collaborative research with industry, provides disease diagnostic services, operates fish hatcheries and fish culture facilities, and develops protocols for safe interprovincial and international stock movement and for the introduction of new genetic resources. The degree of assistance varies by region.
In the area of fishery management the department conducts habitat reviews and, in some instances, supplies a limited numbers of eggs and smolts to the industry. The department also supports aquacultural development projects in eastern Canada, particularly under regional development programs, and undertakes licensing in some areas of Canada.
Other services that Fisheries and Oceans conducts for the benefit of the aquaculture industry include implementation of the national fish inspection program, provision of relevant market intelligence and analysis to other governments and to industry, and the promotion of Canada's interest in the fisheries trade throughout the international community.

Some other federal departments implement a whole slew of programs most of which are national in scope and are accessible to fish farmers. The purpose of most of these initiatives is to promote research and development, economic and business expansion. These may also benefit from tax incentives.
The Department of Fisheries and Oceans is recognized as the federal department responsible for fish farming. It has developed a two-pronged strategy to assume its responsibilities. Firstly, in co-operation with provincial governments, to take steps with a view to ensuring the orderly development of the industry, and secondly to carry out programs and activities in support thereof.
In response to representations made by the industry, the various ministers of fisheries in Canada have agreed to intensify the federal-provincial coordination to ensure the orderly development of the fish farm industry in
Canada. They agreed, and their proposals were adopted by the first ministers in 1986, that memoranda of understanding on the development of fish farming should be negotiated between the federal government and each individual provincial government.

A memorandum of understanding is meant to serve two purposes. First, it establishes a joint agreement and understanding of federal and provincial administrative responsibilities for regulation, while reducing the overall administrative and legal burden on the industry. Of particular interest is the move to establish one stop licensing and leasing of commercial aquaculture ventures.
Second, it sets out a co-ordinated and co-operative approach to government support for the industry. This approach is important, given the concern of certain interests with respect to aquacultural development. A memorandum of understanding outlines the respective roles of the federal and provincial governments in areas such as research and development, education, training, leasing and licensing, fish health, stocks and statistics.
The federal government has to date signed memoranda of understanding with the Northwest Territories, Nova Scotia, Quebec, Prince Edward Island, Newfoundland, British Columbia and New Brunswick. Negotiations are under way with other provinces and the Yukon.

This bilateral approach also serves to recognize the particularities of each region and its fish farm industry.
By supporting this industry, the two levels of government are seeking the same objectives, namely, to diversify the production and improve the quality of fish products in Canada, as well as improve the regularity of commercial fish supply both in Canada and abroad.

All our goals in support of the aquaculture industry are based on a number of principles, and the principle of first order must be a clear and comprehensive regulatory framework. This implies joint responsibility, in fact co-operation to ensure that we maintain a balance between regulation and development. Over-regulating
March 13, 1990

this industry would only lead to limiting its potential in a very competitive market.
Aquaculture is a young and dynamic industry which needs government support. This support is already in place. Fisheries and Oceans is working to develop a positive environment conducive to the evolution of a world-class aquaculture industry.
The Canadian aquaculture industry has made considerable progress in establishing a widespread reputation for high quality seafood products. Fisheries and Oceans is working with the industry and the other levels of government to meet the challenges and opportunities for this industry to become a world leading nation in aquaculture.
Compulsory labelling of the aquaculture product is not required; furthermore, it probably would not work out as too many loopholes would inevitably occur. Because of its critical self-interests, the aquaculture industry is doing its utmost to guarantee the quality of its products. With one of the finest inspection programs in the world, Canada is assuring consumers that the products of all our fisheries meet some of the highest standards of health and safety in our country and abroad.

Mr. Speaker, I was disappointed and somewhat surprised to hear the remarks of the hon. member for Delta. I wondered whether he was reading the same resolution that I was and that the hon. member for North Island- Powell River introduced. He seemed to be talking about a different subject entirely.
The resolution introduced by my colleague from North Island-Powell River clearly states:
-should establish labelling regulations that would require the labelling of farm-reared salmon and steelhead prior to marketing, and regulations that would require labelling in restaurant menus, to permit consumers to select between wild stock and farm-reared salmon and steelhead -
In his remarks the hon. member said that this was over-regulating the industry, that we should depend on the market, and that we should let consumers make the decision as to whether they want the wild stock or farm reared.
That is precisely what the resolution asks for. It is exactly what he wants. He wants consumers to know what they are buying. They make the choice. They may
Private Members' Business
decide they want farm reared or they may decide they want wild. The reasons may be totally ill informed or uninformed, but nevertheless the argument is that they should have that choice.
I suspect all members have had people in their offices as I have who have argued that the flavour of the wild stock is so much better than the flavour of the farm reared. There may be others who would argue the other way. I do not know if it has something to do with my age or the way in which I have conducted myself in the past, but franldy I cannot tell the difference. Nevertheless, there are consumers who say that they can tell the difference.
All the resolution is asking is that they know which one they are actually paying for when they buy it and whether they are getting the one they are paying for. There are some who will argue that the nutritive value of the farm reared as opposed to the wild stock is better, and others will argue that the wild stock is better.
I have heard these same arguments and participated in similar arguments with respect to organically grown food and food grown with inorganic fertilizers. I know enough about it to be satisfied in my own mind that there is no difference from the point of view of nutrition.
However, we do not tell people that they are not going to know what they are buying. Certainly organic food is clearly labelled in most instances as such, and consumers pay more for it because they believe that it tastes better or that it is better from a quality point of view. They have the right to make that choice. They have the right to pay for the difference if they want to. That is all that my hon. friend is asking for: the right for people to know what they are buying when they buy it.
The hon. member for North Island-Powell River mentioned that the environment is quite different. Wild stock is raised and spends a good deal of its life in much colder water. It selects the food that it eats. It ranges over thousands of miles in its growing process, so there is quite a difference in the food that it is getting. I do not say that that makes it any better or any worse. I am simply saying there is that difference.
They do get a lot more exercise. Because of the cold water and the exercise the flesh should be firmer. Again, I do not know whether that makes any difference but you and I, Mr. Speaker, should have the right to know when we are buying salmon or steelhead whether it was raised

March 13, 1990
Private Members' Business
in a little puddle of water in a pen or whether it was raised in and allowed to range the wild ocean.
There is a lot of talk about disease. Certainly Canada is doing everything it can to maintain the quality of farm reared fish and animals alike. We do not know whether we are doing everything that has to be done but we are working at it. We do not know the stress factor. Certainly we know that with 295 of us in this House sometimes the stress is much greater than when there are not quite as many of us here. When those salmon and steelhead are crowded, as I say, in relatively small puddles of water, there is a great stress factor. Does this make any difference? I do not know, but again the consumer should have the right to know what he or she is paying for.
Farm reared fish should be cheaper to produce. They are not because of a lot of problems they are having in the industry in many cases. Nevertheless, they should be cheaper. Farm reared fish should not be sold at the same price as the wild stock. If consumers are getting a product that is being produced more cheaply, they should pay less for it and know what they are getting. They should not be paying top prices for fish that are produced more cheaply when they think they are getting wild stock fish.
The hon. member for Delta was concerned about over-regulating and about the imposition on the industry of having to label. All we are saying is that it is a different product. Whether it is nutritionally different, I do not know. Whether the flavour is different, I do not know. I do not know in what ways it is different, but there is no question but that it is raised in a totally different environment under totally different conditions. There may be questions of flavour and nutrition. If this resolution is supported by the House and acted upon, individuals will know exactly what they are paying for.
I agree with most of what the member for Delta said. Let the consumers make the choice, but they can only make it if the product is labelled so that they know what they are buying.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to rise and participate in this discussion today about the very dynamic and young Canadian industry of aquaculture. I compliment my colleague, the
hon. member for North Island-Powell River, for bringing this important subject before the House with his motion M-546. I suppose I should apologize for my voice. Hopefully it will hold out to the end.
At a time when the global market-place is posing challenges for most resource based nations, Canada is in a very exciting position with its new resource which has enormous potential. We have seen tremendous growth in aquaculture in Canada over the last 15 years. Indeed from 1984 to 1987 we saw a 17 per cent increase in the industry representing today a $50 million industry in Canada. Forecasts suggest another 1,000 per cent increase by the end of the decade which we have just begun.
A combination of factors has fuelled this expansion: the growth of world-wide demand for seafood, the need to meet this demand with production from new sources such as cultured fish, the increasing reliance by fish processors on aquaculture products which they see as a dependable year-round source of quality seafood, and a widespread recognition of the high quality of Canadian cultured seafood products already regarded as a major source of increased domestic and international supply.
Atlantic Canada plays a very full part in this well established aquaculture industry. We have salmon, trout, mussels and oysters, and we are now diversifying into scallops. Nova Scotia is a leader in the area of aquaculture having as well developed Irish moss as an area within aquaculture.
As of 1988 aquaculture has directly produced some 1,500 jobs in Canada and it is anticipated that by the year 2000, 5,000 Canadians will be directly employed in the aquaculture industry. This is a part of the tremendous work in job creation that has gone on in the last five years in this country. Not only is direct employment significant in aquaculture but indeed indirect employment has come through related industries and the production of the necessary equipment.
We need to make more progress toward producing all the necessary fishing equipment here in Canada. That can have a tremendous impact on job creation as well. I speak of building cages, equipment, netting manufactur-
March 13, 1990

ing, feed processing and services in the area of marketing distribution and fish health just as some examples.
There is also a potential down side in aquaculture and we must be very careful in its further development. A number of public concerns have been brought to my attention as a member of Parliament from an area in which there is considerable aquaculture development. People owning adjacent properties have a very active concern in whether or not an aquaculture site is located just off their properties.
Indeed there has to be approval under the Navigable Water Protection Act, but at the same time it seems to me that people who own properties adjacent to the ocean should have a somewhat more significant say in whether or not licences are approved to develop aquaculture right off their own properties. I can relate to this as I live on the ocean myself. There is definitely a need for public consultation on every single aquaculture application that takes place.
There is concern with respect to the impact of aquaculture developments on traditional fishing. For example, earlier this past fall there were applications to develop some aquaculture sites for mussel development near the town of Lockeport in Nova Scotia. This would potentially interfere with the lobster fishery in that area and very legitimate concerns were articulated by the fishermen who have fished there for many years.
We have to be very careful in the development of this industry which at a time when our fishery is facing difficulty has tremendous potential for job creation and the creation of wealth.
One thing that I think is highly significant about aquaculture is that it is an industry that is resource driven. We find out what the market wants and then we develop a means to produce what is required.
It seems to me that this is one of the areas in which we have been falling down in the development of the fishery in Canada. We tend to go out and catch what is there and worry later about whether or not anybody actually wants to buy it, or indeed whether it is commercially viable. We hear much talk in the House about fish allocations that are either left in the water or made available to foreign nations whilst ignoring the fact that we cannot force Canadians to go out and catch fish for which there is no market, or for which they cannot make a reasonable
Private Members' Business
profit or return on the investment that they have made in order to harvest those fish.
We have to continue to look to the future in terms of market development, and aquaculture provides a marvellous opportunity for developing new sources of fish as well as the development of secondary processing of it.
My hon. friend's motion deals specifically with salmon. Aquaculture has been one means whereby we have rekindled the trout industry and the salmon industry in southern Nova Scotia, the area which I have the privilege to represent in this place. We have seen some very successful experiments taking place. My hon. friend from Nanaimo-Cowichan spoke earlier of the differences in the flavour of the meat and the environmental factors that can come into play.
While on the one hand there is the potential for a response to market demand, at the same time we have to recognize that we have a better opportunity of assessing the possibilities for future harvesting because it is a bit more like farming: you know what you are planting and you know what you are going to harvest.
However, we are still subject to vagaries of the environment. That is why environmental protection is so important. The Environmental Protection Act brought forward by this government during the previous Parliament will play a very important role in allowing us to develop an aquaculture industry. We are safeguarding our coastlines and ensuring as best as possible that our oceans will remain clean so that they can produce as much as they can. I am very encouraged to see this Parliament discussing the subject of aquaculture and its potential.
With respect to the specific motion brought forward by my hon. friend, while there is a certain inclination on my part to agree with the sentiment implied in his motion, I have, with all due respect, some reservations as to the wisdom and potential benefits of further regulating an industry that some would suggest is already over-regulated to an extraordinary degree. I believe-and I think that it is consistent with the philosophy of this government-that government's role is to support and to assist but not unnecessarily to intervene in the carrying on of business and in the exploitation of our Canadian resources.

March 13, 1990
Government Orders
It seems to me that to do as this motion suggests, to impose mandatory labelling of cultured fin fish, is unwarranted for a number of reasons. First, I think it is clear that the quality of the product that we are producing through aquaculture is very high.
For example, in Nova Scotia mussels have become a very big industry. When I was a child in Hubbards we did not even use mussels for bait and yet today they have become one of the delicacies of the Atlantic fisheries. I would suggest that a lot of the people who eat mussels cannot tell the difference in taste between a cultured mussel and a wild mussel, though the cultured ones tend to be of a more consistent size.
The industry is also already highly regulated. Goodness gracious, everybody involved in the fishery knows how highly regulated it is. I am not sure we need to add to that. Enforced labelling would be an administrative nightmare, I would suggest. I do not think we really need this sort of thing, not to mention an added cost with no value added benefit from the point of view of the consumer. I am not sure people wish to have prices added on to things that are already very costly.
While I can respect the sentiment put forward by my hon. colleague opposite, I would much prefer to see the money that would go into administering the bureaucratic system which would have to be set up puf toward research. We know the outstanding record of this government and this Prime Minister with respect to research.
