speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure today to enter the debate on Bill C-21.1 would like to spend the majority of my time talking about the government's contributions, the variable entrance requirements and, if time allows, the penalties that are being imposed on those who are unfortunate enough to have to quit their job.
I listened to some of the members opposite speak on Bill C-21. They did not talk about bill itself. What they talked about is that dreaded Senate, that other place, and the fact that it has no right to be sending amend-
March 13, 1990

merits to this House for us to consider. It would not have been necessary for the Senate to send amendments if this particular government had the courtesy to allow us to debate this issue more fully and, therefore, the time to propose our own amendments.
One of the things that this government has continually said is that this legislation is better than the one we have presently in place. That is something that I take exception to, for the simple reason that if $2.9 billion is removed from the system and the government itself states that by the year 1992 it will be in a deficit position of $3 billion, what does that tell you? It can tell you only one thing: there are other objectives and other reasons for this particular piece of legislation.
This legislation is there for one reason and for one reason only, and that is for this government to get out of the business of supplying this particular social safety net for the workers of Canada. There are no other reasons that a government would put a particular program of this magnitude in jeopardy by the year 1992.
Perhaps it would be interesting for the people at home to note that in 1992 there will be another election. The people on this side will likely have the mess of trying to do something with this particular bill, if it is so unfortunate that it be passed.
If this piece of legislation goes into effect, there are going to be some ramifications for the working men and women of this country. The most important one, the variable entrance requirement, relates more specifically to the have-not regions of Canada. The variable entrance requirements were put there simply because this country has a difference in economics. Not all regions of the country are the same. My hon. friend across the way would say that Newfoundland has greater economic difficulties than northern Ontario. Those residents of northern Ontario say to me on a regular basis that their economic situation is much different from that of Toronto. Those in southern Ontario would say that their situation is a lot different from that of Montreal, Vancouver or Halifax.
One of the largest cornerstones of this particular social safety net is the variable entrance requirement. The variable entrance requirements are something that Canadians and governments in the past have put in place because there are different regional unemployment
Government Orders
conditions due to economic situations in the various regions.
For example, northern Ontario, is considered to be a resource-based part of the country. Forestry, tourism and mining are the three important resource-based industries that make our economy grow. What happens if you take one of these large pieces of the puzzle out of the picture, Mr. Speaker? You get mass unemployment. There are no other jobs to go to. In Montreal, if a plant closes down, a worker with the correct training can go down the street and find the opportunity to get another job. In northern Ontario, as in Newfoundland, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, when you lose your job in a single-industry town, you are stuck. You need a social safety net, the type of program which will allow people to keep their pride as Canadians, which will allow them to get by that cyclical problem which occurs in regions where resource-based industries are located. Those are called seasonal jobs. We all have them in our areas.
The issue is that there are those who do not accept the fact that Canada is the same no matter where you live and that these variable entrance requirements have to be maintained and remain in place.
Let us take a look at what is going to happen with this particular bill as it relates to the variable entrance requirements. Under Bill C-21, instead of a requirement of 10 to 14 weeks, it would be 10 to 20 weeks. Regions of 6 per cent or less require 20 weeks, while regions of more than 15 per cent would retain a minimum entrance requirement of 10 weeks.
The regional benefits, under Bill C-21, would affect northern Ontario claimants in that every time they make a claim for unemployment insurance they would lose 13 weeks of benefits. When you take that into a small, unpopulated area like northern Ontario, and in particular, the riding of Kenora-Rainy River, that simply takes $3 million out of the economy. That is a quick figure of $3 million. When you do that, there are some ramifications. I think that members opposite who are not fortunate enough to live in areas with the beauty and magnitude of northern Ontario, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, should think twice before they vote in favour of Bill C-21, because it will change the way people in the regions of Canada look at themselves. Let us take a look at what the situation is.

March 13, 1990
Government Orders
One of the things to consider is the effect of this particular change in the unemployment insurance program. Under the proposed 62-regions system, which would go into effect under Bill C-21, claimants in 45 regions would require more than 14 weeks of insurable earnings based on seasonally-adjusted three-month average of unemployment rates for the month ending November, 1989. Only in eight regions would the minimum 10-week entrance requirement apply. Under the old VER rules, the minimum would have applied in 32 of these regions. Therefore, this particular bill will affect 150,000 of our constituents in a short period of time. That is an enormous change from the old bill.
One of the effects of that will be the shift to welfare. We talk about the fact that once people cannot collect unemployment insurance, they have certain alternatives. They can either move or look for other means of having dollars to support their family. If they cannot get employment in their particular region, or because of their economic situation as an individual cannot afford to wander off to Toronto or Montreal or some other area where perhaps the unemployment rate is not as high, what choice do they have? Their choice is welfare.
They will go to the municipality and the province and simply say: "You'll have to look after me". I say that that is not acceptable. I say to the Government of Canada that we have an obligation to the people we represent to maintain a system where people feel comfortable as Canadians. Therefore, when times are hard, we will be a caring and loving society and look after them.
We cannot simply say: "Move to Toronto". People in northern Ontario do not want to live in Toronto. We cannot afford to live in Toronto. Housing is so expensive that no one would want to move there at this time to try to make a fresh start with a young family. For all intents and purposes, perhaps they do not even have a job to go to at first and have to hunt for a job. The rent is so high, a move is not feasible. So what choice do they have?
For the government to state that the changes in the unemployment insurance system, the variable entrance requirements, are an improvement to the old bill and therefore putting forward this new legislation is going to be an improvement, is rubbish. We all realize in this
House that there are other reasons for this particular piece of legislation being put in place.
I find it very difficult to go back to my constituents and say that we have revamped and improved the unemployment insurance program. It is very difficult for me to say to my constituents that it is improved when I know that on average a person in northern Ontario will have 13 weeks less of insurance that he or she so badly needs in those areas where you find natural, resource-based industries which in certain periods of the year cut back and put people out of work.
There is another area of importance in northern Ontario. I am speaking of the unemployment situation of the native people there. Native people, historically, have a much higher unemployment rate than people in the non-native communities. In my riding, I represent roughly 14,000 aboriginal people. Those people have rates of unemployment ranging from 40 per cent to 90 per cent, depending on the community.
The government makes it more difficult to collect unemployment insurance in those regions. Once, if a person was lucky enough to be a guide for a particular tourist camp for 10 weeks or worked in the forests for 10 weeks, then he or she could collect unemployment insurance. As some members have indicated, they could even get involved in a training program or a make-work program under the old Liberal government which allowed them to accumulate sufficient weeks so that they would not be on the welfare rolls. This gave them a sense of achievement, belonging, the sense of having something to offer Canadians. Now what you give them is welfare. Where would 14,000 aboriginals go for a job in northern Ontario where roughly 10,000 of those 14,000 live in isolated communities to which you have to fly. What do I tell them? Move to Toronto, you have no choice. That is ridiculous. We know it, they know it, but the government seems to think that is fine. Do not worry about them, the government of Ontario will look after them.
That brings me to the other area which the citizens of Canada should be aware of. This bill is just a disguise to pass programs that the federal government historically has been responsible for and is now passing on to the provinces. The government tells the province: "You look after it. They are your citizens. We are getting out of the program".
March 13, 1990

When I read something that states that by the year 1992, if this bill passes, this program will be $3 billion in deficit. When I read that, it made me think that there are no choices available to the worker when he or she gets laid off in this country. If this government is not prepared to put certain dollars into this program, then it is saying to the employer and employee that they have to.
We all know that employers feel that they pay to the UI program to the extent that enough is enough. We have heard that on numerous occasions and I think all members of Parliament would say that they have listened to the small business person and the large business person say that one of the reasons Canadians cannot compete with the Americans is because the amount of dollars we pump into these extra programs and the hidden costs of keeping these employees is too high.
What we are hearing from the government is that sooner or later in 1992-93 when it becomes evident under the new program that there is a deficiency as far as the dollars put into it are concerned, the employer and the employee will either have to kick in more or we will have to reduce the amount of funds we pay to an already small amount. If you were ever so unlucky as to collect unemployment, Madam Speaker, then you will know that it is very difficult to raise a family of two or three, or even look after yourself, pay the rent and feed yourself with the amount of dollars paid through that program.
If we cut the program even more because the government no longer has any responsibility in the program then the workers will be forced into a position of having to stay on welfare, or also something which is very sad in this bill, possibly having to stay in a job where the working relationship between the employer and the employee is so bad that psychologically it would be better for that individual to quit. This government has stated that in this country you do not quit a job. You stay there whether or not you like it, even though there are situations when at times you have no choice but to quit.
The changes in the penalties in this particular legislation change from six weeks disqualification to a minimum of seven weeks to a maximum of 12 weeks plus two weeks waiting period; a reduced rate of benefit from 60 per cent of insurable earnings to 50 per cent. We do not give criminals sentences that long. I cannot understand
Government Orders
why someone who has to quit a job because of situations not of his or her making would be put in a situation where they cannot collect for three months. Not only that, but this can be carried over for six years. I would like to see them give penalties and longer sentences than that to people who steal in stores. A person who happens to quit his or her job is given a six-year penalty. I think that is shameful. Canadians know what this government is up to and when it comes to 1992-93 they will remember, if this government has the audacity to pass this legislation in its present form.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-NON-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have listened to the debate on this amendment to Bill C-21 with great interest. One of the speeches that I found most striking was yesterday when the Minister of State for Employment and Immigration said that she and this government listened to the workers.
When they listened to the workers did they hear the workers tell the government to dump the burden of paying for unemployment insurance on their backs? Did the workers say to this government: "We need training, but we don't need government, our own tax money, to pay for it?" Did the workers tell this government that they want to have shorter eligibility for unemployment insurance that they have paid for? Did they tell this government that they want their unemployment insurance program decimated? I think not.
When I was on the tour with many members who sit in this House, group after group and individual after individual Canadian told us over and over again how important any changes to unemployment insurance are to them. They believed and hoped that the government would care enough to enhance the program, not decimate it. One should not be surprised, however, that the government does not listen. People should not be surprised at the level of disdain at which this government holds working people. Consistently during the hearings and in the debate we have heard these terms from the government: relocation, re-education, behaviour modification. Those words coming from this government with the mandate it has and the commitment it made are shocking, disgusting and, in my view, unacceptable. If

March 13, 1990
Government Orders
George Orwell had a vision when he wrote 1984 the vision was of the government on that side of the House.
Yesterday, we met with the labour coalition that has been referred to a number of times during this debate. The people we met included Shirley Carr, president of the Canadian Labour Congress; Louis Laberge, president of the Quebec Federation of Labour; Jim McCamb-ley, president of the Canadian Federation of Labour; Gerald Larose, president of the Confederation of National Trade Unions; Kitty O'Callaghan, president of the Canadian Teachers Federation, Lorraine Page, president of the Quebec Teaching Congress; Kathleen Connors, president of the National Federation of Nurses' Unions and Louis Lacroix, president of the Canadian Conference of Teamsters.
This group represents 4 million dues-paying workers, both employed workers and unemployed workers. If that is multiplied by 3.6, which is the average family in this country, that is 14.5 million Canadians. Up until Friday, the coalition tried to have a meeting with the minister and this government. They were denied the opportunity to meet with them.
I would like to put what those labour centrals had to say on behalf of working people on the record. Kitty O'Callaghan, president of the Canadian Teachers Federation, talked about kids who are disadvantaged because of unemployment in our communities. She talked about kids who come to school hungry and ill-equipped. As a result of that, they are unable to fully participate in school activities. Not only that, they are unable to perform at full potential. Her concern is that today one in six kids in Canada is already living in poverty, and that coupled with the UI cuts, the transfer payment cuts in the budget, the claw-back of family allowance, and education cuts, kids today are out selling candy bars and other things to buy needed equipment for their schools. Not only are they disadvantaged, not only are they finding it difficult to reach-

speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-NON-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext: I did that when I went to school. What nonsense. They have been doing that for years.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-NON-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
It will be your turn soon. I am sure the Speaker will recognize you.
It is evident that members on the other side of the House also hold poor children in disdain and that is the tragedy of what this government is putting before us.
Kathleen Connors, president of the National Federation of Nurses' Unions, talked about the front-line deliverers of health care, the nurses. She said that they see the direct impact of unemployment on the local health care system. They see when there is not sufficient income for appropriate food, when there is not sufficient income for appropriate health care, and when unemployment causes family stress, family violence and suicide. She said that between the EPF transfer cuts and the unemployment insurance cuts that we are seeing in this bill, the impact will be devastating.
Lorraine Page, president of the Quebec Teaching Congress, said that we need to invest in professional training, but that must not be done by asking the unemployed to pay for the training fund. She said that we need to enhance financing of the education sector, not privatize it as shown in this bill, and not cut it in the budget for education. She said that women, in particular, who are in precarious jobs are unemployed first and unemployed longest. She talked about eligibility and the fact that the increased demands in this bill would make it much more difficult for women to become eligible. She said, and it is very true, that of the one in six kids in this country who is poor, usually, statistically, they come from single-parent, women-led families. Those are the ones who will be affected first and the ones who will be affected most by these cuts.
Gerald Larose, president of the Confederation of National Trade Unions, said unemployment insurance is the main mechanism to reallocate riches from the well off to the more fragile, and that when you weaken the system, as this bill is going to be weakening it, you weaken the regional areas even more. He said that this is a system designed to privatize unemployment insurance, that this government clearly no longer wants to fund unemployment insurance and is copying the American model.
Despite statements during the election campaign and in the free trade agreement itself that governments have to interfere less in the free market, and despite statements by this government that that is not really true, we are finding ourselves again and again with legislation that is tailored to the American model to accommodate the free trade agreement. Bill C-21 is an example of the big lie that took place to get votes in the last federal election.
March 13, 1990

Louis Laberge, president of the Quebec Federation of Labour, said that this government is responsible for plant shutdowns, one after the other. Instead of helping workers, the government is reducing the time available for unemployment insurance and increasing the time it takes to become eligible. Ele said that workers are aware of how far Bill C-21 is going, but it will take time for workers to really appreciate the impact on them and to become angry enough to revolt. He said that this bill is so bad it is hard to find words to explain it.
Jim McCambly of the Canadian Federation of Labour said the removal of $4.2 billion for general revenue responsible for this funding may destroy the unemployment insurance program, one of the better systems in the world. When talking to people from other parts of the world, they are impressed, or were impressed, with our unemployment insurance system. The fact is, after this bill is finished with Canadian workers, it will not be something to be proud of, but something to be very worried about.
Mr. McCambly talked about the impact of unemployment on seasonal, cyclical, and disadvantaged workers. He feels that this legislation is going to hurt very badly those workers. He said that for the first year it may not be too bad, but wait until the second year. The government is banking on those people who are working not being able to visualize being unemployed so that it can get through this bill. Once it does, it will be too late.
Louis Lacroix, President of the Canadian Conference of Teamsters, said that this is more than a bad bill, this is a philosophical debate. The government is no longer participating in the unemployment insurance program. It is the privatization of social benefits in the country and this is one of the very clear steps in the government's plans.
Shirley Carr, President of the Canadian Labour Congress, unequivocally stated that she would be going to the wire fighting this bill. The CLC pointed out that unemployment insurance is fundamental to the economic and social security of all workers, unionized and non-unionized, full-time and part-time, private sector and public sector. Bill C-21 destroys many of the principles on which the unemployment insurance system
Government Orders
has been built. Its most basic purpose of insuring workers against the loss of earnings is seriously undermined. The tripartite financing of UI by employers, workers, and government, developed over the past 50 years, is destroyed by this bill.
Government contributions of $2.5 billion for UI extended benefits resulting from high regional unemployment will be withdrawn. About $300 million of government subsidies for UI fishery benefits will be transferred to premium payers. Fifteen per cent of UI premiums, about $2 billion a year, will be used to finance the purchase of training courses, resettlement, business start-up, wage subsidies and other labour adjustment programs now financed from general government revenues.
Bill C-21 is not good for working people in Canada. Bill C-21 is not good for employers in Canada. The only people the government has heard say that Bill C-21 is good is themselves.
The government is abandoning the social contract-I think it is important to note, the sacred trust-that was made with Canadian workers and employers. It is evident now that the government has never had the intention of listening to Canadian workers.
I would like to tell the government that the impact of Bill C-21 is so bad that time will prove our opposition. We will not let up in that opposition. It may pass the bill, but the opposition will not let up. We will target the government and we will remind workers over and over again of who destroyed the system to which they contributed for a working lifetime and on which they depend. We will remind the 520,000 Canadians who will be affected. I will certainly work with my colleagues to remind the 60,000 British Columbians who will be affected, and I will certainly make it my mission in life to remind the 37,500 workers in my region of Vancouver and the lower Fraser Valley who will be affected. We will be reminding them of the $144 million that will be lost to the B.C. economy, that the safety net that gives them the opportunity to go out and look for other work has been removed, and that the burden is being shifted on to their backs and the backs of the provinces. We will not let up. The men and women working in this country deserve better.

March 13, 1990
Government Orders
I would ask that we consider the people who do not sit in nice surroundings such as these. We should consider the people who work on the shop floors or shift work, which occasionally this House has an opportunity to try. At least we get an afternoon shift to one o'clock in the morning.
I would ask the members to think about working in the dirt and grime in the mines and in the unsafe working conditions. Think about giving your life to that labour and then having someone come along and snatch it out from under you, like one could snatch a carpet, saying that what they are doing is good for you.
It is time that government members spent a little bit of time on the shop floors with working people hearing the kinds of concerns they truly have. They should hear the kinds of fears they have about where the economy of this country is going, where their future is, where the future is of their children and how they are going to survive the clawbacks, the UI cuts, the GST, this budget, and free trade. What is going to be left by the time we get to the next general election?
