subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-NON-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to rise today to speak to the motion moved by the government House leader on the Senate message on Bill C-21.
The legislative initiative undertaken by the Minister of Employment and Immigration represents very tangible progress in the area of employment reform. I would like to congratulate her for it.
First, I would like to take a few moments to remind hon. members of the provisions in Bill C-21 that I support, and why. To me, Bill C-21 represents part of an approach, a reasoned strategy, well thought-out and carefully designed. As a major reform of public policy it is the right way to go.
I have always thought that for far too long in this country, social and economic policy were piecemeal, a bandage here and some ointment there. The result of this rather haphazard approach was policies absent of direction, devoid of parity and often, in the end, ineffective. Today, more and more Canadians are calling out for social and economic leadership as we move towards 2000.
This is no more true than in the area of labour force development. The Minister of Employment and Immigration clearly understands that when it comes to unemployment insurance, for example, what may have been appropriate for a resource-based economy of the sixties and seventies is no longer adequate. Today, we see that, thanks in part to initiatives by this government such as the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, the Western Diversification Office and others, we have an economic
March 13, 1990

base that is increasingly well-rounded and, indeed, quite vital and diverse.
I know all members and all Canadians share with me a sense of great pride when we speak of economic prosperity. It seems to me that the creation of a broad economic base is only part of the story. If we achieve through our economic policies a certain measure of success in diversifying our nation's means of production, then does it not stand to reason that our social, labour force, and workforce policies should operate in tandem?
We know, for example, that our resource-based economy of 20 years ago demanded very little by way of skills development. Technology changed slowly and workers easily kept pace with workplace demands. But training has assumed a critical role in today's high technology era. A skilled workforce is essential for our businesses to compete successfully in the global market-place of the year 2000.
To turn our backs on the challenges of the next millennium is foolish. To be paralyzed by the dogma of the status quo is hardly economic leadership. This bill represents a very sensible and thoughtful approach to labour force development. It is an approach very much in keeping with the Canadian way. These proposed changes to our unemployment insurance system represent a flexible and balanced response to changing times. It is consistent with the commitment to contribute to economic prosperity. Equally, it ensures that those in our society who are disadvantaged are helped and encouraged to be full participants in our society's economic activity.
As one of my constituents in Barrie said to me the other day: "Edna, what we have is unemployment insurance, but what we need is employment insurance." It is understood that these reforms, by their very nature, are designed to help workers and to assist those who require special assistance to play a full and satisfactory role in the workforce. After all, that is the very essence of the Canadian Jobs Strategy.
I want to discuss for a moment some of the particular initiatives designed to meet the specific circumstances of women, older workers and the employment disadvantaged. For example, the strategy is providing a financial boost to a training program for social assistance recipi-
Govemment Orders
ents that already has a proven track record in helping them to become economically self-reliant.
Through this program, the federal government works in tandem with the provincial governments to help social assistance recipients acquire the skills and the work experience they need to find good jobs at good pay. We, on this side of the House, are prepared to support an additional $50 million under the strategy. That, combined with the $50 million spent through the Canada Assistance Plan and matching funds from the provinces, promises an additional $200 million to prepare an estimated 20,000 additional social assistance recipients for productive employment.
I am particularly pleased to note that the strategy addresses the needs of older workers for whom the job search is often a long and frustrating process. We will be injecting an extra $40 million into the continuing employment option which provides financial support for up to three years to employers who hire and retrain displaced workers.
In addition, we will be doubling the budget of the Industrial Adjustment Service which works with companies to deal with the problems of obsolete skills, the challenges of changing technologies, and finding alternative employment for laid-off workers. Its total budget will now be $30 million.
Bill C-21 contains another very important change that older workers will welcome with open arms. It enables workers over the age of 65 to collect benefits if they otherwise meet the unemployment insurance criteria. With more and more Canadians choosing to extend their working lives, this change is an idea whose time has come.
The strategy also opens the door of opportunity for more women. For example, we are allocating an additional $65 million for promoting human resource planning programs in the private sector. These plans will include employment equity components which will broaden prospects for women.
It is my personal hope that details being worked out now at private sector consultations under the auspices of the Canadian Labour Market and Productivity Centre will enable us to improve the apprenticeship program and train more women in non-traditional occupations. In conjunction with the private sector, we hope to develop an entiy level training program for jobs in growing

March 13, 1990
Government Orders
industries, particularly in areas in which women already have a large stake.
Bill C-21 also proposes changes in special unemployment insurance benefits that will not only help women but also make the program more relevant to the needs of today's workforce. These changes include, in addition to the current 15 weeks of maternity benefits, 10 weeks of parental benefits for natural and adoptive parents, shared between the mother and the father as they deem fit, and the proposal for more flexibility and access to 15 weeks of sickness benefits.
I would like to say that I have received a lot of correspondence from my constituents who are young mothers-to-be. They know that if Bill C-21 is not passed before the birth of their children, they will not be able to take advantage of its generous provisions for maternity leave.
The strategy has also taken into account the concerns of women's groups in another matter, the question of what exactly constitutes just cause for quitting one's employment. Under Bill C-21, people who quit their jobs without just cause stand to lose between seven and 12 weeks of benefits. However, anyone who has justifiable reason for quitting, such as being the victim of hazardous working conditions or because a spouse has found employment in another city, will not face these penalties.
In response to appeals from women across Canada, myself included, the Minister of Employment and Immigration has added an amendment to Bill C-21 which provides legislative expression of just cause. When the government introduced the labour force development strategy, it did so to help both the unemployed and Canadian businesses by creating a better match between skills employers need and skills workers have. We know this is just a start, but it focuses our attention on the education and the training which are needed to equip people for the demanding requirements of a modern, global economy, and that will enable them to participate fully in our society. More and more of us who have witnessed the massive changes brought about by the technological revolution appreciate that skills training remains a key means of preparing our workforce for the constantly evolving complexities of the job market.
All of us understand that if we are ever to compete effectively in the global economy, we must ensure that the labour force of the 1990s is not only highly skilled, but capable of adapting to an evolving work environment brought on by technological and demographic change. This challenge requires the co-operation of the public sector, the private sector, professional associations and, yes, unions to pool skills and experience and get involved for the good of our country. Government cannot do it alone. It is essential to establish links between the schools, industry and the community to provide invaluable insights for our youth into the world of work and its demands.
The government has listened seriously to the recommendations offered by the Senate regarding Bill C-21. While there are many concerns which all members should have about many of the suggestions in the message before us, some recommendations are worth including in Bill C-21. For example, we recognize the impact which illiteracy has on Canadian workers and on employers. The lack of basic skills is an impediment to further training. For that reason, the idea in recommendation one is worth including in this bill.
Senators have said that they welcome the commitment of the government to producing an annual plan which will show members how unemployment insurance funds will be spent to train and develop people. In recommendation four, they have asked us to amend the bill to ensure that the minister will provide specific details in this plan. It will do no one good to create centralized plans which are too rigid or detailed to respond to changing times. At the same time, a reasonable level of detail should be provided. Therefore, the response which the government proposes to the Senate's suggestion is a fair one.
The Liberals in the Senate seem to believe that the only purpose of unemployment insurance is to pay people to wait for their old jobs to come back. We believe that unemployment insurance needs to become an active program which invests in people. Training courses, financial help to move to a place where there are more jobs, and assisting claimants to start businesses, are wise investments. This government wants to let people get out of the unemployment trap.
March 13, 1990

In closing, let me say how proud I am to have played a role as a member of the legislative committee which travelled the land studying this bill. I now know with certainty that the proposals contained herein respond to the needs and the aspirations of Canadians entering and participating in the workforce as we move towards 2000.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-NON-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I am duty-bound to rise tonight on closure at third reading of Bill C-21, an act to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-NON-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext: It's not third reading.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-NON-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
The legislation before us, referred back to this House by the other place, would fundamentally alter one of the basic aspects of universality in Canada. The bill would remove the federal government from funding the unemployment insurance program, dramatically restructuring our social safety system. It is a Conservative assault on the Canadian way of life.
The legislation would increase the required number of weeks needed to collect unemployment insurance and lessen the actual number of weeks a person will receive entitlements. The legislation would alter the minimum entrance requirements for workers seeking financial support from the current 10 to 14 weeks of employment to an incredible 10 to 20 weeks of employment. This means that, even though the federal government has removed itself from paying into the program, the Tories are still calling the shots and making it tougher on Canadians, saying: "You have no choice. You will have to contribute more and receive less."
The changes in the legislation before us mean that over 150,000 Canadians will lose their entitlements and over 750,000 working Canadians will have their entitlements reduced. Under this government, the same case is being repeated time and time again. Canadians are paying more and more in taxes, and are receiving less and less in entitlements and services.
The government is removing itself from contributing to the UI system. The government intends to replace its $2.9 billion contribution with increased employee-employer payments. Under the proposed legislation contributions by employers will rise to $3.15 for every $100 of earnings, a total of $3.48 more per week than what employers presently pay, or $180 more per year.
Government Orders
Contributions by employees will also rise. As if the hardworking Canadian was not already paying enough, under the new legislation employees would pay $2.49 more per week than at present, an increase of $129 more per year. Add to this the additional cost of at least $1,000 a year which Canadians will pay towards the proposed goods and services tax. All this is at the worst possible time, when one considers our poor economic outlook, not to mention the condition of our east coast fishery.
The qualification period for receiving entitlements, or the eligibility period, as the government likes to call it, for employees who in many cases lose their jobs through no fault of their own will rise dramatically. The new scale will be based on the average rate of unemployment in a given area, as was the case under the old rules. The difference is the amount of weeks required in order to qualify for entitlements.
In my own city of Hamilton, Ontario the unemployment rate for February, 1990 was 5.3 per cent. This means that under the proposed rules a person needs 20 weeks of work to qualify for entitlements, whereas under the old rules the worker needs only 14 weeks to qualify. The new rules would also mean that the same worker would receive fewer weeks of entitlements. In Hamilton, the same worker who is laid off and who would fortunately have 20 weeks of work under his belt would receive only 17 weeks of compensation. Under the old rules the worker would have received at least 20 weeks. This would only be the case if the person was successful in gaining employment and was able to hold the job without his job moving south of the border.
In the hard pressed regions of our country, people will find it increasingly difficult to receive entitlements, let alone find a secure job. On the east coast where the government has sold out the Atlantic fishery, workers will now be required to have 14 weeks of employment compared to only 10 weeks under the previous rules. The Conservative government members opposite ask the question: What is so wrong with these changes?
The Senate has made it all very clear. In its amendments the Senate proposes that Ottawa continue to guarantee the annual $2.4 billion federal subsidy to the system rather than allow the cost to be put on to the backs of the Canadian workers and their employers. The amendments would also stop the government from making it harder to obtain entitlements in areas of high

March 13, 1990
Government Orders
unemployment and from cutting the time that make recipients eligible.
The government House leader said: "The Senate is acting as if it forgets who won the 1984 and 1988 elections." I ask this: Who gave this government the mandate to carry out this system of injustice? I also ask this: Why has the unemployment rate in St. John's, Newfoundland risen from 10.4 per cent last year to 13.2 per cent this year? Because the Conservative government has abandoned the east coast.
Out west in the prairies the government has abandoned the family farm. In some cases workers there will now need 18 weeks of employment to qualify for entitlements, instead of only 12 weeks which is presently the case. Clearly, under the Conservative government Canadians end up paying more and getting less.
Let there be no mistake, we are not talking about hand-outs here. We are talking about payments from insurance premiums. Canadian workers pay into the system with their own money. As we know, the system would be sustained by workers and employers under the new system. So when a person is laid off in St. John's, Newfoundland or Victoria or Hamilton they expect to be covered until they find a new job. This legislation changes the system of redistribution of wealth in this country.
For example, let us take the present crisis in Atlantic Canada. What happens to the young couple with two children when both parents have finally succeeded in getting a job in the local fish plant but suddenly find themselves out of a job after five weeks of work? Because of Conservative government mismanagement this family of four would be in jeopardy because the two parents would not have had enough weeks to qualify for the entitlements for which they had paid.
There is one person from Newfoundland with a terrific job, but whom voters would certainly like to forget. I am speaking of the Minister for International Trade. It was he who, during the 1988 election campaign, promised that no new changes were planned for the unemployment insurance program.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-NON-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Did he say that?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-NON-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext: I have the exact quote. He said: "No one is planning any changes in the UIC program. There has not been any change proposed to us since we dealt with the Forget commission. We are not contemplating any changes."

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-NON-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext: I can't believe he said that.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-NON-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
What deception. What deceit. The truth is that the government is using the pretext of "adjustment" to finance its deficit reduction plan, which is not really a plan at all since it cannot control it all at the expense of unemployed Canadians.
The government claims that the solution to unemployment will be training programs for the unemployed. Are the unemployed supposed to be thrilled and excited about this? The Conservative government's much talked about training programs are a sham if there are no jobs to be filled. The Conservative government's programs rank sixth in terms of content and effectiveness when compared to programs of OECD countries.
Hard working Canadians will pay for training without any assurance that they will benefit from that training. The idea of training workers is also tied into the concept of education, research and development. The more basic education a person has the easier he or she is to train. The more research and development there is in the country the more spin-offs and jobs are likely to be created. However, under successive Conservative budgets these two important features of growth in our society have been curtailed, slashed, cut by this government.
Under the Conservative government funding for research and development has decreased. Prior to the 1984 election campaign the Prime Minister made all kinds of spending commitments and promises. He said that, if elected, he would double Canada's R and D effort by the end of his first mandate.
However, the percentage of Canada's Gross Domestic Product spent on R and D fell from 1.37 per cent in 1984 to 1.32 per cent in 1988, and is expected to be lower still in 1989 figures. In fact, Canada's R and D efforts now rank well below the efforts of OECD industrialized nations.
Other countries know the value of research and development and know that R and D plays a great part in the strength of economies. The Canadian government
March 13, 1990

could and should play a much more active role in the promotion of research and development, as well as education.
The government likes to boast about its commitment to education. Frankly, its commitment is negligible at best. This year the Conservative government introduced massive cuts in transfer payments to the provinces, making it harder for them to finance education, among other things.
How can the government hope that Canada can have a system of full employment when it is not creating the tjqje of national infrastructure needed to promote increased growth in our country? The cumulative effect of Conservative government cuts to the provinces for post-secondary education, including R and D, up to 1989, totals $8.9 billion. In addition, the government hopes to cut over $7.4 billion to the provinces over the next five years, bringing the grand total of cuts to the provinces to over $16 billion.
I would like to return to some of the more substantive aspects of the bill and the amendments and the reason why there is all this criticism in the House tonight. Canadians should know that the amendments we are speaking about tonight were not conceived by the Senate. They are the focus, they are the pinnacle of all the information provided to it by groups and individuals with whom the Senate consulted.
But what does this government know about consultation? Labour groups from across this country have combined forces against this particular legislation. These groups representing no less than four million working Canadians believe that unemployment insurance is fundamental to the economic and social security of all Canadian workers. They believe that because of the new changes to the act workers do not have the same amount of insurance they once had. This government, if it has been able to do anything with this bill, it is to unify labour organizations against it.
Labour organizations have repeatedly tried to meet with the Minister of Employment and Immigration, but without success. The minister turns her back on millions of Canadian workers, not only by altering the system of federalism, as one labour official put it, but by refusing Canadians the democratic right to be heard. We do not have to go into that again tonight when we are dealing with this motion of closure, when we are forced to have
Government Orders
our say within just a few hours when the government lowers the boom and that is all there is to be said.
Once again the Conservative government is proceeding blindly toward a dark future for the Canadian worker. The labour movement is also questioning, and rightly so, the restructuring of our social fabric, the very system of redistributing wealth in this country.
Not only does this legislation alter the concept of universality, but it could have the effect of physically breaking apart communities in this nation. By placing such rigid and strict conditions on Canadian workers, the government is effectively saying to them: "If you can't find work in your community where you may be a boy scout leader, where you may be a ball team coach, where you may be teaching kids ballet, then you have to move to Toronto, or you have got to move to Montreal. You have got to move to where the jobs are".
A healthy country, a country that shares in understanding of redistributing the wealth from central Canada to those regions that need our support, through no fault of their own-they are unemployed because of work being seasonal by nature-must depend on a strong local economy, wherever that may be in this country. They have got to remain healthy.
Bill C-21 all but destroys what is left of small town Canada. What is to become of our country? Thank God for the other place, that House of sober second thought.

speakeroldname: Mr. John A. MacDougall (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-NON-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to speak tonight. The government has listened seriously to the recommendations offered by the Senate with regard to Bill C-21. While there are many concerns which all members should have about many of the suggestions in the message that is before us, some recommendations are worth including in Bill C-21.
For example, we recognize the impact which illiteracy has on Canadian workers and employers. The lack of basic skills is an impediment to further training.
I would like to take a moment to review the region of the country that I represent, an area where the resource base industries are the backbone of the community. It is an area where we have good times and bad times. In fact it is an area where we are going through some very

March 13, 1990
Government Orders
difficult times. The reason for that is that northern Ontario and regions such as northern Ontario rely heavily on mining, forestry and agriculture. In these three areas families in my riding have grown up. They have been part of the mining community, part of the forestry community and part of the agricultural community. Their grandfather, their father and now their son have had the opportunity to work in these areas.
In areas such as mine the opportunity of being paid well is recognized. The pay in these areas is usually substantial. The opportunity is there to work in the mines for a very healthy wage as long as you are 16 or 17 years old. The thoughts and the feelings of individuals over that timeframe is that they never have to worry, that they will have a job in the mine until they retire. This has been the feeling for the last 50 years in my area. The same is true in the forestry sector.
But times have changed, and in changing times technology changes. One of the greatest problems we face with the adjustment of the unemployed in northern Ontario and across the country is that the technologies that they have learned, whether it was 20 years in a mine or 25 years in a sawmill, have changed. A lot of these workers dropped out of school with very little education. Their only skills were acquired in the job that they are doing. The unfortunate part for them in terms of training is that there was never an opportunity for them to take part in it.
For that reason the idea in the first recommendation is worth including in this bill.
The senators have said that they welcome the commitment of the government to produce an annual plan which will show members how UI funds will be spent to train and develop people. That is what we are looking at in the riding of Timiskaming where individuals have worked in the mining community where technology is now changing and advancing. We are in a competitive world. We are no longer looking just at northern Ontario having a gold mine. We are working on an international basis where we have to be competitive. Because technology changes are before us we have to be able to spend money in training and developing people for that. The
same is true for the agriculture or the forestry side of things.
In recommendation 4 senators have asked us to amend the bill to ensure that the minister will provide specific details in this plan.
It will do no one good to create centralized plans which are too rigid or detailed to respond to changing needs. It will do no good in a country this size, whether we are looking at British Columbia, Yukon, Newfoundland or northern Ontario, to have a rigid, centralized plan. That is not what we should be looking at. At the same time a reasonable level of detail should be provided. Therefore the response the government proposes to the Senate's suggestion is a fair one.
In the eighth recommendation the Senate has also asked the House to consider removing a subsection of the UI act which has been in place for almost 20 years. That subsection would allow the Governor in Council to remove benefits for self-employed fishermen from the UI act at any time.
With the concern shared by ail Canadians for the problems in the fishing industry, the request for added protection for these benefits is understandable. The message which the House will send to the Senate should accommodate these improvements in Bill C-21.
But much of what is in the message from the Senate cannot be accepted. We have been given a set of recommendations by a Senate which is dominated by Liberals which do nothing more than tie the hands of the government. These amendments would force us to spend money which we do not have, in ways which may not be the best for the working people who will be helped by Bill C-21.
The second recommendation would make the government use money from the Consolidated Revenue Fund to pay for training courses for unemployed people and for new measures like allowing claimants to use funds to start businesses.
The Senate seems to believe that the only purpose for UI is to pay people to wait for their old jobs to come back.
I have been here since 1982.1 have had the opportunity in that number of years to deal with unemployment problems in my riding. Between 1982 and 1984, I sat in opposition. I had the opportunity to see the government of the day giving out job-creation programs. These
March 13, 1990

programs back then applied, as long as you cut grass, cut trees, painted fences or shovelled snow. That was the policy of the day. It gave you a period of time in which to collect these benefits, so that maybe if you were fortunate enough you could go back to work at your old job.
We believe that UI needs to become an active program which invests in people. Training courses, financial help to move to a place where there are more jobs and assisting claimants to start businesses are wise investments.
When this government took power in 1984 we were concerned with giving people the opportunity to get out of that unemployment trap.
Prior to the Conservative government taking power in 1984, 89 per cent of the jobs created by the then Liberal government were part-time jobs. That means that individuals had to work for three months or six months, and in that time frame they may have had the opportunity to go back to their old job, or maybe they did not. Maybe they were unemployed and looking for another program that they could get involved with again.
Since 1984, 85 per cent of the jobs that this government has created are full-time jobs. That involves 1.5 million people who are working today, more than had been working in 1984. Some 948,000, or 60 per cent of them, are women. When Flora MacDonald was the Minister of Employment and Immigration, she set out the guidelines for this government for what we believe is the way that we should be going. She set up the Canadian Jobs Strategy, giving the opportunity to Canadians who wanted to work to be retrained. Under that program we developed Communities Futures where it is the local people who are involved. They know what the concerns of the regions are, whether it is in Timiskaming, St. John's, Newfoundland or Whitehorse. Those are the individuals who know what adjustments should be made. In my area I have four of them and they work very, very well.
We are looking at retraining so that those individuals who happen to be laid off, unfortunately, have the opportunity to be retrained for a full-time job. We also
Government Orders
look into job development, a program that works very, very well to ensure that individuals will have that opportunity for whatever areas they are looking at. Industrial adjustment programs give the opportunity to the employer, the employee and government to work together.
I think that Bill C-21 does an awful lot to adjust. One area that I look at which is of great concern in regions such as mine is in regard to those who are unemployed. A region such as mine stretches over a vast area with a very low population but ties it to cities such as North Bay and Timmins where the unemployment numbers under the old bill have us tied to the good economic times there. So they are not really sound figures in terms of those who may be unemployed in the area.
Bill C-21 gives us the opportunity to ensure that exact numbers will be shown and that those who require the unemployment insurance plan will have it there.
The third recommendation stops the government from developing innovative approaches to getting people back to work. It also offers new appeal rights to claimants which will make the system more complicated. There are just two more examples of how the Liberals in the Senate are willing to play games with the unemployed.
What we are dealing with is individuals who are in .really hard times, individuals who do need help.
When the government introduced the Labour Force Development Strategy it did so to help both the unemployed and Canadian business by creating a better match between skills employers need skills workers have.
Sometimes, the things which will produce the best results do not fit all the demands of the UI act. For example, if a person is starting a business they are not eligible for UI. Bill C-21 gives us the flexibility to make UI more responsive to today's needs by experimenting with new and better ways of helping the unemployed.
While much of what the Senate wants to do in its fourth recommendation on the government's annual developmental plan for UI can be supported, one aspect certainly cannot. The Senate wants the power to approve or reject the plan. No one in this House can seriously accept the need for such a new power.

March 13, 1990
Government Orders
The fifth amendment cuts back one of the basic principles behind the bill by relaxing the penalties for people who quit their jobs without just cause or who are fired for misconduct. In response to sincere concerns about the definition of just cause for quitting a job, the House approved the amendments of the Minister of Employment and Immigration to Bill C-21 to ensure that people would not be penalized unfairly. The Liberal dominated Senate wants to change this House's decision to strengthen the penalties for people who quit. They want to send a signal to people that it is all right to quit jobs because UI will pay. In my mind that is like looking for cash for life. We must reject this type of thinking.
The sixth recommendation from the Senate demands that payments made to groups who manage programs for unemployed people be paid from the developmental uses budget of the UI. This government has been steadily improving the responsiveness of training programs ever since it was elected. We have many partners in designing and delivering these programs, such as community training groups which include employers and educators.
In my own area we have taken training programs with regard to miners in order to give them the opportunity to upgrade their skills so that with the new technology out there they are able to go to new modern mines where they can get full-time employment. A lot of mines have been open for 35 or 40 years and use old technology. Once they close down individuals do not have that new technology. The same can be said about a waferboard plant in my area. We are looking at developing a program with the company, the employees and government to ensure that with the new technology that is now available these employees will have an opportunity to retrain.
We can look at heavy equipment operators of which there is always a shortage. I could on with a long list of opportunities in which the government is working with community training groups to ensure that the opportunity of full-time stable jobs will be there.
When these groups perform services on our behalf, it is only fair to charge those costs to the UI account in the same way. That is all the clause that we are talking about was designed to do.
Recommendation 7 would do one thing, but one thing with a major impact on the country's deficit. It would force the government to pay a large share of the costs of the unemployment insurance with money that we do not
have. No one can seriously suggest that the government should spend money on a program just because it used to do so. Yet the Liberals in the Senate are willing to see the deficit rise by more than $1.5 billion a year for a range of amendments in its message to this House.
What we are dealing with is fairness. We are dealing with a major problem that faces this country. This is a problem which causes us to adjust our entire workforce, a problem which which is causing us to adjust to the climate around the world. This is nothing new. It is happening in other parts of the country and around the world. The old mentality of spending money to get out of the problem will not work. The Liberal-dominated Senate is willing to spend money but it is not recommending what the proposals should be.
With recommendation 8 we return to the grab for power which the Liberal senators are making. This government is willing to amend the UI act to better protect fishermen, a group whose benefits have not been touched by this bill. It cannot be willing to go along with a scheme to play political games with the government's ability to make regulations.
The House of Commons cannot permit the Senate to expand its powers.
The ninth recommendation would reverse a decision of this House. We agreed in this place that the cost of UI should be borne by those who benefit, workers and employers. The Liberal-dominated Senate again disagrees. When everyone in Canada seems to understand the deficit must be controlled, they are willing to spend and see it go up and up.
The bill which this House passed was a sincere attempt to balance many different interests in order to improve UI in a realistic way. The amendments which the government is offering in response to the message from the Senate are part of that improvement.
However, we must reject amendments from the Liberal senators who are content to act irresponsibly to increase the deficit, remove innovation from the program and delay needed changes. This House must say no to these games.
Bill C-21 is designed to encourage more and better training of working people by the private sector. C-21 is designed to use UI funds to create new opportunities for jobs and to make UI a more active program. This is a major improvement over confining UI to passive, reactive measures. But UI is still a program which is
March 13, 1990

responsive to the different employment needs of communities, across this country.
The government has ensured that UIC is a response to the regions needs. In areas where unemployment is high the vast majority of claimants will not see any changes in their benefits. We recognize that many of the jobs in areas such as Cape Breton, my homeland, western Newfoundland and northern Ontario, where I live, are important to the people of the communities. UIC is another important form of income support. For this reason people in these areas with higher levels of unemployment will still need and will be able to get unemployment qualification benefits.
I am honoured to have had the opportunity to speak tonight. I think it is vital that we pass this bill, that we deal with the opportunities for stability in this country in retraining, and that we give Canadians the much needed changes in the Unemployment Insurance Act.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-NON-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to rise to speak on this bill and in particular on the amendments proposed by the upper House to Bill C-21, an act to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act and the Employment and Immigration Department and Commission Act.
I should like to begin by addressing the amendments very specifically. Amendment 1 seeks to include literacy instruction in the training programs provided for under this bill. I fully support this amendment. Illiteracy creates a great obstacle to those who need a higher level of training to adjust successfully to economic changes in Canada. As the world advances toward a highly technological state, workers will need to be able to read and write if they are to meet the challenges that lie ahead.
Thus workers on unemployment insurance who need basic skills must be allowed access to this type of training while receiving unemployment insurance benefits.
Amendment 2, dealing with the development uses provisions, seeks to ensure that the government finds a better way of financing an increased training level of the Canadian workforce than by redirecting moneys away from the unemployed. Using funds from the unemployment insurance program to purchase training courses, to start a business or to provide income support to those
Government Orders
who are temporarily unemployed undermines the program's basic role.
Amendment 3 also deals with the developmental assistance provisions. These provisions are the primary benefits that the unemployed would be paying for through drastic cuts to their benefits. The bill gives the commission great latitude on the details of the developmental assistance programs and hence the commission in the future might be able to do things contrary to requirements generally set out in the Unemployment Insurance Act.
Amendment 4 deals with clause 20 of the bill. This deals with the preparation of an annual plan to provide an estimate of total unemployment insurance expenditures and of total expenditures on developmental uses.
Because the reporting requirements are lax, there is the possibility that money used for training might be reallocated from one region to another. The amendment calls for more detail in the plan so that expenditures will be shown for each province and for each unemployment insurance region and that distribution of funds can be monitored.
Further, the amendment includes a provision ensuring that members of Parliament and senators have an opportunity to approve the plan.
Amendment 5 seeks to keep the disqualification period for people who leave their jobs without just cause to a maximum of six weeks rather than have a disqualification period of seven to twelve weeks as proposed in Bill C-21.
By imposing a minimum disqualification period higher than the present maximum, the government is telling workers that they must remain tied to their jobs regardless of the circumstances. This is unacceptably restrictive and could lead those employees who suffer some form of harassment to remain on the job despite intolerable circumstances because they fear losing all income support for up to three months.
Amendment 6 seeks to ensure that the costs of contracting out, as allowed for under Bill C-21, be charged to the new "developmental uses" portion of the unemployment insurance fund. This is to ensure that such contracting out would fall inside the 15 per cent limit for developmental uses so as not to further erode the proportion of the unemployment insurance fund reserved for direct income maintenance payments to the

March 13, 1990
Government Orders
unemployed. It would also prevent too much privatization of the program.
Amendment 7 seeks to prevent the government from obtaining financial immunity contained in Bill C-21. The government has been a financial contributor to the unemployment insurance fund since it began in 1940. In the 1980s the government paid approximately 23 per cent of total program costs per year. Yet, in the 1990 budget the government announced that effective January 1, 1990 all unemployment insurance expenditures would be financed by premiums alone.
Yet the requirement for federal government contributions is the key to the success of our present unemployment insurance program. The withdrawal of government financing would move us closer to the inferior American model.
The federal government has a responsibility to address regional disparities and to help bear the costs of increases in unemployment which often results from government policies. Thus federal fundings must be maintained.
Amendment 8 seeks to ensure that steps are taken to protect benefits now provided to self-employed fishermen and to ensure that the government is committed to maintaining this vital program.
The Unemployment Insurance Act was amended in 1956 to extend coverage to self-employed fishermen and to provide that the government, not the unemployment insurance fund, was responsible for making up the difference between premiums collected and benefits paid to self-employed fishermen. Bill C-21 proposes to place the full cost of fishermen's benefits on the UI fund which, as I have already pointed out, is to be financed by employee-employer premium contributions alone. Thus the full cost of the fishermen's benefits would be borne by all other contributors to the fund.
I would like to quote the following statement of the Fishermen, Food and Allied Workers Union: "Business groups will be fighting tooth and nail in the years to come to take the position that since the government is out they regard themselves as having to subsidize fishermen's unemployment insurance and they will say this is not fair and we want out".
At a time when the Atlantic fisheries are in crisis the government should be furthering its support, not withdrawing it. Hence I fully support amendment 8.
Amendment 9, the last amendment, deals with variable entrance requirement. It was introduced to the unemployment insurance program to link regional unemployment conditions to the number of weeks of insurable employment required to qualify for benefits. As the unemployment rate of a region increased, the number of weeks of insurable employment necessary to qualify for benefits decreased. But this variable entrance requirement has been allowed to lapse by this government and so, since January 6, 1990, a uniform 14-week entrance requirement is in effect for all regions of the country irrespective of their levels of unemployment. That is definitely unfair.
Bill C-21 proposes a 62-region system and in only 8 of these regions would the 10-week minimum apply. Under the old rules the minimum would have applied in 32 regions.
The proposed changes to the number of weeks a claimant may receive unemployment insurance would reduce the maximum duration of benefit entitlement in most cases. For example, in the region of southern Manitoba, in my home province, claimants would lose up to 13 weeks of benefits.
The government is implying that unemployed people are in a position of their own making and with proper incentives could find jobs. Such thinking misses the point. It is not incentives that are necessary but jobs themselves.
Thus I agree with Amendment 9 that Table 1 and Table 2 of Bill C-21 be modified so that the highest unemployment regions would escape the ill effects of these new government proposals.
Before the federal election in November 1988 members of this government dismissed as nonsense suggestions that the Tories had a hidden agenda to cut unemployment insurance or other social programs after the election. The government broke its promise.
During the election the government also promised to develop high quality programs to help the many people who will lose their jobs because of free trade and other
March 13, 1990

economic changes. However, rather than using funds from general revenues as is normally the case, the government will take the money away from the unemployed. That is its solution. All workers will pay for training without any assurance that they themselves will benefit from the training. Training is the responsibility of government and must be funded.
It is the poor and disadvantaged people who already have difficulties in finding secure jobs that will be hardest hit by these changes to the UI program. It is because these people are "last hired and first fired". It will be seasonal workers, young people, natives, new immigrants, new citizens, visible minorities and the disabled people who stand to suffer the most from these proposed changes. Many people in these groups unfortunately are poor and the most vulnerable.
These changes to the unemployment insurance program will also adversely affect not only the economic status but the psychological health of many Canadians. The stress of unemployment compounded by absence of benefits can lead to physical illness. Thus reductions in regular UI benefits would lead to increases in health care costs and, more important, would make more Canadians ill. This is happening at a time of reductions in financial transfer payments to the provinces for health care costs. Where is the heart of this government? How will these new costs due to the ill effects of reductions in the unemployment insurance program be absorbed?
The government has estimated that $3 million will be cut from current UI regular benefits. Since it is known that changes to the UI program will cause illnesses linked to general economic distress, there will be increases in health care costs.
This government should admit that its decision to change the UI program is not only harmful to the health of Canadians but is counterproductive economically.
I should like at this juncture to respond to the response given by the government House leader in reply to the message from the Senate respecting this Bill C-21.
I submit that the government committed some flaws and errors in logic in its analysis. I would like to point these out. First, I submit that the government is wrong in its interpretation of the application of various Standing Orders it has cited to sustain its position. There is nothing in Standing Orders 79(1), 79(2) and 79(3) and
Government Orders
Standing Orders 80(1) and 80(2) that prohibit the Senate from making amendments.
It is clear from the intent of these Standing Orders that only the House of Commons has the right to decide on matters of expenditure.
The Senate proposed certain amendments that this House may decide upon. The Senate never intended to take away from the House the power to decide. The House could decide and should decide. There is a difference between the power to propose amendments and the power to decide on the substance of those amendments.
I therefore ask the House to pass judgment on the merits of these amendments to which I have alluded earlier. Whether the proposed amendment is to get funding from the Consolidated Revenue Fund and whether it is in the best interests of Canadians and the program are the questions that this government must answer. This government can decide if it wants to; the government cannot hide behind a technicality. The government's interpretation of the Standing Orders on the application of these amendments is also wrong.
Second, the government is attempting to camouflage its difficulties to be accountable to the people respecting the absence of heart with which it has produced this bill. It tries to deflect this uncaring attitude by discussing the accountability of the other place to the people.
The government appears to say that because members of the other place are not elected they are therefore not accountable to anyone for their actions. The other place, whether or not the government likes it, is responsible to the people of Canada to exercise sober and serious thought on bills sent to it by this House. This is a constitutional requirement.
Would the government try to insinuate that the Supreme Court of Canada, because it is also an appointed body, is not accountable to the people? Surely no one would make that suggestion. We should debunk once and for all the fallacy of using the non-elective nature of the constitutional Senate as the basis for saying that it is not accountable to the people.
If I may add, if there is really no place for the Senate why has the Prime Minister continued to appoint members to the Senate? The House and the government must not continue to sing the song and dance the dance

March 13, 1990
Government Orders
about the Senate. It must address the real issues that the amendments bring to this House.
I submit that the sentiments echoed by the proposed amendments coming from the other place are the sentiments coming from the people of our country.
I would like to ask the following question: Which should prevail-the heartless principle of the bill where the government abdicates its responsibility for funding, or the caring principle for Canadians who deserve in moments of difficulties due to unemployment which is not of their own making direct funding benefits from this government? You will agree. Madam Speaker, that a heartless principle must at once surrender itself to a principle that cares.
Bill C-21, if not amended, is fundamentally unsound. It is basically unkind and fails to echo the conscience of Canadians. The proposed amendments from the other place restore the kindness and reflect the sentiments of many Canadians. We heard submissions from a coalition of union movements and from church organizations, telling us what to do or what to tell the government to do. Those sentiments are embodied in the proposed amendments coming from the other place. We should thank the Senate for its boldness and sensitivity.
Perhaps I may conclude with a quotation from the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops. Monsignor Charles Valois appeared before the Senate committee and said:
The federal proposals contained in Bill C-21 are based on a disturbing hypothesis. Human labour and workers are viewed as a commodity to be bought and sold, recycled, moved or removed from the market-Emasculating the unemployment insurance plan at the very time when it is most needed is unacceptable morally and politically.
That is the challenge to this government: accept the amendments from the Senate and the government will be doing what Canadians want it to do.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Reid (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-NON-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise tonight to speak on Bill C-21, a piece of legislation that has attracted a lot of attention in this country. Needless to say, it has attracted a lot of attention in my own province of Newfoundland and Labrador.
Questions have arisen about what the government has done with this legislation. I note that the questions have risen as to whether or not the government had what some call a mandate.
There are certainly lots of quotations floating around about who said what and when. This government has made a commitment and I think most governments have probably shared the commitment. This government before the last election made a very clear commitment that it would move to improve social programs, that programs which needed to be made better to help Canadians in a more effective way for the benefit of as many Canadians as possible would be part of the agenda of this government.
I believe Bill C-21 addresses that. Bill C-21 looks at some of the fundamental differences between this government and my friends opposite. My friends opposite would have us say to Canadians: "You have what you have now and, despite all that is happening in the world, despite the changes in the world, we are not going to make it any better. We are going to leave you where you are now". Everyone tells me that the unemployment insurance system should be changed.
I would like to see much broader changes in the unemployment insurance system. I would like to see a whole different system. I recognize that that day is not here right now. I do not think this House is ready for that. I do not think this country is ready for that, but it will come with time. The essence is to keep moving, keep changing and keep evolving because that is what will lead to develop of social programs for Canadians that in the long run are the programs we need to meet their needs.
My friend for Gander-Grand Falls this afternoon was very good as usual, erudite and certainly on occasion came close to fact and dealt with realities. He said a number of things that unfortunately had been said repeatedly in my province and bear some correction. There have been a number of things said in a number of places. I just want to touch on a couple of them just to make sure we are talking about the same thing. This is not a judgment question particularly. This is what is happening.
For most of the people in my province, if the government can have this legislation passed, if the will of this House is respected and Bill C-21 becomes law, we will have a variable entrance requirement which recognizes that in certain parts of the country people are more
March 13, 1990

disadvantaged and there are less opportunities to work. If the legislation can be passed into law, the people in my province for the most part will need 10 weeks to qualify, which is what it is today.
I would be dishonest if I said we have not changed the benefit period. The benefit period has been affected. If you add up in the standard way the qualifying period, the penalty period and the benefit period, you arrive at 51 weeks. The average period on benefit in Newfoundland and Labrador is something less than 30 weeks. A remarkably few number of people go straight through the system and a surprising number who do requalify. Let us be sensible; 51 weeks is what we are talking about.
We heard today about the line with great expression and movement of arms and hands. It depends on what side of the line you live. The law says it is where you live, not where you work.
It has always been that way. To suggest that this legislation changes that is ridiculous, but we get this great expanse of toing and froing and moaning about how the line changes and you have to qualify where you live. It has always been that way. Nothing has changed.
I appeared with the committee when it was in St. John's, and one thing we were consistently told was that you have to change the economic regions. What is happening is that with the three economic regions in Newfoundland and Labrador, we had the city of St. John's with its unacceptably high but relatively low unemployment rate affecting the rest of the Avalon Peninsula. Therefore the people on Bell Island where the unemployment rate is tragically at 75 per cent were having to qualify with the same conditions as the people of St. John's where the unemployment rate was somewhat under 10 per cent for a while. Under the old regulations you would go from 10 weeks needed to qualify all of a sudden to 16 weeks. I cannot call that fair. That is not responsible. That does not let people plan. That does not let people know what is happening in their lives, so we changed the boundaries.
No constituency in Newfoundland was affected more than mine. No people were more divided than those in my riding. I will say that I supported what the unions, the labour councils and many others said to the committee in St. John's, which was change the line, because we have to

recognize the economic realities. People have the opportunity to get employment.
The response of the government was to address the needs of those who needed it the most. When my friend talks about the line and and moving things around, we must be clear that it has always been that way and nothing has changed.

We face some very difficult economic challenges with the crisis in our fishery. We see one-industry towns come under attack. We must have flexibility for our workers, options for people to deal with, options before us so that we can put together packages. More and more we are seeing government departments combining their resources and combining their programs. More and more we are seeing federal and provincial governments able to put different pieces together to come up with solutions to our problems.

Mr. Speaker, I hope my friend from St. John's East will stay a minute. My colleague from Nickel Belt in the New Democratic Party has given me the opportunity to speak behind my friend from St. John's East. Let me say to my friend from St. John's East and say to the House that I first met this gentleman when he was still at a young and tender and unsullied age. He was but a young 15 or 16-year old. He was sitting across the floor from me in

the Colonial Building in the youth Parliament of Newfoundland and Labrador.
In those days when passion burned in his veins, when his blood ran hot, when the salt-water boiled up and demanded to be heard, it was not as a defender of a corrupt and bankrupt regime that he spoke but as a Newfoundlander who believed in his people and demanded to be heard. The fundamental change that has occurred, and he bears a heavy burden-it is a heavy cross that he carries now-is that once as a young and sullied Newfoundlander he was a voice for Newfoundland wherever he would be heard. He has now become the apologist of Ottawa to Newfoundland in the House of Commons. I want to tell him the apology just expressed will not be accepted by the people of Newfoundland and Labrador.
What are the facts? This member rises up to his full height, an inch or two shorter than me, and with his greatest of indignation tells Parliament and through Parliament the people of Canada what a great and wonderful thing is being done for the people of Newfoundland. They are being trained. How wonderful. He cited two examples of four fellows fixing up a church and a couple of other people going through a genetic lab at Memorial University.
Not a word was heard from the member for St. John's East about the people on the great northern peninsula of Newfoundland and the historic community of Port au Choix who cling to the rocks with their fingernails on the edge of the ocean trying to scrape a living from the land and the sea. Not a word for them.
Not a word for the people who live on the south coast of Newfoundland, not the city of St. John's, but the south coast of Newfoundland where there is not even a road connection. St. John's is but a blast they have to endure nightly on the local news.
Not a word for them nor a word for the people on Twillingate Island on the northeast coast, nor a word for the people of Lock Harbour and the Bay of Islands, nor a single uttered word for the people of La Scie on the Baie Verte peninsula. He has got two examples in St. John's of training programs. Of course what is good enough for St. John's is good enough for all of Newfoundland. I am here to tell him that Newfoundland is not our echo of what is good for St. John's.
I want to tell the member for St. John's East that if he wants to deal in fact, deal in fact. When it comes to rhetoric those of us from Newfoundland are quite capable of matching the rhetoric that has been heaved across this floor.
What are the facts? A $51 million cut to the province of Newfoundland and Labrador. That is the fact. Fifty-one million dollars. The member opposite wants us to get so caught up in his emotion that we will allow, happily, $51 million to slip out of the pockets, not of those who have in Newfoundland, not out of the pockets of the merchants of Newfoundland, not out of the pockets of the academics at university with their sinecure, safe and secure jobs, good people that they are, not out of the pockets of the bureaucracy of Newfoundland, the people who administer these wonderful training programs, not out of the pockets of the Crosbies of the world, but out of the pockets of the poorest of the poor in Newfoundland.
And there is not a word from the member for St. John's East for the poorest of the poor. We have just heard from a member whom I instinctively and intrinsically generally have some empathy for, because I think he is in a hell of spot, defending this regime. The tragedy is that his own area, the Avalon Peninsula, is that part of Newfoundland most devastated by Bill C-21. It is the area which sees the greatest increase in the requirements for qualification for UI, and there is not a word from that member.
Let us talk about these training programs. You have rural communities where unemployment, seasonally, is 50 per cent. And some bespectacled young fellow, well intentioned, shows up from the local CEIC office because he has a mandate from Ottawa. God knows, he knows it is a fool's errand but, nevertheless, it is his mandate and he must carry it out. He walks up onto the local wharf and he says: "Boys, we are going to train you. And if you can develop a training program, we are going to give you some financial support. And if you cannot develop a training program, we cannot help you".
Well, what has happened? With very rare exceptions, and there are a couple of rare exceptions, we have either seen areas that traditionally have shared in a national program and played a role in a useful national program, being cut out of it entirely, because they do not happen to have a technical college on their doorstep, or we have seen farcical training programs designed merely to quali-

fy and to get access to some community development funds. That is what has happened all too often, in rural Newfoundland.
It takes the nerve of a severe toothache to stand in this House, to be from Newfoundland, and be engaged in the political life of the province, to have a degree of awareness about the political life of the province, and to suggest that there are some great and wondrous training programs going on in Newfoundland today. That is a farce. That is not true. That is a false representation of the facts. That is a distortion of reality. It is a disservice to the people of Newfoundland and Labrador, to make that kind of suggestion in this House.
I know my colleague opposite from St. John's East must be severely out of touch, must have breathed too much of the rarefied air, must have been so moved by the splendour of this Chamber and the stained glass windows that reality has become distorted for him, as he looks at these programs with rose-tinted glasses. I know that in a serious, sober and honest moment, having been exposed to the light of day, the member for St. John's East could never make such a foolish and wanton declaration of nonsense in this House of Commons. I know that for a fact, Mr. Speaker. I am hoping he goes home soon and stands on the leeside of Bell Island, in a strong wind and clears his brain of these foolish notions.
So what is the reality? What is happening is that an otherwise fine human being, an otherwise decent individual whose instincts, although they have been absolutely repressed, are otherwise right, has been corrupted by the necessity of defending the indefensible. That is what has happened. Members opposite are being forced to stand on their hind legs-and when they are from the opposite side it is their hind legs that they stand on, whereas for most of us it is just two-and defend the indefensible.
This is a government that is being driven by budget considerations to slash spending. There is no over-all economic policy here. There is no over-all social plan here. There is no over-all determination to train people and make them more employable here. There is merely a Minister of Finance who said, "I need $2 billion". And having declared he is going to cut $2 billion, he then left

it to the Minister of Employment and Immigration to impose those cuts.
The Government of Canada is getting out of the business of unemployment insurance.
That is important to me because as a Newfoundlander I recall the words of the Minister for International Trade, the member for St. John's West, the mentor of the member for St. John's East, who said in advance of the election campaign that the government had no plan whatsoever, not the slightest notion of changing the unemployment insurance program. It is the same gentleman who was trotted out to say that there was going to be no change and no cuts to education spending, who also said that there was going to be no cuts to health care. He told us there would be no cuts to Canada's social programs. It would not happen. None of this was part and parcel of the free trade deal. There would be no cuts to transportation subsidies. What do we have? We have here the completion of the free trade pact. He does not want to be seen to be negotiating away health care so the government cut it unilaterally. He did not wish to be seen negotiating away education so he cut it unilaterally. Nobody will ever accuse the Minister for International Trade of having negotiated away our social programs at the table with the Americans in definition of subsidy because we gave it all away in advance. We destroyed those programs.
It is a transparent and desperate measure. This government knows that the people of Canada will rise in literal rebellion as they see the nature and the collective values of this nation, that which distinguishes us from our neighbours to the south, being destroyed at a negotiating table. The way to avoid that spectacle is to give all of those programs away and destroy them in the name of budget cuts. The government can then tell the Americans that we don't need to negotiate UIC, we're out of the business. We don't need to talk about regional development programs because we are out of the business. We don't need to worry about tourism develop-

ment because we are out of the business. We are now imposing cuts so that within a few years we will have a privatized health care system.
Do you know what else? Universities cannot afford to function any more because we have cut them too. I will bet you they will be privatized in short order. So you do not need to negotiate away our so-called intervention in the economy because we got out of our participation as a government in the economy. The job is done.
Now that is what is going on in every walk of Canadian life. It is not the disappearance of government initiatives that we have seen. It is not a reduction in the bottom line deficit that we are seeing. Although in individual terms it is, it is not even the disappearance of necessary dollars from the pockets of those most poor amongst us that we are seeing.
What we are seeing is the evaporation of what makes Canada a country, what distinguishes us from every other nation of the world and in particular our neighbour to the south. We are seeing the evaporation of the kind of mentality and values that make me as a Newfoundlander proud to say that as proud as I am to be a Newfoundlander, I am prouder still to be a Canadian because I share some values with people from every province and every region of Canada. I have them in common and I know that together, collectively, we build a better country.
Those values are being eroded. No amount of rhetoric by members opposite, no amount of smoke and mirrors, no attempt to try and sell this as a training program, and no attempt to try and convince those who are being affected that somehow their lot is being improved will change that. This government has given up on Canada. It sees this nation merely as so many bits and pieces on a monopoly board to be manipulated to suit the bottom line.
We in the province of Newfoundland, and I know all of my colleagues in this party and those with some better sense in this place, reject that kind of vision for Canada because that is no vision for Canada.
There has been a lot of debate in this place about the role of the Senate with respect to Bill C-21. There has been a lot of debate about whether or not the Senate should supersede the rights of Parliament and so on.
Let me say that I accept, embrace and endorse the notion, unquestionably, that the elected member, those who are directly accountable to the people, have a role in
the government of this land that cannot be shared in equal measure by those who are appointed to the Senate. I do not dispute that.
Let me say that when you see your country, not slowly, not bit by bit, but in giant leaps being dissipated, when you see the glue that holds us together being melted, when you see the pieces that make a whole beginning become askew, when you see neighbour turn against neighbour-and that is what has happened in Canada- because there is such profound frustration with the government that people have exercised that frustration and have made it felt by turning on their neighbours- and when you hear communities say: "We are English only" others say: "We are French only" others taking up petitions protesting by the tens of thousands our visible minorities in this nation, it represents a profound sense of fear in the land, profound frustration. Canadians know they do not have the opportunity to cast judgment on this government for two and a half years, and in their anger and frustration and, yes, in their fear, neighbour has turned against neighbour.
If we in our party have a message for this government and for the people of Canada it is this: That we will use every legitimate means at our disposal as a party and we make no apologies to stopping this kind of legislation, to amending this kind of legislation, to reforming this kind of legislation. We know there are Canadians out there who are frustrated, feeling abandoned by their national government, who we know have a sense that that which they have held dear, and those values that we have collectively embraced are disappearing. We say to them: Do not despair. Do not turn neighbour against neighbour. Do not become intolerant of those who are different. Maintain that sense of what you want your community and your province and your country to be. Join with us in fighting this policy not only in Bill C-21 but, in fact, right across the board to rewrite the values of Canada, to reduce this nation to nothing other than a piece of real estate on a monopoly board, to reduce our values to dollars and cents, to reduce this nation to a piece of merchandise, to be marketed, sold and where every program, every group and every region has a financial value attached.
No country can survive if we measure those who make a contribution to it purely in financial terms. No country can prosper if we attach a miniscule value to those who live in the last outpost and the farthest outreaches of the land. The citizens who live on the bill of Cape St. George, the citizens who live on Cape Spear, that piece
March 13, 1990

of Canadian real estate reaching farthest out into the Atlantic Ocean, for those who live in Prince Rupert or Smithers on the other side, those who live in Chimo in Quebec or in Iqaluit on Baffin Island, the value they bring to this country and the contribution they make to this country is every bit as important as that contribution of any citizen who has the privilege to occupy a seat in this place.
When we make national programs we must make those programs bearing in mind that Canadians live in communities from sea to sea, and that the flag of Canada must be raised and raised with pride in every one of those communities and that when the Government of Canada makes policy, it must reach out to people in every part of this land. We must understand always that the inherent wisdom, the native intelligence, wit and brilliance of those people who live in our rural economies and rural communities are not fooled by this defence of Bill C-21 by the member for St. John's East. Let us reject this bill intelligently, or let us at least amend this bill intelligently. Let us begin to restore this tattered and
