speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-21 does more than change some of the rules of the Unemployment Insurance Act. It will implement the Labour Force Development Strategy. This strategy, as announced on April 11,1989, is an important initiative of this government and will make a real improvement in Canada's ability to compete in the world economy.
The projected expenditures under the current UI program are estimated to be $12.7 billion for 1990. There will be no change in the over-all size of the UI program once the changes have been implemented. Spending reductions within the UI will occur primarily in three areas; changes to the program entrance requirements, benefit duration and penalties for voluntary quitters without just cause.
Additional spending will be made in more generous benefits for new parents, expanded coverage to workers over age 65 and an increased use of the UI program for development purposes such as skills training.
As a former businessman and an employer, I applaud the changes that have been proposed. As an employer I was often disappointed by employees who worked only long enough to qualify for the benefits of the UIC. These changes in program entrance requirements should weed out the lazy from the system and gear it more for those for whom it was intended. Second, as an employer I was concerned by the lack of skills training available to many employees. The additional emphasis on this area through UIC will greatly address this concern.
The primary responsibility for the skills training of the employed people should rest with the employers and their workers. This government intends to stimulate their commitment by promoting and reinforcing private sector training, thereby strengthening the competitiveness of the Canadian industry.
A total of $230 million is available in the Labour Force Development Strategy to increase training activity by the private sector through co-operative programs. The government's objective is to stimulate an additional private

Government Orders
sector training effort of $1.5 billion a year by 1994 to bring the total to approximately $3 billion per year.
This increase is needed is needed to raise the relative level of Canadian private sector training to that of the United States. We are placing greater emphasis, through new UI development uses, to help the unemployed improve their job prospects through skills training, self-employment and relocation assistance. The support for training and other developmental uses will be increased from the present 2 per cent to about 10 per cent or $1.4 billion in total UI expenditures. Developmental uses of UI funds will also include such things as relocation assistance, self-employment, entrepreneurship assistance and re-employment assistance.
As I stated earlier, I have in the past been discouraged with the incentive to not work which exists in the UIC. There have been changes to the minimum requirements for qualifying for benefits which should greatly address this concern. In addition, a greater flexibility has been added to the system to compensate for regional differences in the unemployment rate. For a government which is often labelled as uncaring and unfeeling, this is a very sensitive approach to the needs of Canadians. In my province of Manitoba, the minimum requirements for receiving benefits will vaiy from 10 weeks in the north to about 18 weeks in the south where jobs are more plentiful.
According to the 1987 data, this would affect less than 1 per cent of the claimants. On total, the average number of weeks benefits that will be paid to claimants will be 35. This amounts to four months more than the average claimant uses. That is, those who are using unemployment insurance as a temporary source of income until they find a new job will see no change to the benefits available to them. However, those individuals who have taken advantage of the system will suddenly find themselves receiving fewer benefits.
I do not believe the majority of my constituents, or Canadians in general for that matter, would be offended by such a change. We have stiffened the penalty to those who quit jobs simply because life is easier on unemployment benefits. Reduction in benefits to people who voluntarily quit jobs had to happen.
However, the Liberal Senators want to change this decision. They would like to send a signal to people that it is all right to quit jobs because UI will pay. As an employer, a taxpayer, and as a member of the House of Commons, I reject that way of thinking.
Unemployment insurance exists in this country because the citizens of this nation have strongly held beliefs in the work ethic and in a sense of fair play. A person should have the right to find a job and earn a living to support a family. When that right is taken away from them, they should be provided with a temporary source of income until they can find a new job. This is the only fair and just thing to do.
However, Canadians are like-minded in their opinion of individuals who take advantage of this belief for their own personal desire to avoid working for a living. In my opinion, the changes to the UI bill are a step in the right direction, returning the UI system to its original purpose of providing income support between two jobs.
I support Bill C-21 because of this. I find myself deeply troubled by the actions being taken by the members of the other House. The Liberal has-beens in that place feel they have some inexplicable authority to override the elected House of Commons concerning the legislation of what are constitutionally referred to as money bills. I, for one, can find only two reasons for their position. It is either a question of legal authority or moral authority. On both counts, I find their reasoning lacking.
First of all, with respect to legal authority, I believe my colleague the hon. Minister of State, has clearly enunciated the weaknesses of their position. As he stated, Section 53 prohibits the Senate from amending money bills. In this regard, he noted that Standing Order 80 of the House of Commons states that only the House of Commons has the right to direct, to limit and to appoint such bills which are not alterable by the Senate. I believe that this is just too clear to even debate.
There is no doubt that Bill C-21 qualifies as a money bill as it is responsible for the collection of money from individuals for the express intent of distributing said moneys to citizens through the offices of the Receiver General. In this area the authority of the Senate would seem to be quite clear.
March 13, 1990

The Senate has argued that the Monarch and the Governor General have the right, regardless of Section 53 of the Constitution and Standing Order 80, to override all legislation from the House of Commons. In the strictest sense, they are probably correct. However, the Monarch and the Governor General no longer have the role in legislation they may have had a few centuries ago.
Obviously, the reason for this change is the democratic principle which dominates the functioning and beliefs of the society we live in today. The Senators, regardless of their misguided belief, are not elected representatives of the people of this country. Any powers they may think they have via the Constitution, are based less on sound constitutional principle and convention than they are on delusions of long-departed power.
Allowing the Senate to override the House of Commons at any time, and particularly with regard to a money bill, would set a most dangerous precedent. The principles of democracy would be completely undermined by such an action.
In this particular case, the Senate has recommended the government spend an additional $2 billion on unemployment insurance. This kind of expenditure is absolutely unacceptable in a day and age when spending restraint is essential to help this country recover from the legacy of Liberal over-spending which created our outrageous national debt.
This fiscal unacceptability of their recommendations, however, are overshadowed by their desire to exercise powers for which they have no mandate from the people of Canada. The consequences of allowing the Senate to proceed on its course unchallenged shake the very foundations of democratic principles.
As elected representatives of the people of Canada, we in this House, from all parties, cannot allow them the luxury of this one transgression. Programs spending was way out of control by 1984 when this government came to power. By that stage, the Liberals were spending $16 billion more than they were taking in in revenue.

Who did they figure was going to pay this bill? Their current recommendations indicate that they have not figured that out yet. Our government, however, has figured it out. The bill is to be paid by you, by me, and by all the citizens of this country.
Since 1984, we have taken drastic measures to correct the utter lack of respect for the taxpayers of this nation. We have turned a $16 billion annual deficit in program spending into a $9 billion surplus. Mr. Speaker, I have listened all afternoon to the debate. My friend and colleague for Gander-Grand Falls entitled his speech on Bill C-21 and the proposed amendments from the Senate, "Which Side of the Line Do You Live On". I want to make my comments in terms of "Breaking the Faith with Canadians".
The speeches this afternoon started with the government House leader. He attacked the Senate, he attacked the constitutionality of the Senate. He waxed the most eloquent I have ever heard him wax. He made a very good speech attacking the Senate. Canadians watching will think that the Senate is really the issue in this debate. I want to say at the outset very clearly that it is not the Senate. Up in northern Ontario when we are hunting moose we do not get distracted with rabbit droppings. The Senate is not the issue here, although the government would like Canadians to think it is.
The issue here is C-21; breaking the faith with the Canadian people. Why have I focused on Bill C-21? The New Democratic Party, in its criticism of C-21, correctly said that the provisions were Draconian. First of all, the government removes itself from participating in the unemployment insurance program. It is breaking the social contract, a contract which was entered into in the 1940s between government, employers and the working force of this nation. It saw its flowering, as it were, in 1971 when the then Minister of Employment and Immigration, Biyce Mackasey, introduced an amended unemployment insurance program, which is the one we have today, or had if C-21 gets passed.
In that Unemployment Insurance Act of 1971 the coverage was broadened, the contract expanded. We included school teachers, the armed forces and fishermen, and we expanded the coverage. We introduced sick benefits and maternity benefits. The government picked up the cost of the unemployment insurance program if the national unemployment level went above 4 per cent. That was the contract, a contract that said to the workforce, the working men and women of the country:
March 13, 1990

"If you become unemployed through no fault of your own, here is the safety net." The government participated.
Along the way, because of government's inability to achieve full employment, the unemployment rate in the country rose and the government found itself putting more and more bucks into the unemployment insurance program. From about 1975 or 1976 right through the period of 1980 to 1984, the Liberal governments of the day consistently moved further and further away from the social contract.
It was a principle of gradualism. Gradually, more and more of the cost of carrying the unemployment insurance program was sloughed on to the shoulders of the employers and the employees.
From the principle of gradualism, we have this quantum leap which is Bill C-21. The Tories have done in one fell swoop what it took the Liberals some 15 years to accomplish. In Bill C-21, the government removes itself completely from any responsibility, from any participation in the contract for unemployment insurance.
Now the Tory government can say: "Well, we don't have any more interest in what the unemployment rate is because the government now doesn't have a financial finger in the pie." One of the greatest arguments for having government participate with employers and employees is that whenever the cost to the government goes up, it makes it stop to think about its programs, particularly the whole question of full employment. This government has kissed any dream of full employment good-bye. There is no opportunity anymore for that.

Take, for example, the effect of C-21 on the Avalon Peninsula. Under C-21, 10,000 would not qualify and 5,440 would be losing weeks. Mr. Speaker, I have listened to a lot of debate today and yesterday. There are really two issues here. One is regarding the substantive provisions of Bill C-21. The second is related to the constitutional process involving the Senate and revision of bills passed in this House.
I would like to deal primarily with that second concern, because I think both require some addressing here in this Chamber. Frankly, when I hear the impassioned and eloquent speech from the hon. member representing Nickel Belt and the answers that have been given to many of the points he has raised in this House, it makes me reflect again on why we even need in our Parliamen-taiy system any other chamber to be busy with the kind of legislation that is coming here when the issues are represented by this legislation are receiving veiy full debate right here in the Chamber of popularly elected representatives.

Mr. Speaker, it has always been said that the Senate's role is to study legislation dispassionately. Recently, however, it has become a place for political dealings where people use their position to defeat bills that were passed democratically by the elected members.
The Liberal senators said that they had established a special committee to give those who had not appeared before our legislative committee a chance to express their opinion. Then why did the 54 witnesses chosen to appear before the special Senate committee represent groups or individuals who had already appeared before the legislative committee of the House?
Why did the special Senate committee decide to hear the representatives of groups who had already opposed almost all the government's proposals?
And why didn't the special committee of the Senate consider the views of recognized experts on unemployment? Because the Liberal senators want to show only one side of the question. They want to scare the public and have no interest in taking a serious look at the real, positive impact of this bill.

The Minister of Employment and Immigration told the committee that its findings indicated it had failed to raise a single new point of any substance in the bill.
The special committee of the Senate is also determined to delay the process for as long as possible. The provisions of Bill C-21 consider regional needs in areas of higher unemployment according to a scale that makes the system more straightforward and more equitable for all claimants. Instead of passing Bill C-21, however, with its variable entrance requirement, the Senate Liberals decided to wait. This means that many people who would otherwise be eligible for unemployment insurance today cannot receive those benefits. Canadians know perfectly well that the Liberal senators who represent the majority in the Senate are the only ones to blame.
Canadians also know that Senate Liberals are preventing many people, including mothers and fathers of newborn children, from taking advantage of expanded benefits under this legislation. There are people who depend on these benefits, and the Senate is quite content to let things drag on.
Canadians will recall this is the same group of Liberal senators that prevented the passage of other bills for political reasons.
We are now certain of what we already jrnew. The demands of the Senate Liberals had no reasonable basis and were meant only to scare the public and needle the government. We cannot afford to let ourselves be manoeuvered into this kind of position again, Mr. Speaker.

Yesterday, the government House leader, also speaking largely about the Senate and its role in a democratic state like Canada, referred to a book entitled The Modem Senate of Canada written by E A. Kunz. From that book, the minister quoted many extracts but the one which I would like to refer to and pick up on is the following. For anyone who wants to compare, this appears at page 9093 of yesterday's Hansard:
But these arguments and counter-arguments respecting the Senate's financial powers, although theoretically interesting, are now-a-days little more than examples of academic pedantry and to discuss the Senate's right to revise the Government's financial program in terms of conflict is really to present a very misleading picture of its
functions in the modern state. On the contrary, the Senate has acted in full understanding of the meaning and implications of responsible government and accepted as binding upon itself the proposition that it should not unduly disturb what has come to be called "the balance of ways and means"; or, as Hopkins says, ' 'that it would be inadmissible to tamper with the overall financial program submitted by the Government in its budgetary proposals in such a way as to effect a material change in the budgetary surplus or deficit envisaged therein. "
The key part of that, in my view, is this reference to the modem Senate of Canada having acted in full understanding of the meaning and implications of responsible government.
The country has, somewhere on our public agenda, and have had for decades, the issue of Senate reform. It is currently in abeyance, pending the outcome of the Meech Lake Accord. One of the things that this whole debate is doing is raising to a much greater prominence before Canadians this enduring, unfinished bit of Canadian business, this hold over from an entirely different era representing a totally different perspective on government, the Canadian Senate.
By its most recent actions, when you take them in the same flow as we have seen with Bill C-22 previously, or borrowing bills that were held up costing Canadians some $14 million a day every day they were delayed in the Senate, and many other things that have happened in the other place since 1984 where the majority is of a different political persuasion from the popularly elected majority in this Chamber, it has brought into very sharp focus the fact that we Canadians have been unduly long in making the right final decision with respect to how constitutional government shall be structured in this country.
The origins of the Senate, if I could just go back to that, really come from what could only be called archaic conservativism. Way back prior to Confederation, the whole time when the family compact was in power, the pre-eminent position of the church and the conduct of affairs of state, the garrison mentality, the colonial economy, there was an effort to replicate here in Canada the social order of pre-revolutionary Europe. That archaic conservativism was supplanted not by really radical ideas. The rebellions of 1837 both in Upper and Lower Canada were repelled and replaced by Confederation conservatism. It was another idea.
March 13, 1990

There were places where this primitive conservativism lingered for a while, most particularly in the province of Quebec, supported by the doctrines of ultramontanism. It continued for a long time where the women only received the right to vote in 1940, where a department of education was not established until the early 1960s, and where finally the role of the modem state swept aside even those last remaining remnants of an archaic conservatism.
The one lingering vestige of that pre-Confederation, early 19th century thinking, can only be found today on the banks of the Ottawa River here in Ottawa, the Senate of Canada. This idea that there has to be an appointed Upper House that can supervise and control the actions of the tempestuous, popularly elected, democratic assembly is a notion that may have fitted a much earlier Canada, but it no longer fits this country.
The example we have with Bill C-21 typifies that, but it is only one example. In fact, all the provinces that had appointed upper Houses have abolished them. Some of the provinces, for example, the province of Ontario where politics is always seen in very pragmatic terms, opted for an elected upper House. Under our Constitution of 1841, the province of Ontario or Canada West at that time, had an elected upper House. We continued with that until 1867 when again the pragmatic Conservatives and pragmatic Ontarians decided no, let us be done with this; it makes no sense to have an upper House either elected or appointed, and it was dropped from the constitution of the province when Ontario came into Confederation in 1867.
Prince Edward Islanders are known to be contrary-minded from time to time. When the Liberals are in power in Ottawa they elect Tories to come here. When the Tories are in power in Ottawa, Islanders elect Liberals to come here. Islanders have always displayed a healthy degree of independent-mindedness. They too, in the mid-nineteenth century, decided if an upper House we are to have, let us have an elected upper House. In the Constitution of Prince Edward Island they changed it in order to have an elected Upper House. Again, Prince Edward Islanders, having found out that an Upper House of whatever kind, elected or appointed, fit very poorly in our system of representative democracy and
Government Orders
simply was not needed, wisely decided to reform their Constitution and let the Upper House slip into the mists of history where it rightly deserved to be obscured.
Only at the federal level have we still with us an appointed Upper House.
We have seen this question of reforming the Senate as an agenda on the political debates of this country for decades. The understanding that Kunz refers to in the other place is that those who have been appointed to the Senate will always act within the very narrow tolerances of a truly parliamentary democracy. They have largely enjoyed office by not disturbing.
It has been an irony that people have pointed to the Upper House and have said that while it serves a good role, we want it to do more. Whenever the Upper House does something and exercises power, there is an outcry. This is not only something when the Progressive Conservatives form the government of Canada, as is currently the case, but I recall this having been a cry that was heard at various times back through the 20th century in Canadian political history.
The point is that we are only happy when the Senate is docile. The moment that it begins to get involved politically in legislation and begins to take these initiatives, people in this country, who are all democrats whatever party they are in, quite rightly resent this development as being most untoward.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government House leader stated yesterday that his government cannot accept the Senate amendments to Bill C-21, a bill to change the unemployment insurance benefits to the workers of the country.
By rejecting all the amendments but one, the government is saying that all Canadians must accept Bill C-21 in its original form. Before getting into the substance of what I want to say with respect to this, along with my friend and colleague who was trying to raise a point of order, I would like to compliment and thank the Senate for having the strength to take this bold move to reject this legislation. I compliment it for using the wisdom of its years of experience in this very important social area. I thank the Senate, instead of chastising it, for its belief in the institutions of the country that have made Canada great, and particularly the social policies which it is trying to protect in this legislation.
Bill C-21 is wrong. It is wrong in principle, wrong in what it proposes, and wrong in its philosophy. This bill will change the insurance of the income of our workers in the country. It will change what they have come to expect and deserve. This is a bill the government promised it would not pass in the House.
The Prime Minister said in 1984 that social programs in our country are a sacred trust. He told Canadians during the last federal election in October 1988 that there was absolutely nothing that would prevent the government of Canada from maintaining all of its social programs. The Minister for International Trade told The Evening Telegram of St. John's on October 14 that after consulting with the Prime Minister, he could confirm and assure Canadians that "no one is planning any changes in the Unemployment Insurance Act of this country".
My colleague from Hamilton in his comments earlier outlined more of the substance of the speech of the Minister for International Trade on that particular date. The minister assured the country and Canadians on many occasions that nothing would happen with unemployment insurance. That was before the election.

The fact that we are debating this issue points to the contradictions in the words of the Prime Minister and the Minister for International Trade.
I said the word "contradiction" and, Mr. Speaker, you know as well as I that we both come from areas where a more explicit word would be used to say what happened prior to the election in terms of what the Prime Minister promised to the people of this country and in terms of what the Minister for International Trade promised the people of Newfoundland. We could be more expressive. I would like to use that word tonight, but I am sure that you would think it unparliamentary, so I will just say that those words were contradictory to what they are doing here today.
We on this side of the House are once again compelled to bring to the attention of Canadians the inconsistencies and the contradictions between what this government promised during the last election and what it is delivering here today.
The government will no longer contribute to the unemployment insurance fund of Canada. Instead, the financing burden will be placed on the shoulders of all Canadian workers and all Canadian employers.
The estimated government cost of unemployment insurance expenditures is $2.9 billion. By abdicating its responsibility to pay unemployment insurance contributions this government will force employees to pay an additional $1.2 billion in their premiums, and employers will be forced to pay $1.7 billion in additional contributions. This government will pay nothing. This is an abdication of responsibility for a fundamental and basic social program that Canadians have earned and deserve and have come to expect.
Not only will workers be paying more; they will be paying more and getting less. The changes to the unemployment insurance system will shrink the safety net by making more stringent the qualifications to receive unemployment insurance and the period for which benefits are paid. Obviously it appears that the workers in our country need protection.
Under the present system, total entitlements include initial benefits, that is, one week of benefits for every week worked, plus regional benefits. Under the new legislation there is only one set of benefits calculated using the regional rate of unemployment and the minimum entrance requirements.
Government Orders
Let us look at what this does to the regions of this country, and particularly the people in the region that I represent, the people of northwestern Ontario. With an average unemployment rate of 7.6 per cent, they will witness an increase in the minimum entrance requirement from 12 weeks to 18 weeks under this new system. That is an increase of 50 per cent.
Northwestern Ontario will see the duration of entitlements reduced from a minimum of 26 weeks to 18 weeks, and a decreased maximum of 50 weeks to 41 weeks in benefits. In other words, workers in northwestern Ontario will be paying much more and, as I said earlier, be getting much less.
Like so many other policies of this government, for example its GST proposals, its new taxes which have been implemented over the years, what it has done to the passenger rail service in the country, what it is doing with the rural post offices and now the changes to the unemployment insurance program, they show a complete disregard for northern Ontario, a complete disregard for rural Canada and a complete disregard for the small cities in this country.
Did this government consider what sort of an impact such changes would have on the rural Canadian economy? Many local industries and firms are set up to employ seasonal workers long enough so that they can apply for UI benefits. Under the new system these firms will have to make the choice of laying off workers without enough weeks to qualify or retain those workers for a few additional weeks increasing their costs. Most firms could not afford the latter option and remain competitive, which again shows that our workers need protection.
Further evidence of this government's ignorance of northern Ontario can be found in its plan to put $800 million back into the job training program. The government failed to mention that between 1984 and 1989 it cut training programs in this country from $2.2 billion in 1984 to $1.5 billion in 1989, a decrease of over $700 million. Yet now it is putting back $800 million by taking the money out of the unemployment insurance fund. This will be paid by the employers and employees of this country. Using simple arithmetic, the government takes out $700 million in 1984 and puts back $800 million in 1989. It does not even respect the cost of inflation in this program. This is just another issue like the goods and

March 13, 1990
Government Orders
services tax issue. It is trying to mesmerize all Canadian workers with its use of figures.
This government claims that by offering training programs through this system it will allow the unemployed to use UI as a trampoline, not as a safety net, that it is a springboard to do greater and better things than the job that they have lost. Supposedly the unemployed would be launched into new productive careers by taking advantage of these fantastic training programs.
How will residents in a single-industry town in northern Ontario and other sections of Canada use this springboard of opportunity to advance themselves? How can they expect to train someone for a job that does not exist in these single-industry towns? When the single industry closes down there are no jobs left to be trained for.
What it causes and what we have been talking about in all smaller communities is the loss of our young people to the bigger centres. This new, improved Unemployment Insurance Act is just going to augment this system. It will move our families out of the small towns into Toronto, Ottawa, Montreal and other large centres. They cannot find a job, the training program, or the job the training program will provide other than by moving into these large centres.
Moreover, how can you realistically expect to retrain older people such as our grain elevator workers and ship workers who have little or no other experience? What I am talking about here are people who are going to be losing their benefits and are just over the ages of 40, 41 and 42 and up to about 50. What are they going to do for the balance of their careers, the 15 productive years after they are laid off? Can you train these people for jobs? Can you offer them something that would make their lives more independent than they are today?
What about sawmill workers? This government can remedy the problems that exist in the sawmill industries of Canada, especially northern Ontario, by eliminating the export tax of 15 per cent, thereby ensuring that there will be no unemployment in these fundamental industries. Yet, it refuses to invoke clause 9 of the memorandum of understanding signed and embedded in the free trade agreement which causes distress among sawmill workers not only in northern Ontario but in British Columbia, Alberta and the Atlantic provinces. All it has
to do is invoke clause 9 and get rid of that memorandum of understanding.
What about our new Canadian citizens or older immigrants who may have some difficulty in speaking either the English or French language well? What sort of retraining will we be able to offer them? It is obvious that these workers will now be paying into a system from which they have no guarantee or receive any benefits or qualify for these training programs.
I do not need to remind you, Mr. Speaker, that northern Ontario as well as other parts of Canada is not renowned for its high tech industries. This policy encourages those who are able to be retrained to move away from rural and small town areas in pursuit of further training and better job opportunities in large cities. It will encourage the youth in small town Canada and in rural Canada to leave their homes, their parents, their loved ones, their grandfathers and grandmothers to seek employment in the large centres where they may not want to go.
I had the privilege of attending a conference on this matter in Timmins, Ontario just a short while ago at the invitation of the Premier of the Province of Ontario and his ministers. The subject of the three-day conference was the losses in our communities of our young people.
Did this government take into full consideration the implications of adopting such an unemployment insurance system? Did it calculate the impact it will have on the seasonal workers in Canada who rely so heavily on UI payments though through no fault of their own? Was any thought given to the impact these measures will have in small communities where students will be driven to leave to seek employment elsewhere in this country?
What will happen to the small businesses in these communities which are dependent for their livelihood on the existence of that community? How will these small businesses absorb the extra costs of UI? Many of these questions and more obviously have not been addressed by this government, nor does this government want to answer them.
In closing, I just want to re-emphasize that this government is negligent in this area. It imposes its will on the Canadian people again. We realize more each day that this government does not care about our small cities, about rural Canada, nor does it care about our single industry towns. It certainly does not care about the

north. It certainly does not care about small business. This government, by this legislation, certainly does not care about the workers.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-NON-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to speak tonight on the revisiting of Bill C-21 to the House.
I did have an opportunity as a member of the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration to spend some time dealing with the bill in its original form. As part of the legislative committee I travelled with the committee and had the opportunity to hear about Bill C-21, to hear from the people across Canada, from nearly 200 different groups that made representations.
We have also had the opportunity to hear some very eloquent and sincere arguments both for and against Bill C-21. The problem I have with many of the approaches taken by some of my colleagues is like trying to paint a picture. It is easy to do it if all the paint you have is black or white, but there is no issue facing the government today that is that simple. We are not looking at black or white. Surely these members have recognized that there is a need for all shades of grey. When we are faced with difficult choices and decisions to be made, there has to be a balanced approach. We cannot just advocate black or white. We cannot just advocate the simple answers.
First, I should like to cover some of the reasons I think that there is a need for the changes the government is proposing. Second, I should like to say why these changes are not only reasonable but in fact very wise.
Most people would recognize and agree that the need for changes to the UI act is readily apparent. Let us look at the demographics in the workforce in Canada. They have not stayed the same. If we think back even to when I was younger and starting out in the workforce, we see that the numbers of people who were in the workforce and the kinds of jobs and training required have changed dramatically.
Let us take a couple of examples. First let us look at the women in the workforce. Who would have thought 30 years ago that more than 60 per cent of the women in Canada would be active participants in today's work-
Govemment Orders
force? Women's participation in the workforce has more than doubled in the last 20 years.
Who would have thought we would be approaching a time when the seniors of this country would be not just a minority, but in fact approaching the point where they could be a major segment of the population in Canada? What is surprising is that more and more of those seniors actually want to work. They want to work longer than our parents did in the past. Any system that we in this Government of Canada adopt has to be able to suit these changing demographics.
For the past 20 years we have seen a dire shortage of jobs for our youths. One of the most heart-rending situations you could face in Canada over the last 10 or 15 years was seeing well trained young people who wanted to work but who were having a very, very difficult time finding suitable jobs. Those times are changing. We are going to be reaching a point in time in the next few years where there will again be a shortage of young people qualified for the jobs required of them.
We have had changes on the job scene itself. Everyone recognizes that we have far more service jobs now than ever before. We have jobs that require high training. Some people have even suggested that there will be in excess of 30 per cent of the workforce requiring education past high school. Some 20 years ago this would have been unthought of. It would have appeared ridiculous.
The fact in our workforce today is that there is not just a need for training for high technology jobs. There is a need for retraining. Many of these workers are going to be re-entering the workforce in different ways which require different training. There is a requirement for this government to address those changing needs.
Then there is the recognition across Canada by a high percentage of the population. In fact in excess of 75 per cent of the people in Canada has indicated that the government has to reform the unemployment insurance system. They recognize that there are misuses and unfortunately even abuses in the system. These misuses and abuses require a reformed system. As a government we have to hear what the people are saying. We have to see what is happening to the system, and we have to make some of those changes.

March 13, 1990
Government Orders
The biggest message we have heard in this regard coming from industry, people in the workforce who are dealing with it on a day to day basis, is that we have to reintroduce into our unemployment insurance system an incentive to work. Many people who know the workforce and know the jobs are there are saying that we are getting dangerously close to motivating or encouraging people not to work rather than the reverse.
In talking about Bill C-21, unemployment insurance and any changes to it we must go back and recognize the primary reason for the unemployment insurance system of today. It is geared to those workers who are out of work but who are willing, available and anxious to work.
I think another point has to be discussed before we can reach any solutions in the reform of the UI scheme as seen in Bill C-21, that is the recognition by the House and by people across Canada of the need for restraint.
When the Conservatives took office the Government of Canada was using 32 cents of every tax dollar to pay the interest on the debt. If this government had not exercised restraint or had not taken the actions that it has, the interest on the debt would now be taking 50 cents on each dollar and would be fast approaching the point where it would be 60 cents and 70 cents. Nobody in Canada wants that situation to occur. It is not only necessary, but it is essential that we recognize the need for restraint and we exercise it.
Several speakers today have talked about the hardships we are imposing on our workers. I should like to make the point that the real hardship we could impose on the workers of Canada is if we do not get our debt under control, if we let the interest payment on the debt rise to the point where we do not have the dollars to exercise sovereignty in Canada or continue to pay the benefits to which the people of Canada should be able to look forward.
In achieving restraint in Bill C-21 there was the need by the government to recognize that it is possible to achieve more and spend less. Some people say that is ridiculous, that of course you cannot do that. Companies across Canada and the United States for the past 15 years have been finding out that in fact you can. Our search for excellence has taught us that not only corporations but also government should find it possible to be able to achieve some of the things that we need to achieve and still exercise the restraint that we know we should be exercising.
We cannot necessarily afford any more to do everything we want. We have to be able to make tough decisions. It is time for choices. It is time for us as the government to try to achieve a balance between the changes and improvements we want to see in the program and what we can afford, what the dollars will allow us to select.
The original design of the UI system was for shortterm protection of workers who were unfortunate enough to find themselves out of work, out of the workforce and needing protection and some form of guaranteed income until they could get back on their feet. We still need that protection, and any balanced program will ensure that it is retained.
The more innovative part of Bill C-21 involves the choice between passive and active programs, programs that are going to address the real needs of the workers who find themselves out of work. Those workers do not just want their unemployment insurance cheque every week. Workers who are truly searching for and wanting a job would like to be able to find that job. They would like to have an unemployment system that will respond to whatever their needs are to ensure that they get that job.
The people who will require this are people my age, and in some cases younger, who have found themselves out of the work that they have done since they were young. They do not want unemployment insurance; they want jobs. They want their dignity back. They want their pride. That entails assistance. This government must be in a position to provide that assistance. Bill C-21 puts that flexibility in the system so that we can respond.
There are women, as I mentioned earlier, entering and re-entering the workforce in record numbers. In many cases they also require special assistance, orientation and in some cases special training.
We have all seen the tragedy of an industry that has had to shut down. There are unemployed people requiring special assistance. Whether it be training, relocation assistance, you name it, this government should be in a
March 13, 1990

position to help them find work, not just provide the unemployment insurance dollars.
Finally, in making choices we have to recognize that there are regional differences in Canada. Not every one of our areas in Canada has the same job opportunities. This government recognizes that the differences between the various regions should be recognized in Bill C-21. Those who have more opportunities, those who are able to find work, should not expect the same levels of support as those people in areas of Canada where jobs are not as readily available.
The government has put together in Bill C-21 a good package, a balanced package, and a package that contains a lot of wisdom, for not only does it provide all the flexibility, all these improvements to the system, it recognizes that it cannot do it all alone. We all know the government cannot administer these programs totally on its own and do it successfully. It has brought in a good balance of private consultants or private firms that have a role to play in the employment scene created by Bill C-21.
Industry is going to be motivated and encouraged to play a bigger role. The communities are going to find that they are essential in the decision-making process under Bill C-21. Colleges, local as well as regional, will become involved in this process.
The bill has been put together wisely. We have travelled. We have heard what Canadians have had to say. We amended the bill. Now the Senate, which is supposed to be providing the wisdom and sagacity that we would expect from a senior House, has tried to destroy this delicate balance created in Bill C-21. That we cannot allow.
This bill was designed to provide work for people. We want a nation of working people, not a nation of people who lose their jobs and do not know how or have a government prepared to give them the assistance they need to get back on their feet and into jobs.

Mr. Speaker, I think the member who just spoke described the government accurately as a government that does not know how to get people back to work.
I am standing to oppose the motion of the Liberal Party which is to amend the message to the Senate. We will be strongly opposing the message the government
Government Orders
wants to send to the Senate, which is to get on with the passage of this veiy bad piece of legislation.
In the debate so far we have heard a number of extraneous points, a number of points which may have some bearing if we were examining a reasonably good piece of legislation, but we are not. We are looking here tonight at legislation which is bad for the people of Canada and which must be defeated before it leaves this Parliament.
An analysis has been done of the effect of this legislation region by region. I should like to draw the attention of the House to the effects on Victoria and Vancouver Island.
First, the average unemployment rate on Vancouver Island and in Victoria was 11.9 per cent in 1988. The number of persons receiving benefits under UI was 51,270. The number who will not qualify as a result of this bill would be 3,070. The number who will lose significant weeks due to the higher entrance qualifications is 4,430.
Accordingly, the total number of Canadians living in Victoria or on Vancouver Island who will be affected by this legislation is over 7,000; some 7,500 residents in our area will be affected by this bill. Across Canada, 519,877 Canadians will be adversely affected by this bill.
These are not the Canadians who are driving the third family BMW in Toronto or who are paying $300,000 or $400,000 for houses or condominiums in South Oak Bay. These are Canadians who already live for the most part on the borderline of poverty in this country. Most often it will be single women, single parents or teen-aged children trying to get their first jobs, or working Canadians trying to support a family and live on the edge of economic survival in the country. Or, it will be those in Atlantic Canada whose centre of economy has been ground down by the policies of this government and of the Liberal governments that have preceded it. We have a bill which attacks those on the margins of economic survival in the country.
It has been suggested by speaker after speaker on the government side that this debate is really about the Senate. I do not owe any brief for the Senate. In fact, I know a close relative of mine whose lifelong ambition is to be appointed to the Senate so that he could rise in that

March 13, 1990

place and move its abolition, a sentiment with which I entirely agree.
In this case, the Senate is doing a service to the people of Canada by turning this bill back. It gives the people of Canada another opportunity to understand where this legislation fits in the economy policies of the government.
There are already 1.6 million Canadian youngsters who live below the poverty line. There are over four million Canadians living below the poverty line. This bill goes to the heart of the Tory agenda because it will add, not subtract, to those numbers.
We have to see this bill in the context of Conservative economic and social policy. We have now had almost sue years of Conservative government since 1984.

speechtext: You never had it so good!

speechtext:
My friend says we never had so good. If he would come with me to talk to the people of Victoria, or go around the country and ask people whether they have ever had it so good, he will get his answer.
The fact of the matter is that the economic and social policies of this country are a disgrace. As I sit and watch the Minister of Finance as he stands in his place virtually every day to answer questions about the country's economic policy, it is interesting to reflect on a book written in the late 1960s or early 1970s by David Halberstam entitled, The Best and the Brightest. This book described how the best-educated and best-tr^iped people in the United States managed to get that country into the Vietnam disaster.
As I reflect on the government and those behind it, the financial wizards and the best brains in our corporate sector who persist in pushing the government along the economic and social path that it has taken, I must say that "the best and the brightest" in this country are leading us into a dangerous, economic situation. The complacency of the government, when it says that we never had it so good, in the face of the clear facts of housing shortages, unemployment, abuse, poverty, and cutbacks in social programs, is a disgrace. Let us look at what its agenda is.
First, reduce social programs. That is part of its agenda. Second, weaken the progressive tax system and change the balance in our tax system so that it favours the rich as against the poor and the middle income groups. It is a clear fact. Just ask the middle income earners how much tax they are paying now compared to the taxes they paid in 1984. Look at the facts of cutbacks
in the tax rates and the opening of further loopholes in the tax system that this government has brought in. Now we have the GST, and it will not explain to a single person in the country how the GST is going to help the middle income earners. In fact, the Conservative chairman of the finance committee boasted that the only people left in the country to tax are the middle income earners. As for the rest, it does not make any difference.
The third element of its economic policy is the privatization of the economy. Fourth, it wants to set about the integration of our economy with the United States. Also, it wants to maintain unemployment. The previous member spoke about trying to reduce unemployment. It is a clear, systematic, intentional policy of the government to maintain unemployment at higher and higher levels. That is its economic intention. An article recently in The Economist magazine made that very clear.
Finally, it is part of the government's agenda to strengthen the position of the multinational companies in the Canadian economy. That has very clearly been part of the Conservative agenda and that is what it has put in legislation which it put through the previous Parliament.
Let us look at the effect and how the government done this with the particular steps it has taken. It had a so-called tax reform package in the previous Parliament which reduced the total number of tax brackets and particularly reduced the rate payable in the upper brackets. It reduced corporate taxation in the country. It eliminated elements of capital gains tax and the government has completed the Tory tax reform, or is in the process of completing the Tory tax reform, with the GST.
The second part of the steps the government has taken to implement its agenda is the free trade legislation. Over the last couple of years-certainly the last year-and-a-half- the government has maintained a high dollar which has had a bad effect out my way, for example, because a high dollar hurts tourism and exports. It has maintained high interest rates. That high interest rate policy is beginning to have a negative effect on small business, potential house purchasers, and unemployment levels. The high interest rate policy is not a mechanical policy that it is following, but an intentional policy of the Bank of Canada, supported in this House by the Minister of Finance and the government. The clear intention is to increase unemployment levels in this country so that, in their terminology, the economy cools off. When saying that, the government is speaking of the
March 13, 1990

economy of southern Ontario and it is finally getting its wish in that.
