What would we do, the hon. member asks. I guess the government is so bankrupt it now has to turn to the opposition and ask us what we would do. I will be advising the hon. member in a minute exactly what we would do about it.
Let me continue with the step-by-step Conservative agenda and how the government is proceeding with it. It has in fact instituted a systematic set of cut-backs on social policy and social programs in the country, of which this bill is a veiy important part.
It has placed no limits on private debt while attacking the social programs which are developed in the public sector. I can speak with some feeling on this. I am one of those Canadians who found himself in private debt, and debt more than I could handle. There are millions of Canadians who, without a qualm, get talked into additional debt by the various institutions in the country. There has been no Conservative control on private debt because the Conservative philosophy accepts the idea that increased private consumption is a good and systematic economic policy. The effect of that kind of overheated private consumption is to drive up house prices, to fuel inflation, to devastate our environment and to knock our economy out of balance. What do the Conservatives do in response to this? They turn around and cut public programs and social programs. That has been part of their intentional agenda.
The Conservatives really believe that a good society rewards the rich and penalizes those who are less fortunate than themselves. That is the Conservative philosophy. I give them at least this much, they understand what they are doing. It would probably be worse if they really believed that they were doing something for the good of the country. What they know they are doing is changing the face of Canada. They are changing it into a country which is even more beset with inequality. They are increasing the poverty levels in the country. I have
Government Orders
here the figures of Canadians who use food banks. There are 378,000 different people per month use food banks in the country. That is an absolute disgrace in a country with our wealth. If the government had any sense of responsibility to the people, it would be focusing its attention on those problems, not on making the rich richer, as it has done persistently in every policy it has introduced since it took office.
We are faced as well, with an economy in which the wage levels have increasingly gone down in real terms for most Canadians. The kinds of jobs that the government has visited on the people are not the jobs which a Polar 8 project would introduce. I am pleased to see the Minister of Justice enter the House. She is now the senior political member from British Columbia. I hope she will take an opportunity this evening to encourage the House to believe that maybe the government is going to do something either to revive the Polar 8 project or at least to put in its place a shipbuilding program on the west coast that would provide the kinds of jobs Canadians need and are entitled to. That is jobs with some kind of economic future, which pay a decent wage, and which permit the possibility of a pension and of purchasing a home of their own. Instead what the government has done so often is to cut out those kinds of jobs letting them be replaced with part-time, poor-paying jobs in the service industry. That is the face of Canada for millions of Canadians.
The government has, in fact, continued and added to the public debt of the country and to the deficit. That too is part of the Conservative agenda. To say the government has not done it intentionally is to simply fly in the face of the facts. Not only has it maintained high interest rates which are a major burden on the taxpayers of this country, but in addition the government has failed to tackle some of the highest spending areas in the budget. In defence spending, for example, over $1 billion is spent in maintaining troops in Europe, long after they have served any useful military purpose. Now they provide, clearly, even no diplomatic purpose.

March 13, 1990
Government Orders
If the government would seriously attack the debt problem it would begin attacking those kinds of useless expenditures. Instead, it is maintaining those expenditures, not because they contribute in any way to peace, but because when it comes to the crunch, the government will do whatever is necessary to please the government of the United States. It has done so in its economic, social and external policies. We just have to look at the way in which the government caved in to the United States on Panama. It was the only government in the western world outside of Margaret Thatcher's government that had the nerve to support the breach of international law involved in the invasion of Panama. Soon we are going to be getting the renewal of NORAD. That is going to be coming before the House. Any bets on what the government is going to do about that? Of course, it will supinely reinforce the NORAD agreement and just put it through for another five years, without any consideration or debate in the House.
A few minutes ago an hon. member asked what our policies were. What we call for is a completely different direction in economic and social policy for the country. What we say first of all is that the underpinnings and purpose of economic policy must be fourfold.
First, we must ensure that our economy is environmentally sustainable. Everything must become secondary to that. We must now begin a serious, planned, comprehensive transition to an economically sustainable environment. We cannot afford to wait any longer to fulfil that objective and that must become the primary objective of government economic policy.
Second, and in keeping with that, social equality must be the objective of our economy. We can no longer accept poverty in the midst of plenty. We must ensure that every step we take makes this a better, fairer society, that the spending and economy we have will be addressed to that problem.
Let me finish by outlining the other two points very briefly. Third, we must ensure that our economy provides a decent living for all Canadians in which they have some worth and some ability to participate in the economy. And, fourth, everything we do must contribute toward the ending of poverty around the world. This is our program and we urge it on the House.
Mr. Francis G. LeBlanc (Cape Breton Highlands-
Canso): Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have the opportunity, even at this late hour, to debate once again in the House the provisions of Bill C-21.1 am glad to be able to speak to the veiy excellent work of the Senate in its review of these changes to Canada's unemployment insurance system.
I am glad too to be able to explain here and for the unemployed in my constituency who, since January, knew they required four more weeks to qualify for UI but could not understand why. I am glad to explain to them the purposes of the stand that we, in the Liberal Party in the House and in the Senate, have been taking in opposing this legislation.
On several occasions during the last two months I have been confronted by constituents who found themselves with 10 weeks but without the 14 weeks they suddenly needed after Christmas to qualify for UI benefits. Why could they not get benefits? They were told it was because the UI bill was in the Senate and they had to wait until it was passed. They would ask: "What is the hold up?" I would have to say that there was a principle involved. The principle had to do with the fact that this government was no longer going to be contributing to the UI program and that was going to weaken the program in the future.
They would give me a puzzled look and say okay and that they would be patient. But I never thought I was able to explain properly the consequences of the thrust of this legislation. In particular, the decision by the government to withdraw entirely its financial contribution to the UI Program and to transfer the financial burden of this program entirely to the fee payers. I never felt I could adequately explain why this particular change, which appears to many to be nothing more than a bookkeeping change, so dramatically altered the character of the UI program, why it is so dangerous to this most vital component of our social safety net and why I should prevail upon the indulgence of those unemployed in my constituency to be patient.
I am glad to have one more chance because the changes contained in this bill, in particular the changes embodied in the Archaean phrases of clauses 52, 53 and 56 of Bill C-21, in essence knock out one of the pillars of the UI program. They are the first step, I think, to the dismantling of a national social insurance program in the country. Bill C-21 is the thin edge of the wedge, to coin a popular expression. It is the first step down the slippery slope of privatizing, decentralizing and, eventually,
March 13, 1990

Americanizing the unemployment insurance system, of undoing one more strand in the subtle garment of national social insurance programs, national infrastructure, and equalization payments which hold the country together. It is philosophically linked with the free trade agreement, the abandonment of VIA Rail, other changes that have weakened our regions and weakened the country from one end to the other.
The current UI program, which has been in place since 1940, is financed by three partners: employers through their premium contributions; employees through their premium contributions; and the federal government through the Consolidated Revenue Fund which itself is financed by our taxes.
In 1989, for example, the government contribution was $2.9 billion out of a total UI expenditure for Canada of some $12.3 billion. The government contribution is more important than this share would suggest. It pays for UI benefits which arise from conditions of higher than average unemployment rates. When unemployment rates rise across the country, as they did during the 1981 recession, the share of UI benefit costs paid for out of government revenues rises substantially.
As well, in regions of high unemployment like Newfoundland, Cape Breton and other parts of Atlantic Canada, large portions of Quebec and northern Ontario, the west, and northern Canada, a large part of UI benefits comes from government contributions. This is because the weeks of so-called regional extended benefits-weeks of UI benefits which are related to high unemployment rates-are paid for from government general revenues. That means that for an unemployed worker from Inverness in my constituency, the first 10 weeks of his UI benefits are paid for out of premium revenues; the second portion, if he has enough weeks, is paid for out of premium revenues; and the third portion, often involving the largest share of his benefits, are paid for out of government revenues under the current program.
This feature of the UI program allows the federal government to stabilize the national economy by directing money through UI benefits to individuals in communities that need it most when it is most needed. This
Government Orders
keeps our regions alive and it keeps our communities alive. It allows the federal government to contribute quite naturally to stabilizing the economy of the country. It is one of the pillars of our macro-economic policy and it is one of the pillars our our social policy.
In addition, the federal government finances UI benefits to self-employed fishermen. It finances these out of general revenues to the tune in 1989 of some $261 million. Why? Because the situation of seasonal fishermen and the communities they live in is regarded as unique. Again, the UI program is how the federal government is able to support a way of life in many parts of Atlantic Canada.
I would urge the members opposite to read the transcript of the Senate committee hearings in Canso. They should read the testimony of Claude Sangster, an inshore fisherman from New Harbour in Guysborough County, or Edison Lumsden from Canso, or Keith Lettington from Drum Head. They should read their testimony to see if they have any doubts about the importance of this feature of the UI program to our east coast fishery.
One of the fundamental thrusts of Bill C-21 acknowledged by the Government House Leader yesterday is, and I quote:
(I) a shift to full financing of the UI program through employer and employee premiums.
This thrust is embodied, first, in clause 52 of Bill C-21 which, by replacing Section 118 of the current UI act, ends all federal government contributions to the UI program including in particular the contribution to regional extended benefits. In fact, the concept of regional extended benefits and the financial stake of the federal government to lower unemployment rates through contributions to UI benefit payments related to high unemployment is ended with Bill C-21.
Second, with the passage of Bill C-21, the government no longer contributes to the financing of special UI benefits to self-employed fishermen. Henceforth, these benefits will be financed out of general UI premiums. In addition, as the Senate discovered, this entire component of the UI program which is hived off from the rest of the UI Act can be altered and, for all intents and purposes, abolished by a simple Order in Council. That is without even consulting Parliament. The government

March 13, 1990
Government Orders
accepted the Senate's suggestion for not eliminating fishermen's benefits without consulting Parliament, but we can see the handwriting on the wall.
What will happen if Bill C-21 is adopted without the Senate amendments? Before saying this, I should say that one of the key Senate amendments which the government refuses to accept would bring back the principle of government contribution to the UI program, at least in part. This is one of the recommendations which would prevent the erosion of the program that we are going to see if Bill C-21 is adopted. Let me explain.
If Bill C-21 is adopted without amendment, the entire cost of the UI program will be funded by premiums. Employee premiums will rise from $1.95 to $2.25 per $100 and employer premiums will rise from $2.73 to $3.15 per $100. The Minister of Finance has fixed this rate for the next three years in the last budget in 1989. With the changes on the benefit side, it will be harder for many unemployed to qualify for benefits. They will qualify for fewer weeks and face higher penalties for quitting and a whole series of other changes related to the cut-backs in the unemployment insurance benefits amounting to some $1.3 billion.
I want to focus the attention of members on the evolution of the UI account. This is something which has received very little attention. At the current premium rate, the government has admitted that the UI fund, which is now in surplus, will move into a deficit position by the end of 1992 to the tune of some $3 billion, according to the Deputy Minister of Employment and Immigration. Three billion dollars is more than one-quarter of the total UI expenditures for 1989.
How will this deficit be financed? Either premiums will have to rise or benefits will have to be cut further. It will be that or the government will have to kick in out of general revenues. But we already know the orientation of the government, so we can pretty well rule out the third option.
What should we expect? It would be a simple matter to jack up premiums for fishermen's benefits or cut down drastically on the benefits paid to them. The government has said it would not do this, but it can easily be done
without even consulting Parliament over the summer holidays when there is no one around to oppose it.
Next, how about cutting drastically benefits that go into high unemployment regions like Atlantic Canada? That will save some money. We know that the government's business friends, who as employers will pay the majority of the UI fund, want to cut back on UI benefits. They want to make UI more like insurance and they can legitimately say: "Since our premiums pay the majority of the funds in the account, why should we not decide?" Can you blame them? Indeed, they might well ask: "Why does the government have any say in the management of the UI account at all?" After all, he who pays the piper calls the tune. This government has stopped paying the piper, so why should it call the tune?
Anyway, since UI is becoming more like private insurance, why not go the next step? How about turning it into a Crown corporation, or maybe privatizing it completely? Then we can start to see what happens. With no financial stake in holding a strong national unemployment insurance program together, one which stabilizes incomes, supports regions, and provides benefits to the hinterland regions of the country during periods of high unemployment, the federal government has abandoned one of the roles which it has had since the thirties as a principal feature of its economic management. It will enable the government to abandon the regions completely. That is the thrust of this legislation.
The next step is to let the quality of the unemployment insurance program benefits drop in order to have a level playing field with the United States. That is what we said all along was the ultimate aim as a result of the free trade agreement.
This is the agenda under Bill C-21. This is the agenda we have been trying to expose and which the government is moving towards with these changes as surely as night follows day. It is time that Canadians wake up and realize what is happening to them. It is time for this government to wake up and realize that it is dismantling the very essence and fabric of this country. That is what is happening with the changes to Bill C-21.
March 13, 1990

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-NON-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to participate in the debate on Bill C-21.
The subject in a broad perspective, as I see it, breaks down into the following general areas of discussion. First is the role of the Senate in the rejection and delivery of this bill back to the House from the other place.
Second is the subject of premium changes and the withdrawal of the federal government subsidy to the unemployment insurance program.
Third is the area of increased training and the shift from support to preparation for re-employment.
Fourth is the increased maternity benefits, the inclusion for the first time of workers over 65 and the introduction of disincentives to abuses, misconducts and failure to be employed. Last is the general philosophy of the government in its approach to employment and unemployment and the introduction of the intensification of the work ethic in our countiy.
First, let us consider the role of the Senate. As has been said already this evening on more than one occasion, it was on November 6, 1989 that this House passed Bill C-21 and sent it to the Senate. It was February 14, better than three months later, when the Senate finally did report this bill back to the House.
It is not a very cogent demonstration of urgency, serious intent or concern for those who have suffered the loss of significant benefits from Bill C-21 which would have become effective during the first week of January.
The Senate heard 60 witnesses in 11 weeks, 54 of whom had appeared before the House of Commons legislative committee. The legislative committee heard 200 witnesses in four weeks. The serious intent and the sense of urgency and dispatch with which the subject has been addressed by the Senate left a great deal to be desired.
I think some of the amendments from the Senate being debated indicates that there has been some room for sober second thought. In the area of illiteracy, it is the kind of recommendation one would expect from a responsible Senate. I certainly speak with respect for the members in the Senate individually, although as a body I believe that their motives and their actions in blocking
Government Orders
the bill is absolutely intolerable and unacceptable in our parliamentary system.
The Senate plan to more specifically identify the proposed training program is a reasonable proposition and one which the government indicates it is willing to consider and accept. The suggestion that the Senate would be empowered to rule on the efficacy and appropriateness of this annual plan is again absolutely intolerable and unacceptable in a responsible parliamentary system.
The suggestion concerning Recommendation No. 8 that there be a specific alteration to the bill with respect to self-employed fishermen is a reasonable and sensitive suggestion. It is also a reasonable and sensitive response by government that self-employed fishermen are not specifically alienated by the provisions of Bill C-21. In fact, it improved the original Unemployment Insurance Act in that respect.
I refer to the Senate and its penchant for seizing on issues such as this and on the free trade agreement. Fortunately, it caused a general election which the people of Canada took in stride and delivered a very profound message of support for free trade much to the surprise of the Liberal Senate. To confront legislation from this House in the manner as was done with the substance of Bill C-21 is unacceptable.
There is general support in many quarters for a Triple E Senate, elected, equal and effective. I think many more activities of the nature of the confrontation with Bill C-21 might cast a new meaning to triple E in being excessive, expensive and extinct.
The actions of the Senate in what appears to be an outright obstruction of a major bill benefiting those unemployed Canadians most in need, has been seen by many Canadians to be superfluous to the responsibilities and functions of the Senate in the exercise of a power that, while technically appropriate and technically legal, is traditionally inappropriate.
With respect to premiums, the federal government has been paying approximately $3 billion per year to the unemployment insurance fund, $2 billion of which is a subsidy and $1 billion as an employer on behalf of federal government employees. The termination of that subsidy in this day and age of relatively sound and buoyant economic times in Canada with a deficit of $30 billion constitutes an act of not only fiscal soundness and financial good management, but one that is sensitive to

Government Orders
the realities of a self-sustaining fund which is doing very well and operates on a principle of regional equality.
The premiums used to replace the federal subsidy will come from those workers and companies who are in a buoyant condition, employed and active. The benefits of that program will continue to go to those areas of the country where unemployment is high and where workers need support and training. I believe that that is consistent with the philosophy of the government to turn Canada in the direction of paying its own way and of living within parameters that we can afford.
I certainly do support the withdrawal of the federal subsidy to the premium account and I believe the citizens of Canada will also support that initiative. Hopefully, the Senate will support it even though it is beyond their terms of reference because it is a financial matter. The variable weeks of qualification and duration of benefits are very significant. The transfer of a portion of the unemployment insurance fund from a total of $13 billion in support systems to a total of about $1.3 billion in training and re-employment initiatives and a remaining fund of about $11.7 billion for support, the variable requirements, while significant, are relatively reasonable. After all, it takes 10 weeks to qualify for unemployment insurance. The difference between 10 weeks and 14 weeks in the course of a 52 week year is not a major stretch of the work ethic in this country. I believe we will see that this stretching of the parameters will stimulate initiative and will be demonstrated to have little consequence at all because the average unemployment is far below the extreme parameters contained in the old program.
The variable entrance requirement will result in about $800 million being available for transfer to the training and re-employment fund. I believe that the combination of the stretch to a higher work ethic and the provision of increased funds for training and re-employment to help achieve that work ethic is a balance that any reasonable Canadian will find very significant.
I would like to review the range of training and re-employment initiatives that those variable entrance requirements help to fund. The other portion of that $1.3 billion for training and re-employment comes from
the elimination, reduction and moderation of abuses to the system. Many Canadians never use the unemployment insurance fund and fortunately never have to seek its benefits. Their only criticism is that the system is abused, that people have adopted it as a way of life and have found ways to live within it and that the raison d'etre for it are ignored and misused.
The correction of these abuses will generate almost a half billion dollars to be added to the training and re-employment initiatives, going with the variable entrance requirements, totals $1.3 billion. I believe any reasonable Canadian will say that is a very acceptable and commendable change in the focus of the unemployment insurance program, to the modem ethic and vision that Canadians have today of our country.
I would like to review the list of training initiatives that this $1.3 billion will provide. It will add $65 million to human resources planning for work with industry and with non-governmental organizations. One of the areas I have heard mentioned is a commission on human resource development, one which would address the educational aspects of Canadian life and delve into one of the most profound areas of human resource development in addressing the future of our Canadian society.
Another is the addition of $100 million to the Entry Level Skills Development Program where the combination of private sector participation and federal issues such as employment equity would go together to improve the skills and capabilities of a great many Canadians. The Industrial Adjustment Service will receive an additional $15 million, doubling it to a total of $30 million. Employees will work together in terms of new technology in the replacement of obsolete skills and in retraining.
The Community Futures Program will receive an additional $50 million under the Canadian Jobs Strategy budget. This will help communities such as those we have heard of in the very tragic fisheries difficulties in eastern Canada. It will help communities to cope with their problems and will give substance and credibility to the Prime Minister's commitment during the last election campaign when the mandate for this entire program was put on the table. The Prime Minister said that Canada will have the best employment industrial adjustment program in the world. The direction of the initiatives contained in Bill C-21 are in pursuit of that promise
March 13, 1990

and that supporting mandate that was delivered in the 1988 election.
Under Section 26, the unemployment insurance training program will receive an additional $350 million, the continuing employment option and training for displaced older workers will total $100 million. There will be benefits amounting to $40 million for people over 65 years of age who up until now have been denied unemployment insurance eligibility.
Consistent with the Charter of Rights and Freedoms in which men and women are eligible to work to the age that they desire and to the age they can satisfactorily perform, they will be eligible in future for unemployment insurance benefits and can participate in the program, both from a benefit and a premium participation viewpoint.
In terms of self-employment and entrepreneurship characteristics of the Canadian Jobs Strategy, there will an additional $45 million; $20 million to promote new entrepreneurial activity and $25 million for mobility assistance. The very significant improvements to the maternity and parental benefits portion of the unemployment insurance program under Bill C-21 will introduce new benefits worth $450 million, almost half a billion dollars in new support for maternity and parental benefits. How the Senate could hold up this bill for three months and let those benefits lay idle, I certainly do not understand.
If you total all of these initiatives along with some others I have not mentioned, we have a program worth $1.3 billion which is paid for from changes that improve the spirit and the substance of the program in terms of the work ethic and in terms of abuses and disincentives under the old program.
In conclusion, I would like to say that Canada needs to revitalize its approach to employment, enterprise, the changing realities of new technology, the environmental imperative, the developing world and to the more intense trading competition we face as a nation throughout the world. In Canada we have in our unemployment insurance program a safety net that is second to none in the world. Bill C-21 continues to keep it that way. That is important. It is something in which we all believe.
Government Orders
We want to ensure that that safety net does not become a way of life. We want to ensure that Canadians do not get locked into that trap and get captured by the ethic of unemployment. I believe that Bill C-21 accomplishes that. It points us in the direction of new work ethic initiatives, discourages abuse, provides for increased training and re-employment initiatives and provides the best safety net in the world, while at the same time, casting a spirit that does not make that safety net a habit of unemployment and perpetual dependence upon the dole which I believe all Canadians would abhor.
I believe in Bill C-21, particularly as it is introduced and as people begin to experience the qualities and the values of it. Hopefully the Senate, commencing tomorrow, will take their responsibilities seriously and approve the speedy passage of this bill to which all Canadians will give their full-fledged support.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-NON-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to speak on Bill C-21. I would like to voice my opposition on behalf of many Canadians to the vast majority of the bill's provisions and in support of the Senate's proposed amendments.
This bill represents a beginning of privatization of our unemployment insurance system. It represents the undermining of the basic principle of the unemployment insurance system. The fact that most Canadians are not aware of the government's true intentions with respect to the dismantling of our system is unfortunate. The Mulroney government has taken a page from a book authored by other governments that act not for, but against the wishes and interests of those who put them there, the majority of the people they purport to represent.
This government rules by attempting to mislead the public. It attempts to obscure its real motives. In fact, it hires advertisers at millions of dollars to misrepresent the truth. The government actually justifies every action by painting it as an attempt to cut the deficit. What this government does not understand is that it can no longer take the economic ills that it created out on the backs of the low and the middle income earners and the backs of the unemployed.
This government is uncomfortable with debate and intolerant of dissent. It used closure at second reading

March 13, 1990
Government Orders
and time allocation at report stage and third reading of this bill. Once again it has invoked closure to stop, to stifle debate.
Hearings were held across this country at a whirlwind pace, one that guaranteed that many informed Canadians, that many concerned individuals and groups could not voice their objections to this bill. We all know that the government feels such discomfort at the mention, much less the exercise of debate, of public hearings and consultation. It is because it is breaking promises, the sacred trust that it talked about so much during the past election. The government stifled debate because it does not want to be reminded of those promises.
The members opposite do not want to be reminded that in October, 1988 the Minister for International Trade called the suggestion that the government was planning to change the UI system as "complete nonsense". He called it complete nonsense that the government was going to change the UI system. Well, we have seen what the government has done today. It does not like to consult. It does not like to consult because it knows that people will say things like "You promised you would not do this and now you are doing it". People would ask tough questions such as why, why does the government continue to break its promises?
We all know that if the Canadian public had known during the last election what this government had in store for them, the majority of members opposite would not be here. We know this and this is why the government continues to break these promises.
If Canadians had known the Conservative rallying ciy of unfettered access to the U.S. market was a hoax which would mean the undermining of our social programs and the principles of social justice which we hold dear, they would have turned their backs on the Conservatives as they will in 1992 for breaking these promises, or hopefully sooner.
If Canadians had known that the Mulroney government had planned to sell out Canadian farmers and to undermine our supply marketing systems, they would have turned the Conservatives out on their ears. If they had known that the Mulroney government would prove incapable of managing our economy, of protecting the Canadian fish stocks and the Canadian fisheries, they
would have shuddered at the mere thought of putting these Conservatives back in power. If the Canadian people had known that the Conservative agenda for the country was devoid of respect for social equality and economic fairness, unable or unwilling to combat growing racial intolerance and regional strife, then the Canadian public would have ensured that the Conservative members opposite would not be sitting where they are today.
The Minister of Employment and Immigration has stated that Bill C-21 will, and I quote "ensure that Canada is poised to take advantage of the future of unprecedented opportunity and to meet the objectives of competition, confidence, strength, sovereignty and compassion". I find it interesting to say the least that the minister would assert that one of her objectives for Canada was sovereignty and that somehow Bill C-21 met that objective. This bill provides for the elimination of the tripartite financing of our unemployment system.
In withdrawing the government's contribution to the fund, we would be eliminating from our system a practice which is used practically in every other country in the western industrialized world with the notable exception of course of the United States. What a coincidence that in fact the only country in the western world that does not have a system like this is the United States.
Bill C-21 is not about protecting Canadian sovereignty. It is about many other things, such as bringing about a social system that is in line with that of the United States, a social system that was promised to the Americans during the free trade debate. In fact, the real reason for this bill is because of the free trade deal. A commitment was made during the free trade debate to bring our social systems in line with the Americans.
When I hear the Minister of Employment and Immigration defend this bill, it is clear that this bill fits hand in hand with other legislative endeavours undertaken by this government, such as the free trade deal, GST, budget cuts to education, health care, social assistance, women's groups, native publications, the list goes on. Why? I do not think members of this side of the House have to ask that question. I do not think Canadians today have to ask that question. They know. It is because of the free trade agreement.

It is not that the Conservatives have no vision for this country, as we are sometimes tempted to think on this side. It is that the Conservative vision of the country, of what is right and good, is just so isolated from reality and from the minds and the hearts of ordinary Canadians that it is barely incomprehensible.
The Conservative vision of this country is shared by only a handful of Canadians. At election time the Conservatives get together and decide what will they say this year to get elected? They decide what is in their best interests to tell the Canadian public in order to get elected. So they tell Canadians, "We respect the UI system". They tell Canadians all sorts of other things and by golly, just after the election is over they say, "We changed our minds", or "We did not really promise you this".
Bill C-21 is a perfect example. After promising Canadians that they would not change the system and then breaking their promise, after cutting off public hearings and ramming the bill through second and third reading, then ciying foul when the Senate insisted on hearing what Canadians had to say about this bill, people who wanted to speak on the bill. Do you know that there was only one group besides the government who voiced support for the quick passage of this bill? That was the Canadian Chamber of Commerce.
As the special committee of the Senate on Bill C-21 has pointed out, the overwhelming majority of those who appeared before the committee disagreed with the government's contention that the bill would be good for Canadians. In fact, the overwhelming majority of people who appeared before the committee said that Bill C-21 is an attack on the working people of this country. It is an attack on small communities, an attack on underdeveloped regions and an attack on the basic decent foundations of our country.
I think Earl McCurdy from the Fishermen, Food and Allied Workers Union put it well when he said that Bill C-21 is a classic case of blaming the victim.
The unemployment insurance program has been a cornerstone of Canadian social policies since 1940.
Since the beginning, government contributions have formed an integral part of this program. By contributing
Government Orders
to the unemployment insurance program, the Government of Canada is acknowledging its commitment to the creation of full employment.
This is a government which is not comfortable with committing itself to the pursuit of full employment. It is no wonder that, with the free trade agreement, the fisheries mismanagement, the farming crisis we see in Canada today, this government is putting thousands of Canadians out of work. It is no wonder that the government wants nothing to do with accepting a financial incentive in the form of contributions to UI, creating stable, quality employment.
The government must know that its attempt to pass responsibility off to someone else is unacceptable to Canadians.
The government is attempting to pull out of the unemployment insurance program. Who has the government designated to make up for the $2.9 billion a year in shortfall? Employees, employers and the unemployed will have to pay this price.
Premiums paid by employers and employees will rise under Bill C-21.
Unemployment insurance will be harder to qualify for and benefit periods will be shorter.
As witnesses to the special Senate committee pointed out, once the responsibility for UI funding begins to rest solely on employer-employee contributions, there will be pressure to cut the program even further. The government has given up control over the unemployment insurance program. It is giving up the control it promised Canadians, a promise that it said it would keep and a promise, as with other promises, it has failed to keep.
The government is telling Canadians that they will have to pay more for less.
Try telling that to the workers in my riding who are losing their jobs because of this government's policies. The Prime Minister promised them during the election campaign that he would create the best adjustment programs in the world because of free trade.
Where are these adjustment programs? We are still waiting. This was another broken promise. He said there would be the best adjustment programs in the world after free trade. Nowhere have we seen them.

March 13, 1990
Government Orders
Not only has the government not introduced these programs, now it is backing out of the one program that is supposed to represent the government's commitment to the creation of employment.
How can it expect Canadians to believe it when it says that this legislation is good for them? They know better than to believe the Conservative government now.
In closing, I urge this government to accept, not just three of the Senate's proposed amendments, but to accept all these amendments.
These amendments represent the suggestions and the beliefs of many Canadians who were left out of the system, who were not heard by this Conservative government which cut off debate. I respectfully submit that the government should withdraw this bill and should come back again with something much better.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-NON-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise in support of the motion that was put forward by the government House leader. While there are some ideas with which we can agree in the message from the other place, there is a basic conflict between some of these amendments and the total intent of the BUI C-21.
Our government is determined to do more than passively accept unemployment. We must and we wUl help unemployed people get back to work and make it possible for them to contribute to the growth of this country. BUI C-21 has been held up long enough. The needs it addresses are too important to justify prolonged arguments over some of the detaU and some of the recommendations that have come forward from the other place.
The government has listened seriously to the recommendations offered by the Senate regarding this Bill C-21. And, while there are many concerns which all members should have about many of the suggestions in the message before us, some of the recommendations are worth including in the bUl.
For example, we recognize the impact which illiteracy has on Canadian workers and on Canadian employers. The lack of basic skUls is an impediment to further training. For that reason the idea in recommendation No. 1 is worth including in the bUl.
Senators have said they welcome the commitment of the government to producing an annual plan which will show members how UI funds wUl be spent to train and to develop people.
In recommendation No. 4, they have asked us to amend the bill to ensure that the minister wUl provide specific detaUs in this plan. It wUl do no one any good to create centralized plans which are too rigid or too detaUed to respond to the changing needs. At the same time a reasonable level of detaU should be provided. Therefore, the response which this government proposes to the Senate suggestion is a fair one.
In recommendation No. 8, the Senate has also asked this House to consider removing a subsection in the Unemployment Insurance Act which has been in place for almost 20 years. That subsection would allow the Governor in CouncU to remove benefits for self-employed fishermen from the UI Act at any time.
With the concern shared by all Canadians for the problems hi the fishing industry, the request for added protection for these benefits is understandable. I think I share with all my colleagues on this side of the House, and indeed with all my colleagues in the House the difficulties that our fellow Canadians in Atlantic Canada are having. The message which this House will send to the Senate should accommodate improvements in this particular area. But much of the message that we are receiving back from that other House cannot be accepted.
We have been given a set of recommendations by the Liberal senators which do nothing more than tie the hands of the government. These amendments would force us to spend money we do not have in ways which may not be the best for the working people who are going to be helped by the bill.
The Liberals in the Senate seem to believe that the only purpose for UI is to pay people to wait for their old job to come back. UI is not a guaranteed income plan. We on this side of the House believe that UI needs to become an active program which invests in people's lives. Training courses, financial help to move to a place where there are more jobs and assisting claimants to start businesses are wise investments. This government wants to let the people get out of that unemployment trap.
The third recommendation from the other place stops the government from developing innovative approaches to getting people back into the workforce. It also offers new appeal rights to claimants which make the system
March 13, 1990

far more complicated. These are examples of how the Liberals in the Senate are willing to play games with the unemployed.
When this government introduced the Labour Force Development Strategy, it did it to help both the unemployed and Canadian businesses by creating a better match between skilled workers, skilled employers and the skills that workers have.
Sometimes the things which will produce the best results do not fit all the demands of the UI Act. For example, if a person is starting a business, they are not eligible for UI. Bill C-21 gives this flexibility to make UI more responsive to today's needs by experimenting with new and better ways of helping the unemployed. That is what this bill is all about, being responsive to today's needs.
While much of what the Senate wants to do in its fourth recommendation on the government's annual development plan for UI can be supported, one aspect certainly cannot. The Senate wants the power to approve or reject that plan. No one in this House can seriously accept the need for such a new power to that place.
Their fifth amendment cuts back one of the basic principles behind this bill. It cuts back by relaxing penalties for people who quit their jobs without just cause, or who are fired for misconduct. In response to sincere concerns about the definition of just cause for quitting a job, this House approved the Minister of Employment and Immigration's amendments to C-21, to ensure that people would not be penalized unfairly.
Now the Liberal senators want to change our decision to strengthen the penalties for people who quit. The Liberal senators in the other House want to to send a signal to people that it is all right to quit their job because UI pays. We must reject this type of thinking. Enough is enough.
Recommendation No. 7 from the Senate would do one thing, but it would have a major impact on this country's deficit. Members will know the one message that has come clear from coast to coast, is: "Government cut your deficit and cut your debt".
Government Orders
Recommendation No. 7 would force the government to pay a large share of the cost of the unemployment insurance program with money that we simply do not have. No one can seriously suggest that the government should spend money on a program just because they used to do it. Yet the Liberals in the Senate are willing to see all the government's deficit raised by more than $1.5 billion a year for the range of amendments in their message to this House. Well I say, no way.
This government is willing to amend the UI Act to better protect fishermen, a group whose benefits have not been touched by this bill. It cannot be willing to go along with a scheme to play political games with the government's ability to make regulations.
The bill which this House passed was a sincere attempt to balance many different interests in order to improve UI in a realistic way. The amendment which the government is offering here tonight, in response to the message from the other place, is part of that improvement. However, we must reject amendments that increase the deficit. We must reject amendments that remove innovation from the program, and we must reject amendments that delay needed changes.
Let us talk now about improving training and improving unemployment insurance protection. The Liberals in the Senate have spent months claiming that C-21 will lead to destruction of the unemployment insurance program.
This is absolute nonsense and it is not true. Bill C-21 is designed to encourage more and better training of working people by the private sector. Bill C-21 is designed to use UI funds to create new opportunities for jobs and make UI a more active program. This is a major improvement over confining UI to passive reactive measures. But UI is still a program which is responsive to the different employment needs of different communities across this country.
The government has ensured that UI is responsive to regional needs. In areas where unemployment is high, the vast majority of claimants will not see any change in their benefits. We recognize that many of the jobs in areas such as Cape Breton and western Newfoundland are seasonal. For these people and for their communities UI is an important form of income support. For that reason people in these particular areas and in others

March 13, 1990
Government Orders
with higher levels of unemployment will still need only 10 weeks of work to qualify for benefits.
The government has also recognized the special situation of self-employed fishermen. While Liberals suggest that the government is ready to abandon these people the reality is very different.
Another important change the minister has made will make UI fairer by extending UI protection to workers who are 65 years of age and older. Many of these people want to keep working and deserve the same rights as younger workers. That is exactly what this bill is going to do.
But C-21 does more than change some of the UI rules. It will implement labour force development strategy. Labour force development strategy is an important initiative of this government and will make a real improvement in Canada's ability to compete in the world economy.
An active UI program is one which does more than mail out the cheques to people who have lost their jobs. An active UI program provides chances for people to gain new skills. It provides chances for people to explore new opportunities which will help them get and keep better jobs.
The government will work with the private sector to improve the amount and quality of training which employers provide. We want to bring the level of training up to that of our major trading partners.
The government will devote more funds to human resource planning, skills needed by new workers such as improved apprentice training, and the Industrial Adjustment Service and Community Futures. With this money, the government can work with employers, workers, communities and help them better meet the challenges of a changing workplace and a more competitive world economy.
The Labour Force Development Strategy will increase the money available to train people collecting UI so that they can get skills needed for better and more permanent jobs. The strategy will also allow Canada to experiment with new and innovative approaches to meet the needs of the working people. By providing funds to UI claimants to become entrepreneurs or to move to places
where more jobs are available, Bill C-21 will assist individuals and communities all across the country.
It is not always possible and nor is it simple to take the jobs to the people. People need to have the ability to go to where the jobs are. Unlike the Liberal senators, this government is committed to ensuring that Canadians have all the skills they need to be active players in a changing economy. Bill C-21 will make UI a more effective tool in meeting those needs.
People have always been told that the Senate was a place for sober second thought. Recently it has become a place for political games by people who can use their appointed status to frustrate legislation passed by a democratically elected House.
The senators said that they would set up a special committee to let people speak who had not testified before a legislative committee. Why was it that 54 of the witnesses represented affiliated groups and individuals who had already testified before the legislative committee? Why did the special committee in that other House decide to hear from the same list of groups who had opposed virtually everything that this government had opposed? Why did the special committee in the Senate ignore respected experts in the field of unemployment? I guess it is because they wanted to present one side of the story. They did not want an unbiased opinion. They wanted to spread scare stories because they are not really interested in a serious review of the real, positive impact of this particular bill.
The special Senate committee was also determined to delay this process as long as possible. This House passed Bill C-21 last November 6. The special committee of the Senate did not meet for three weeks after that. It did not present its report to the Senate until February 14. That is uncalled for.
Our Bill C-21 recognizes the needs of areas with higher unemployment rates by creating a table which makes the system simpler and fairer for claimants. But instead of passing Bill C-21, and our permanent variable entrance requirements, the Liberals in the Senate decided to delay the bill. The delay of this bill in that other House means that many people who would be eligible today cannot qualify. Canadians know that Liberal senators are the ones to blame for this. It is too bad because
March 13, 1990

those people who do need the support, who do need the training, who do need the assistance and maybe the portability to go elsewhere and get jobs have been held back, absolutely held back.
It has been a pleasure to speak in the House because the UI bill has needed to be reviewed and it has needed to be amended for quite some time. What we are doing is giving flexibility, recognizing the needs of high unemployment regions. We are recognizing the concerns of our fishermen in the Atlantic provinces especially, who are going through some very difficult times, and this government will support them, absolutely.
The one thing that this bill recognizes is the changing needs and that this country has to compete with international global trade. If we are going to have the people in place who can meet our trading partners head on we have got to train them. We have to give them the skills and the tools that allow them to go out there and compete because I will tell you that this country is only as economically healthy as the goods and services we produce and the goods and services that we sell.
In conclusion, we want to modernize the system to meet the current needs and, indeed, our future needs. We want to make a more flexible system. We want to remove disincentives from the system. We want the UI system to function both as a bridge back to employment and an important income support system. We want to address the urgent national need to develop our human resources, including the young, the middle-aged and the elderly, to meet the needs and the challenges in the decade that lies ahead of us. These amendments simply do not address these specific issues.
I want to add my support for the motion that was put forth by the hon. government House leader yesterday and I urge my fellow members to do the same thing.

Mr. Speaker, I sat here on Monday and listened to a speech from the new government House leader. He ranted and raved about the inequities of the Senate and he almost got apoplectic as he ranted about the subject. It was unbelievable. It was one of those performances one expects to see on the stage where one of the actors got carried away, but he got carried away with his own rhetoric.
Government Orders
Mr. Speaker, it is hard for me to concentrate with all this yelling across the way. Anyway, what he did do, with all the ranting and raving, was to display what I can only describe as a profound ignorance of constitutional law and practice.
I think it is time that he listened to some of the reasoned arguments that we, on this side of the House, have put forward in respect of this particular series of amendments. In my view, the government House leader should have studied a little bit before he came into the House and started speaking about constitutional practice.
We know, however, that he is new, and we can forget and forgive. But I want to point out for my hon. friend across the way that this party got a new House leader about a month ago and a month later the former government House leader got transferred. He was turned into mincemeat by our House leader and I can only warn the new House leader for the government that he soon may be mincemeat as well. I would like to turn to what he said. I could quote extensively from him but I would not want to bore any hon. members. I know it was one of the most tedious speeches we have listened to for a long time except that the government House leader went into orbit. What he said was some stuff and nonsense here on page 9093 of Hansard for yesterday. He said:
If I may I will quote from a book by Mr. F. A. Kunz entitled The Modem Senate of Canada which deals with the period up to 1963. We have not had any political scientist look at the Senate since then and I can understand why not.
Those are the words from the government House leader. What an incredible speech, Mr. Speaker.
Let me read from R. MacGregor Dawson and W. F. Dawson's book, Democratic Government of Canada, Fifth Edition, revised by Norman Ward. This is the 1989 edition, by the way, so the government House leader will know that there are political scientists still writing about the Upper House, the other place in this Parliament. I would suggest he get them out and read them. He is the government House leader, he is supposed to know something about this. Anyway, it says at page 63:
Whether or not the Senate has the constitutional power to amend a money bill has long been a matter of unsettled dispute between the two Houses.

If the hon. member had been paying attention, I said it was MacGregor Dawson.
The House of Commons, relying on the British parallel of the House of Lords, has always insisted that the Senate possessed no such power. The Senate, on the other hand, has never accepted this in theory, and in practice has repeatedly made its point, even amending bills which have dealt exclusively with matters of finance.
This one does not, I point out.
In these cases the House has often accepted the amendments, but has added the futile proviso that they were not to be considered as constituting a precedent.
In summary, it may be said that the Senate, although severely handicapped, has been able to do some genuinely useful work. It revises and checks legislation sent up from the Commons-
I could go on, Mr. Speaker, but there is a second book. I would like to read from Professor C.E.S. Franks' book-these are my own copies I should inform the minister-entitled The Parliament of Canada, published by the University of Toronto Press in 1987, another recent work by a political scientist of repute. I quote from page 193 of this work which reads:
The activities of the Senate in its investigative studies and in its revision of legislation are a useful complement to the work of the House of Commons. In both of these spheres of activity the experience and competence of the senators and the freedom they enjoy from the partisan and other pressures of the Commons add a valuable dimension to their work. The Senate has been criticized for being a lobby within government for big business but it would be more accurate to describe it as a defender of the rights of property, a function which it was intended to perform by the Fathers of Confederation.
I could go on again to read further from this learned work, but if the government House leader would like to borrow my copy he would be welcome to have it at any time.
I would like to go on to the rules of the House because that is really where the minister had difficulty. Page 45 of the new Standing Orders deals with this Business of Supply. Standing Order 79(1) provides:
This House shall not adopt or pass any vote, resolution, address or bill for the appropriation of any part of the public revenue, or of any tax or impost, to any purpose that has not been first recommended to the House by a message from the Governor General in the session in which such vote, resolution, address or bill is proposed.
From a simple reading of this rule, I suggest that if the bill in question proposes an increase in the charge on the public revenue, the royal recommendation is required.
All through the day we have listened to speeches from hon. members opposite saying how this bill saves money, it helps the government reduce its deficit; in other words, it reduces the charges on the public purse, on the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada. If it reduces the charges then it does not need a royal recommendation, and yet it had one. Who put it on? I suggest that probably the government House leader had something to do with it and, if he did, I suggest he was wrong and he had better go and check the precedents again.
Second, he relied on Section 53 of the Constitution Act which reads:
Bills for appropriating any Part of the Public Revenue, or for imposing any Thx or Impost, shall originate in the House of Commons.
It does not say they cannot be amended in the Senate. It says they "shall originate in the House of Commons". Bill C-21 originated in this House; it has been to the Senate; and now it is back. It does not say anything in there about the Senate's power to amend a money bill.
The only place where the minister was able to point out something about the Senate's power to amend money bills was in Standing Order 80 of the House of Commons. He read it and he read it as though it were the Constitution. If you turn to page 9096 of Hansard you will see that the minister was clearly getting very, very confused. I think it is safe to say this minister is so far in over his head he is completely lost. After quoting Standing Order 80 he had the gall to say this:
It would be in contempt of this House for hon. members to stand up and say that they do not care what Standing Order 80 says, they intend to agree with the Senate's butchering of this Standing Order.
Imagine a government House leader making a statement like that. It is unbelievable. As I say, his whole speech was unbelievable. Standing Order 80(1) reads:
All aids and supplies granted to the Sovereign by the Parliament of Canada are the sole gift of the House of Commons-
We agree with that statement. This bill is not "aids and supplies". This bill is slash; cut, cut, cut. This is taking money out of the pockets of the poor in Canada, of the unemployed in Canada, of the people who deserve better from this government. This bill is a contempt of the people of Canada, not just of this House. In
March 13, 1990

condemning the Senate for trying to help these people, the government House leader is showing Tory arrogance on an impressive scale.
Nevertheless, I want to turn to the rules relating to this issue because there has been a clear misunderstanding of them. I have here May's twenty-first edition and I would like to read some citations from it.
If the government House leader had been so concerned that these amendments from the Senate were out of order, why would he propose a message sending them back? If they were contrary to Standing Order 80(1), why did he not get up on his feet and instead argue that they were out of order and ask Your Honour to so rule?
I will tell you why he did not. He knew they were in order, yet he tried to pretend in his speech that they were out of order without actually saying so. He went through all this stuff and nonsense, saying that the Standing Order did not properly apply, that somehow it was tied in with the Constitution. He read every section he could find.
He got completely confused and obviously he completely befuddled every other member of the government who spoke on this subject because they have all agreed with the nonsense he spouted out yesterday, saying that the Senate was somehow acting improperly. The Senate has acted within its constitutional rights.
I suggest that any member of this House could have moved any of the amendments that have come down to this House from the Senate. We could have moved them at any stage on this bill, and they would have been in order. The government House leader knows that full well.
In support of that I would like to cite May's twenty-first edition. At page 713 Erskine May describes how it is that Parliament gets control of the public expenditure. It is sanctioned in two ways. I quote:
(1) It is initiated by a money resolution imposing a charge payable "out of moneys to be provided by Parliament" which receives confirmation by specific enactment;
Government Orders
(2) It is subsequently presented to the House of Commons in the form of an estimate which receives final sanction in the Appropriation Act.
It is our submission that the normal practice with Estimates is that they be presented with a message from His Excellency which recommend those Estimates to the House. Based on those Estimates, we grant aids and supplies to Her Majesty.
This bill, the Unemployment Insurance Act, constitutes a charge on the public revenue of Canada, a statutory charge. It is not granted. The moneys for payment are not granted as aids and supplies as defined in Standing Order 80(1) of this House. It is completely in accordance with British constitutional practice.
The Minister of Justice should be listening. She may need this lesson some day, in case within another two weeks she becomes government House leader because the previous one is going to be mincemeat when our House Leader get through with him.

Mr. Speaker, I am tempted to say it is a pleasure to rise to speak on this bill, but frankly it seems, as I reflect over the last several months, that not only I but many other members in this House time and time again have risen to speak on it.
I must say I envy the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands who has just spoken, not so much because of the profoundness or the wisdom of what he had to say, but because of the fact that he had a voice with which to say it. Nevertheless, I shall do my best to make a few observations which I trust will be helpful to this House in trying to make a decision on how best to vote on this very important measure once again before us tonight.
I look back over the history of this bill and I am simply amazed at the litany of times it has come before this House for discussion. Are we to discuss this bill interminably and never get on with any other business of the nation? I do not know what my hon. friends opposite are up to or what their aspirations are, but indeed I do have some thoughts which I will share, if my voice holds out tonight, as to what our friends down the hall are up to.
This bill has been before this House since June 1, and I hope that this is the last time that it is here for our consideration. I must ask: Who are these people down the hall who send this bill back to us so many times? Who are these people who have given themselves a mandate to disrupt the business of this country, who have given
Government Orders
themselves a mandate to ignore and have fun with democracy?
We are told in the history books that when this country was created and the British North America Act was brought in 1867, the Senate was to be a place for sober second thought. I understood that the intention was that they would seek out some outstanding citizens, perhaps some elder statesmen, that these people would sit in the Senate, and that they would review the decisions and the legislation brought forward by the elected representatives of the people. This was some 125 years ago, before we had the same commitment to democracy that we have in this country today. The idea was that what would come from the other place would be wisdom, and not simply the Machiavellian actions of a bunch of hacks.
I regret to say that what we are getting is not contribution to legislation but disruption. I regret to say that they are trying to break the legislative process, and not build and contribute to it. What is happening in the other place is a travesty of democracy. I regret to say that I am one of those few who believes that the Senate could have a very useful role to play in contributing to the democratic process. I believe it should be, as my hon. friend from Calgary has just said, a place of important contributions. Unfortunately, I think they could well lead to the demise, the destruction, and ultimately the abandonment of that other place.
When the senators set up their special committee they said they wanted to hear the people who had not been heard on this issue. We heard from members opposite today about how the legislative committee heard witnesses in a hasty manner across the country.
I must tell you, Mr. Speaker, that I was one of the members of that legislative committee. We heard many, many witnesses. It is interesting to note that 54 of the witnesses that we heard also appeared before the Senate committee. "Had they not been heard the first time", I ask hon. members opposite who were there, some of whom are in this chamber tonight. Of course they were heard. Why did that committee from the other place choose to hear from the same people from whom we had already heard?
I submit-and it is with great regret that I have to pass along this observation-that there were Machiavellian tactics being thought up in the other place. I suggest that the objective in the other place was not to participate, to contribute and to hear what Canadians have said. Canadians in my part of the country are telling me that they want to see an overhaul and a reform of the unemploy-

March 13, 1990
Government Orders
ment insurance system. They want to see an end to the cheating and a discouragement of the cheating. They want to see incentives for people to seek out and take advantage of employment opportunities. They want to see an unemployment insurance system that is active rather than passive in the way it helps people find themselves useful and fair employment in society.
I regret to say that the exercise we are engaged in here tonight is not one that is necessarily useful and helpful but is a redundant exercise forced upon this place by the people in the other place in a highly improper and irresponsible manner. It is interesting to note that we have had other precedents where the other place has dealt with legislation on the unemployment insurance system. It is interesting just for the record to review the track record of the other place with respect to legislation.
I am reminded, for example, that in 1977 there was Bill C-27. The minister of the day was the hon. Bud Cullen. The government was of a political stripe somewhat different from that of the incumbent government in this country today. It is interesting to review the provisions of that legislative back in 1977.
We had, for example, a change from a flat entrance requirement to a variable entrance requirement. We had a reduction in benefit duration for some claimants, a reduction perpetrated by the people on the other side. We had authorization of developmental uses for unemployment insurance funds. What an interesting concept. They should read Bill C-21. They would find the same idea there, including the idea and the use of funds as income maintenance for claimants on approved training courses. What an interesting idea.
The entrance requirement was hotly disputed at a House of Commons committee. Time allocation was used. Imagine that, Mr. Speaker, time allocation used by the Liberal government of the day to effect speedy passage of the bill through the House at that time.
On it went to the Senate, this contentious piece of legislation presenting a lot of the same principles that are quoted in Bill C-21. I know you can guess what happened in the Senate, Mr. Speaker. I know that you expect that the Senate set up a special committee and
toured Canada. It went to little towns like Canso, Nova Scotia to hear what the people thought.
Let me tell you what the record is, Mr. Speaker. It just so happens that the Senate received Bill C-27 on August 2, 1977 and reported the bill without amendment the following day, on August 3, 1977. Is that not a remarkable record to observe?
The following year we had Bill C-14 brought before the House of Commons, again by the hon. Bud Cullen as minister. This was a time when Prime Minister Trudeau wanted restraint measures brought in. What did the bill contain at that time? It is interesting to review the record. It contained higher entrance requirements for repeaters. Say it isn't not so. It contained higher entrance requirements for new entrants. Surely not in a bill introduced by a government of members opposite. It contained a reduction of benefit rate from two-thirds to 60 per cent. Surely they were not suggesting that the unemployed people on benefits should be drawing less money than they were before.
You are not going to believe this one. It contained recovery through the income tax system of a portion of UI benefits of high income claimants. Can you believe it, Mr. Speaker? This was in a bill introduced by a government of the people who now sit on the other side of this chamber.
At committee stage the government estimated that Bill C-14 would result in savings of $885 million in UI benefit payments. Is that not that a remarkable achievement? Now what happened to that bill? They did not wait until it left this place. It was pre-studied for three weeks by the Senate at that time, but rushed through the Senate, all stages with no amendment, on the same day as it received passage in the House, December 22, 1978. By the way, Royal Assent was achieved on that very same day.
What does one conclude, Mr. Speaker, about this history of behaviour with unemployment insurance legislation by those people in that other place? One can conclude but one thing, and that is that legislation in the other place is treated one way if it comes from a Liberal government and another way if it comes from a government headed by the Progressive Conservative Party of Canada. It is an appalling and shocking form of beha-
March 13, 1990

viour. This question can be put: Does this government listen to the people? Does it listen to sound advice?
