I hear my colleagues saying "yes", and they are absolutely, unequivocally correct about this.
This government has listened. It has reviewed with great care all of the recommendations from the other place. I am pleased to say that some good recommendations came from the other place. Because this government listens, some of those recommendations have been incorporated and are accepted in the motion that we put forward tonight. For example, we recognize the impact which illiteracy has on Canadian workers and on employers. The lack of basic skills is an impediment to further training for that reason. Recommendation 1 is worth including in this bill.
One could go on and speak about other changes that are there. For example, one that is of particular interest to me is the one that affects fishermen. In the eighth recommendation the Senate has also asked this House to consider removing a subsection in the UI act which has been in place for almost 20 years. That subsection would allow the Governor in Council to remove benefits for self-employed fishermen from the UI act at any time. With the concerns shared by all Canadians in the fishery, I think it is very appropriate that this recommendation should be accepted because there is no question that fishermen are in a very unique position with respect to unemployment insurance.
As a member who represents some 8,000 people employed in the fishing industry, I have some familiarity with the impact of unemployment insurance on fishermen. I find that people quite often ask me: "How come fishermen are treated differently from everybody else?"
The answer is quite simple and it cannot be repeated often enough. How come farmers and people in the forest industry are not in the same situation? It is for a very simple reason. It is because fishermen are self-employed. They are the only self-employed people included in the unemployment insurance scheme. The reason they are included is that unlike every other industry theirs is regulated directly by the government, and
Government Orders
therefore fishermen are told that they cannot go and fish from time to time. That is why they have the special provision. It is properly there. It should continue to be there, and I am delighted to see that among many things this government has maintained that provision.
I could go on and speak on more of the recommendations, most of which quite frankly are nonsense and most of which quite frankly are clearly and unequivocally intended to do nothing but disrupt the business of the country, nothing but try to destroy the piece of legislation that has been brought before us. It would simply tie up the government and the country and continue to do what those people over there are doing right now, that is, deny the benefits of Bill C-21 to the people of this country.
I think this is an outrageous thing, coming from an area as I do where we are suffering fish plant closures, that plants are closing down and people are being put out of employment. What is the Senate of Canada doing for them? It is forcing them to have to meet 20 weeks in order to qualify for unemployment insurance. That is the concern that those people over there have for the people of Atlantic Canada and the people of the fishing communities. I for one think that it is absolutely and utterly outrageous.
What is their approach to unemployment insurance? What is it they are looking to have done? They seem to think that the only thing unemployment insurance should do is put people on a payout and leave them there until such time as their job comes back again. What happens if you are in an industry where your job is not going to come back again? What happens if you are in a fishing community and there is not enough fish and the plant has to close? The job is never going to come back. Do you just subsidize people forever? No. You have an active program that is going to help them find another approach. The whole thrust of this legislation is to shift from a passive to an active approach in unemployment insurance.
There are many points I have been wanting to make, but I will make only one last point and then I will conclude my remarks. There have been suggestions that this government does not have a mandate to do what is

March 13, 1990
Government Orders
being done in Bill C-21. Nothing could be further from the truth or greater nonsense. Check the record.
Do we have a mandate? They say it was not a part of our 1988 platform. If they check the record they will see that the Prime Minister of this country promised the best adjustment programs in the world. I would like to say that with Bill C-21, together with other measures from the Labour Force Development Strategy, the Prime Minister and the government of Canada have in fact delivered on that program as best they can.
They have allowed us to move our UI system from passive to active, which is something that Canadians support. Interestingly enough, it is something Mr. Timer, the former leader of the opposition, supported when he was running for office in 1984. We have forgotten that and he forgot that. Do we have a mandate? Did Mr. Trudeau have a mandate for wage and price controls in 1974? I do not recall that he did. I remember him saying: "Zap, you are frozen" to Mr. Stanfield and I remember in 1985 that he imposed wage and price controls.
This government has a mandate. It came on November 21, 1988. That is the mandate that counts. That is the mandate that will be renewed in 1993.

Mr. Speaker, it gives me a lot of pain to have to address this subject tonight and the rehashing of the worst attempt at setting back the working people and the unemployed in Canada that we have witnessed in Canadian history for a long, long time.
Yesterday, we had a delegation that met both with the NDP caucus and also with the Liberal caucus, representing not only the Canadian Labour Congress but a number of other organizations, most of them unaffiliated with that Congress. The delegation included Shirley Carr, president of the CLC; Louis Laberge, president of the Quebec Federation of Labour; Jim McCambley, president of the Canadian Federation of Labour; Gerald Larose, president of the Confederation of National Trade Unions; Kitty O'Callaghan, president of the Canadian Teachers Federation; Lorraine Page, president of the Quebec Teaching Congress; Kathleen Connors, president of the National Federation of Nurses' Unions;
and Louis Lacroix, president of the Canadian Conference of Teamsters. This delegation represented in all close to 4 million dues-paying working Canadians.
Their message was very clear to both ourselves and the other opposition party, but that government that pretends to represent the majority of Canadians or the plurality of Canadians, did not even have the decency to agree to meet with the representatives of 4 million working Canadians. That is absolutely shameful, particularly when the subject at hand has to do with one of the most important parts of the Canadian social safety net that this government seems intent on putting the axe to.
Because the government did not see fit to meet and to listen, for the record I want to read part of the statement of those representatives, not all of whom have any strong connection with the New Democratic Party by the way. There are a number of organizations here representing a pretty broad cross-section of working people.
The leaders of this labour coalition opposed to Bill C-21 were meeting with the Liberal and NDP parliamentary caucuses to reiterate their opposition to this legislation. The coalition made every effort to meet with the employment minister and the Conservative caucus but their request was denied. They stated:
Unemployment insurance is fundamental to the economic and
social security of all workers; unionized and non-unionized, fulltime and part-time, private sector and public sector.
In saying this, they were playing the traditional role of working people under the labour movement in Canada, of organized workers, in speaking not only for themselves but for unorganized workers from one end of Canada to the other, because who else has ever spoken for them?
We had challenges from the other side of the House today saying: "You are only speaking for the labour bosses, you are only speaking for those unions that are in the NDP's pocket", or vice versa as they like to put it. That is simply not true, because if you look back through the social and economic history of Canada, virtually no one outside of the democratic organized working trade union movement of Canada has spoken up for unorganized workers in every part of this nation.
They went on to state:
March 13, 1990

Bill C-21 destroys many of the principles upon which the unemployment insurance system has been built.
That is true.
Its most basic purpose-insuring workers against the loss of earnings-is seriously undermined. And the tripartite financing of UI by employers, workers and government developed over the past fifty years is destroyed by this Bill.
I suggest that the government knows that, despite all its prattling, because this bill is just the latest in a long series of economic measures that this government has taken, as did in many ways the Trudeau government before it, to try to push Canadian workers further to the back of the bus. It started with the wage and price controls in October, 1976. Real incomes of Canadian workers have dropped ever since then. There has been a continuous attack ever since that time by successive federal governments to put workers back in what those people over there and sometimes these people to our right seem to think is "their place".
Canadian workers have a right to expect something better of their governments whether or not they vote for them, because any government in a democratic society is supposedly elected to serve the interests of all of the people. To ignore the legitimate needs, aspirations and demands of some 4 million people, to give proper accordance to the security of their members and the people they are elected to represent, is fundamentally wrong in a democratic society.
The delegation went on to state:
In addition to the $1.3 billion of cuts in benefits to unemployed workers, Bill C-21 will shift $5 billion of government financial responsibilities to worker and employer UI premium payers.
In doing that, the government paid no attention whatsoever to ability to pay, neither of working people nor of the business community. Not much has been said about that part of it, but a number of employers have objected to this bill for precisely that reason, especially employers in the small business community.
The entire cost of what is a social program and a social insurance program is now being shifted out of general revenue, that portion of it that used to be properly charged to general revenue of the nation, and being put solely on employer and employee premiums. Those premiums do not make any distinction as to whether an employer is running a profitable enterprise, an unprofitable enterprise, or a marginal enterprise. It is just one other shift away from progressive taxation, whether in
Government Orders
the corporate sector or in the area of individual income tax.
The $5 billion of government financial responsibilities have been shifted to worker and employer UI premium payers. What constitutes that $5 billion? An amount of $2.5 billion of government contributions for UI extended benefits resulting from high regional unemployment will be withdrawn. This is an end to regional equity. How much of this entire attack on the unemployment insurance system and in a sense privatizing it by putting it solely into the contributions of employers and employees is a result of the whole strategy behind the free trade agreement? The exact promises that the Prime Minister made in the last federal election that free trade would not mean a destruction of the Canadian social safety net is obviously false. This is the first major attack in line with that philosophy and commitment obviously made at the time of the free trade agreement that we have seen.
Included also in this $5 billion is about $300 million of government subsidies for UI fishery benefits which will be transferred to premium payers. Fifteen per cent of UI premiums, about $2 billion a year, will be used to finance the purchase of training courses, resettlement, business start-ups, wage subsidies and other labour adjustment programs now financed from general government revenues.
What does some of that financing have to do with income maintenance or unemployment insurance? Training people is fine. It is laudable. We need better and expanded training programs in a wide variety of areas in Canada. But it is a totally improper charge on employers and employees to pay for education. That is something that ought to come out of general revenue, whether through the provinces or through the federal government. There is no excuse. There is no legitimate argument that can be made to have that financed totally out of employer and employee premiums. It simply does not belong there. It is bad social cost accounting.
The delegation went on to state:
Bill C-21 will negatively affect a million unemployed workers. Tens of thousands who would have previously qualified will not even qualify for benefits because of the higher entrance requirement. And hundreds of thousands will exhaust their benefits months before they find a job because of reduced duration.
The proposal to significantly reduce benefit levels and restrict the opportunity to qualify for UI will hit hardest lower income groups, people with short term or part-time employment and disadvantaged regions. It does not provide flexibility for individuals and specific

March 13, 1990
Government Orders
occupation groups to qualify where employment opportunities are periodically weak for cyclical, sectoral, seasonal or regional reasons.
To those of us who come from resource areas of this country like the east and west Kootenays in the province of British Columbia, we particularly understand, and the people we represent especially understand, just how this bill particularly hits and hurts them and hurts the communities in which they live.
The delegation further stated:
The primary purpose of unemployment insurance has been and must continue to be the insurance of workers' earnings while unemployed or on training. The use of UI premiums to finance non-income support programs is a back-door tax on workers to finance programs which should be financed from general government revenues. Several employer organizations have publicly expressed their opposition to this misuse of UI premiums.
That simply reinforces the comments I made earlier and it is correct.
The withdrawal of government funding will also place the pooled-risk unemployment insurance fund in a cumulative deficit position.
We find it totally unacceptable that labour adjustment programs should be financed by cuts in benefits and benefit entitlements to unemployed workers who have paid premiums for insurance against the interruption of earnings.
With this Bill, the government has significantly weakened the principal labour adjustment program in Canada. As the major stakeholder we ask the government to withdraw this Bill. This Bill in no way represents the promises the government made in the last election with respect to unemployment insurance or labour adjustment programs.
That was not a long message that that delegation had to bring to Parliament yesterday and attempted to bring to the government yesterday and to the Conservative caucus. Surely, it is not asking too much that that caucus over there and the government that it supports should have taken the time to listen. Sure the members can say: "We have heard this song before". But it is like the Bourbons in post-revolutionary France. They forgot nothing and they learned nothing. If they have to listen to the same message over and over again in order to
learn something, perhaps that is what they should have done. It is not too late.
We have heard a number of contributions to this debate that seem to suggest that when the Liberal party was in power with Mr. Trudeau and Mr. Pearson and Mr. King before that, and God knows how far back it goes, everything was hunky-dory for Canadian workers. We know, and anybody who knows anything about Canadian history, realizes that that was not the case either. Politics is about bargaining power.
It is interesting to note even though this party and its predecessor, the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation, have never held federal power, it has only been in those times when either we or our predecessor have been high in the polls or have come close to winning a major province such as Ontario, or held the balance of power in this federal Parliament, that we have had any significant progress in any major field of social legislation in the history of Canada. That goes back, Mr. Speaker as you well know, to 1926 when Mr. Woodsworth and Mr. Heaps with only two members held the balance of power. At that time they had a promise from Mackenzie King, the gentleman who said, "Do nothing by halves that can be done by quarters", and God did he ever prove it.
Somebody over there suggests that that is what it is all about. Yes, that is what politics is about to people who do not directly represent ordinary working people across this country, or if they do represent them, do not understand them and do not understand the kinds of problems they have.
There were two commitments made in an exchange of correspondence between Mr. King and Mr. Woodsworth at that time. One was that the government would immediately move to bring in a system of old age pensions. That promise was acted upon rather quickly. We then had to wait from 1926 until the end of World War II, some 20 years until, coincidentally, the CCF was leading the polls nationally across Canada and came within four seats of winning the Government of Ontario, when the Liberal Government finally decided they had better listen to the voice of some political bargaining power and finally act on a promise made in 1926 to bring in unemployment insurance.
There is nothing wrong in responding to the voice of the people as expressed in elections, as expressed in polls

or however they want to express them. There is nothing wrong with that. But when you have governments that only seem to respond to threat and never attempt to lead public opinion because they want to do something that is right for ordinary working people, then there is something wrong with the democratic process. There is a time that politicians ought to lead, not just follow and not just buckle to pressure, even when that pressure is good pressure.
We then had another dearth after the immediate post-war era. There was bit of a lull, except that there were things happening in the provinces across Canada, particularly in the province of Saskatchewan, when despite fierce opposition, hysterical opposition from both Liberals and Conservatives, hospital insurance was established in 1947-1948. We were Bolsheviks, we were Commies, we were pinkos and we were Nazis. Anything that could have been a bad term was hurled at us by both Liberals and Tories right across the country, because we wanted to bring in hospital insurance, old age pensions, and these other things.
Now we have a Conservative government and the Prime Minister has stated: "If we get a second term, you will never recognize this country". Well, they got then-second term. If they continue to get through measures like the one that is now before us and other ones that we have seen in the last four or five years, particularly in the last year and a half, this country will be unrecognizable, but it will not be the better for it.
After that period, we then moved on into the period of Mr. Diefenbaker. He did some worthwhile things. Much more than a Conservative, Mr. Diefenbaker was a western populist. All you have to do is look at the record and see how much time the best known Conservatives across the country spent in trying to shove a knife into his back. But he did listen and he did manage to implement and put in place nationally what the province of Saskatchewan had pioneered earlier.
We then had the minority Pearson years. We had medicare then again established, which was pioneered by Tommy Douglas and the NDP in the province of Saskatchewan, despite Liberal attempts to kick down the door of the legislatures, and fierce opposition from the Conservatives. Everybody got into the name-calling phase again.

Now we have a Conservative government in its second term that seems determined to try to move working people once again to the back of the bus, and entrench in a free trade agreement and in other ways, a right-wing reactionary agenda, which if it is successful, will put this country on the back roads for a long, long time. We do not intend to support that kind of action and we will do everything we can to stop it.

Mr. Speaker, thank you for the opportunity to address Bill C-21 again, and I hope for the last time. First, to give you some advance notice, I want to speak rather briefly on this so as to allow my hon. colleague from Wetaskiwin some time before the vote this evening, I will not be taking the full 20 minutes and I hope those who are following me will extend the same courtesy to my colleague.
The delay in the Senate, which I am sure you have heard referred to many times before as being an unelected and unaccountable body, has resulted in this matter being placed before us in a most unacceptable fashion. At the risk of breaking the heart of someone who might be listening, I might tell you that I have had many mothers-to-be calling me and asking: "When is this bill going to be passed? I am currently employed outside of the home. I am looking for some help that this bill will give me. I know it is a positive thing; it will provide me with an opportunity to raise my family for the length of time that is required as an appropriate period and one that will get our children off and running to a good start and one that will not require institutionalized care at an early stage when children require love, affection and have the desire to be held".
Therefore, there are many people out there who are non-politically aligned and who are looking at this bill with a great deal of anticipation. I encourage all members in this House to respect their wishes, to respect the wish to the natural mother and to respect the fact that this is a matter that is being placed in our hands and subsequently in the hands of the public in the form of a bill that requires only the understanding and good common sense of that other body and I hope that it does respond in a positive sense.

March 13, 1990
Government Orders
In taking the time to prepare a few comments about the subject before us, I could not help but observe that perhaps an understanding of what unemployment insurance is might be of some benefit to those who are debating the bill, some benefit to those who have questions with respect to some of the garbage that has been floating aloft in an attempt to grasp the inattentive with the thought that they might succumb to perhaps a distorted view of some in this House. I want to say that unemployment insurance is very simply a scheme, a plan, an endeavour whereby the employer and the employee get together, by way of an agreement, and insure the fact that once the employee's labour should no longer be made available to the employer, that the employee would be the recipient of some funds that would provide a lifestyle which is deemed by society to be generally acceptable, given the circumstances.
Beyond that, and this bill does provide, and the government has said many times, that should there ever be the necessity to have the government step in and fill in the void caused by an emergency situation which has caused the unemployment insurance pool to dry up, the government will be there. I think that that is the role of the government. The government is there to ensure that if you slip and fall, it is there to pick you up. But, I do not think it is a government's role to tie a leash around your neck and drag it behind you to suit its own political agenda. I cannot concur with that at all. Government should be there to encourage people to be self-motivated rather than having the government pour its own agenda into the mind of humanity and expect humanity to follow it.
The government's responsibilities indeed go as far as Bill C-21. In fact, they go much further than that. Many of my colleagues have made reference not only to the two or three amendments to which the other place has made reference that are deemed to be acceptable but it also goes beyond the simple up-front issues to the more gut-wrenching issues of trying to run a country with a social conscience on one hand, and with a budget on the other hand. There is a mentality which suggests that one can ignore what programs cost, just be up front, be first to commit yourself as a government body or as a political body in the pursuit of a social good, and damn the financial consequences.
Sooner or later you get to a point where future generations are faced with the consequences that I think are placed before us right now. There have been some political parties which have said that they were the first in developing a medicare plan. I understand that medicare has progressed rather rapidly to the point where the city of Regina, some very few short years ago possessed not one CAT-scan machine. We did find that our citizens had to go to Edmonton and to Saskatoon. Finally, the city of Regina obtained a CAT-scan machine. One CAT-scan machine was not good enough. We now have three CAT-scan machines. Three times as many CAT-scan machines as we need, but nevertheless because they are available now, in order to get a proper physical in the city of Regina, you must go and get a complete CAT-scan. If you do not like that doctor's opinion you simply go to another doctor and get another CAT-scan. I do not know how much these machines cost but I am told they are in the millions of dollars. Where is the logic attached to this? Who would dare run on the political platform that we have got too many CAT-scan machines. The simple truth of the matter is that in consultation with specialists in our city we have simply oversupplied in that particular medical commodity. I am not being a medical specialist. I do not know where that all ends.
Yes, socialism running rampant at election time is likely to get you some public support. But on the other hand, once in power how does one pay for all these things? How does one pay for all these so-called benefits that simply take a nod of the head and it is there- we can afford anything. We have this magical machine in the basement of this building that not only pumps out brand new dollar bills, but it pumps out more gold than you and I could ever spend.
The bill before us does address some specific issues that I would like to make reference to, if I have time. They do enter into the area of youth and as well social assistance recipients, just to pick out two of the items of the bill because the bill is rather lengthy and I know others have spoken to it. Given the series of facts, and there are some three or four pages of facts that deal with the plight of youth in our system and deal with the fact that we have a high school drop-out situation that is not tolerable, given the fact that youth are currently entering into the market-place and not properly trained and equipped for a lot of the jobs that the industrial sector

requires of them, it is our goal, through the funding that we hope to raise through this bill, to provide for some additional training.
The same thing holds true for social assistance recipients. I have to relate a fact to you, Mr. Speaker. When I was the Mayor of Regina-you may not believe this but this actually happened-we and the provincial government plotted in an attempt to exploit the funds available to us through the unemployment insurance program. We took some city money, some provincial money, took someone off the welfare roll and said we are going to make work for you so that you can work long enough so you can go on unemployment insurance and collect pogey and rip off the federal system. We are in this governmental system to make sure that those kinds of slippages, or those attempts to rip the system off in fact deplete themselves. We are responsible to the Canadian taxpayer and to the tax dollar to ensure that the benefits that Canadians have elected us to provide for them remain to be a goal that they can attain.
I would like to conclude at an early time to allow my friend from Wetaskiwin to have the floor. I know he has worked many long minutes in preparing a full 20 minute dissertation that I am sure you and the House of Commons would dearly like to listen to. I will conclude by thanking you for the opportunity that I have had to address Bill C-21.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to review this bill in the sense of its stand with the Canadian constitution. Our friends opposite and the government are calling this a finance bill. It is not. My hon. friend for Kingston and the Islands made that abundantly clear earlier this evening.
In 1937, the Rowell commission report outlined the of fairness of the division of financial responsibility between the federal government and the provinces. They did that because during the depression years of the thirties some provincial governments went broke because they were incapable of looking after the unemployed and those who required social payments.
When this report was brought in, an amendment to the BNA was necessary. It is very interesting to note that that amendment was brought in in the summer of 1940 and passed through this House of Commons. At that time, the amendment became 2(A) of the BNA of 1940.
Government Orders
It was added on to Section 91 of the BNA and Section 1 was amended by inserting thereafter Item 2 following the regulation of trade and commerce and 2(a) simply became unemployment insurance.
Let us look at what that really meant. In the distribution of those powers it meant the prevention and relief of unemployment. This is a section from the Rowell-Si-rois Commission report. They were two very distinguished judges, and there were others working on it. This was one of the most intensive studies ever undertaken by any royal commission that we have had in this country on financial divisions between the provinces and the federal government.
I want you to realize that this report encompassed the whole country in those days. The provinces were in terrible financial straits because they carried the burden of the unemployed. They carried the burden of those who needed assistance during those Depression years, without having the financial capability to pay for it.
In the introduction of the Rowell-Sirois Commission report, under the heading "Prevention and Relief of Unemployment as a Federal Responsibility" this is what those esteemed judges said: "The assumption of responsibility by the Dominion of Canada for relief or aid of unemployed employables would entail: (1) Complete financial responsibility."
I repeat for the members on the government side that in 1940 this meant complete financial responsibility by the federal government of this country. Under the second item they were to take over full control of its administration. For efficient administration, it would also be essential to do the following: that the Dominion define employability for purposes of administering unemployment aid.
I maintain that what this government is saying to the employers of this country and to the workers of this country is this: "We are no longer going to pay one red cent towards unemployment insurance programs in this country; you are going to pay your own. You small businessmen out there, you are going to have to pay more to keep up the unemployment insurance fund. You people who are working daily are employed and you are going to have to pay more to help out the others. This is a federal government of cheap skates. We are not going

Government Orders
to put up a single red cent towards the program". The government calls that efficient administration.
Here are some of the other recommendations: that the Dominion have full control of administration of employment aid; that a national employment service be established and administered by the Dominion without prejudice to the right of the province to continue or develop an employment service of its own; and that the Dominion be empowered to establish a system of compulsory unemployment insurance. Again, that refers to the federal government. I want to repeat that this was done in order to take some of the financial burden off the provinces which, obviously, could not afford it.
There is another thing that is very realistic in this whole deal. In the same Rowell-Sirois Commission report one of the recommendations and one of the understandings was that the provinces of this country would have the field of direct taxation to themselves. What is this federal government doing to the provinces today? It is entering into the direct taxation field. That is why you have double taxation.
The GST is going to become double taxation. The GST is a form of direct taxation. The government is robbing the provinces of this country of their basic constitutional right.
The Minister of Justice should listen to this because she is going to be reading it in the days ahead. In fact, she will be reading the history of how the government that she belongs to right now tore down the unemployment insurance system in this country and dumped the burden on to the provinces of this country. Even the Minister for Privatization before a legislative committee one day said to me that the provinces are getting off too light. He said that they should have some debt, too. Because you have good administration, because you are basing your government on the division of financial powers given to you by a royal commission in this country, you must see that this constitutional responsibility has been in the hands of the federal government for 50 years this coming July.
You are giving up that constitutional responsibility. You are backing away. You are not going to accept your responsibility. You did the same thing in the field of medicare. What did you do? You dumped on to the provinces post-secondary education. Then you had the
gall as the government to come forward and say that you are going to train people for another job. Is that not wonderful? You are going to train people for another job but you are taking money away from the provinces when it comes to post-secondary education, which simply proves that you are not all that committed to education at all. What reason do the workers of this country have to think that you are going to deal with them any better under this legislation?
Let us get from the provincial governments down to the municipalities and what effect this bill will have on them. You are going to have the welfare system in full tow at the provincial level because people are not going to get unemployment insurance for the periods that they need it. They are going to have that long waiting period for it. What if someone quits his job? Who is going to clarify why they quit and whether they were justified in doing it? Are you going to force them to work under cruel conditions, under mean conditions, and if they decide to quit their job you are going to take away their unemployment insurance? You are going to put those people on the doorsteps of every municipality across this country.
Here is something else that the royal commission report said 50 years ago. It should benefit this government today. "Nothing in the history of Canadian government has contributed more to the breakdown of public finance, or has been productive of greater waste in the economy than the attempt to hold local governments primarily responsible for unemployment as well as for relief". That was said just a little over 50 years ago.
This government belongs back in the early thirties. At the rate it is going it will put this country back into a recession. You are going to have this same situation all over again where provincial governments and municipalities are not going to be able to afford this.
If the municipalities are loaded with that financial burden, who is going to pay the tax bill? It is going to be the real estate people right in that municipality, the home dwellers, the small businesses, the factories, John Q. Public who buys a new home. They are going to be charged extra taxes. Your local taxes will go sky high to pay your welfare bills. That will be the inheritance of this government, and that will be the inheritance of you also.

Mr. Speaker, I rise in the House this evening to support the motion put forward by the government House leader.
Bill C-21 has been held up unnecessarily at the cost of the economically deprived, unemployed citizens of Canada. We must not delay this any further. I urge this House to support the motion.
Bill C-21 as presented in this motion will improve aspects which are fundamental to deal with the problem of unemployment in this country. It provides provisions for youth, provisions for training, provisions for older workers, provisions against abuse and other initiatives.
I wish to concentrate my comments on these very salient aspects which must be addressed in order to get the unemployment situation under control.
Bill C-21 does more than just change the rules, as other members have said tonight. It is an active program which provides opportunities for people to gain new and more permanent employment.
We support the minister's Labour Force Development Strategy that will be implemented by Bill C-21. Indeed, an important element in any employment strategy is to aim to train non-workers for the jobs available today and tomorrow. This is the initiative of this government. It will
make a strong improvement in Canada's ability to compete in the world economy.
The Labour Force Development Strategy includes the examination of the private sector to improve the amount and quality of training which employers provide. More funds will be devoted to human resource planning skills needed by new workers, such as improved apprentice training, the industrial adjustment service and community futures.
With this money the government can work with employers, workers and communities to help them better meet the challenges of today and to predict the needs of the workplace for tomorrow. All in all, this will result in nothing less than a positive step to make Canadians more competitive in a global setting by securing permanent jobs for Canadians.
On youth, the Labour Force Development Strategy incorporates key labour market facts, and this is seen in its approach toward youth. Studies show that the demand for highly skilled workers will rise dramatically. Of all jobs created between 1986 and the year 2000 it is projected that 64 per cent will require more than 12 years of education and training. Almost half of these new jobs will require more than 17 years of education. Occupations which require lower levels of education and training will represent a declining share of employment growth. To address these facts, the government is proposing an entry-level training program. At maturity it will benefit 40,000 to 50,000 participants a year. Many of the beneficiaries will be young people making the transition from school to work occupations outside of those currently covered by apprenticeship training. For example, financial and business management, computer programming, child care, hospitality and other service sector job areas are possible candidates for this program. Furthermore, there will be extensive consultations with industry, business, labour and interest groups, prior to any decisions regarding the design of entry-level training programs.
Another area of concern to be addressed is the apprenticeship program. Although it is a good model for providing many necessary skills, there are problems with the present system. First, women are not getting a chance under the present arrangements. Only 3 per cent of apprentices are women and they are concentrated in
March 13, 1990

such traditional trades as hairdressing and cooking. Outside those trades, the figure is a mere 1 per cent.
Second, there is as high dropout rate of 50 per cent. These are clearly unacceptable statistics and there must be action taken to rectify the problem. Through the implementation of Bill C-21, we can address this situation. Industry, labour and provinces will be consulted to get a plan of action accepted to remedy the problems with current apprenticeship systems.
It is imperative that governments and industry work together to ensure that this large investment in skills training is relevant to today's needs and is delivered in a cost-effective and efficient manner.
With respect to older workers, the recent demographic study by Health and Welfare Canada clearly indicates that there is a definite age shift and more and more seniors are staying in the workforce. Government programs must reflect society and Bill C-21 aims to do this. Under Bill C-21, the UI protection will be extended to cover all workers, regardless of age. As other members have said tonight, it is also clear from the Charter of Rights and Freedoms that workers cannot be discriminated against on the basis of age. Furthermore, these individuals have much to contribute to business in Canada. Bill C-21 eliminates this discrimination in UI.
In addition, the newly targeted income support and training funds will provide increased training opportunities, essential to ensuring the adjustment of displaced older workers. The stable employment and long job tenure of displaced older workers means that they often have skills unique to the firms in which they have worked. The new Labour Force Development Strategy complements the program for older worker adjustment by providing additional options. UI coverage will be available to all who want to work past age 65 and we wish to encourage those who do.
I would like to turn now to the issue of abuse in the UI system. In my riding I have received complaints from many small businesses, who note the abuse of the present system. One small business owner from Wetaski-win writes: "Possible workers would rather stay on unemployment insurance. Are these people reporting
Government Orders
the fact that they have been offered full-time jobs at a reasonable rate of pay"?
The strategy incorporated in Bill C-21 is designed to protect unemployed workers, and at the same time strongly encourage re-entry into the workforce. There will be counselling provided to ensure the government can communicate its full range of services and programs that might be available and also on the way in which a client's special needs might be identified. It will be through better communication and more opportunities leading to brighter futures for the unemployed, that we shall be able to control abuse.
Before I conclude, I am pleased to note the initiatives this government has taken in respect to native unemployment. There has been several comments on native unemployment in this chamber. Native unemployment is a serious issue and demands attention. To this end and to ensure that program changes reflect the needs of native Canadians, the government has established a task force specifically to analyse the unemployment situation in this sector. If I may quote from their paper:
The demands for change have evolved for a variety of reasons. Increasing numbers of young aboriginal people are reaching labour force age without the skills or training to participate. Aboriginal unemployment rates remain double that of the national average. Aboriginal skill and education levels remain much lower than the national average. Aboriginal people have the highest illiteracy rates and the lowest income levels of any group in Canada. These problems will worsen unless economic, social and human resource development policies and programs get better results.
Now more than ever, it is appropriate to review employment and training programs and services for aboriginal people and explore where improvements can be made to better address their serious labour market needs and to more effectively utilize resources.
In the government's analysis of Canada's workforce, aboriginal people are clearly shown to have substantial barriers in access to the labour market and to be a largely undeveloped and underutilized component. Out of these concerns a native employment and training work group was established. The working group consists of aboriginal representatives from six national aboriginal organizations and from all regions of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to list very quickly some of the representatives. The organizations represented include the Metis National Council, the Union of Ontario Indian Chiefs, Assembly of First Nations, the Metis National Council, Inuit Tapirisat of Canada, Native Women's Association of Canada, Native Council of Canada, National Association of Friendship Centres, Inuvialuit Regional Corporation, Council for Yukon

Indians, Native Employment Advisory Committee, First Nations Technical Institute. Some of the individuals involved were Ray Ahenakew from the Meadow Lake Tribal Council; Richard Arcan, Yellowhead Tribal Council; representatives from St. Thomas University; from the University of Manitoba, Raoul McKay; and Germain Paul from the Native Training Institute of Quebec.
Their first meeting was held last month. I am happy to say that the program has begun positively and with definite practical direction. I welcome this initiative by the Minister of Employment and Immigration.
To conclude, I feel strongly that it is imperative that this motion must be passed. We can no longer deprive Canadians who are presently in the unfortunate position of unemployment from these fundamental steps to secure futures that are offered in Bill C-21. As Maureen Baker stated in her report:
Planning for the future must take into consideration changing
trends in education, family formation, labour force participation, and
ideology, as well as demography.
Bill C-21 has considered all of the above. I strongly urge once again its support in this House.

They have suggested the possibility of what is done in other countries. When someone becomes unemployed, they have a program that is proven to be 65 per cent effective whereby, if the member or the applicant can qualify, he can receive his full amount of unemployment insurance invested in a business. The government will supply them a loan to match that business. They have found that those businesses in which they have participated have had a 65 per cent success rate.
These are the kind of policies we should be talking about. These are the kind of programs that we could bring about to bring some good jobs and some initiative to help people out.
In Preston there is a small apple packing group where people come together to pack apples in the fall. Their normal work time was from October to the end of November. I attended a meeting in Preston. These people were laid off and they were not able to pack apples. When I checked into why they were unable to pack their apples, it was because they found that the American apples were coming across the border at $1 a box less than our Canadian apples. The free trade agreement had created this sort of problem for our people in the West Kootenays. Bill C-21 is not going to address the problems that these people have.
This bill should be scrapped. It should be scrapped now and we should be getting on with trying to bring about some legislation that will help people and not take away from them.
The government has a responsibility to participate in the unemployment insurance program along with the workers and the employers and that is the kind of system that we have been used to. The labour organizations are saying so, small businesses are saying so, and the people of Canada are saying so. The only one saying no is the government, and it is time the government changed its policies.
It is unfortunate that the government is creating the kind of animosity that it is creating across Canada. I represent 14 different small municipal areas and, as I travel throughout my riding, they contact me on a daily basis complaining about this government and what it is doing to them. They complain that they are being called racist. They complain that they are being called uncaring. They complain that they are not given any opportunities

for input on what the government is doing. I want to say to the government that it had better start listening to the people of Canada. The people of Canada want some say on the kind of changes that are taking place.

We have an attack on our social programs. First, we had the clawback on our old age pensions. Now we have the Unemployment Insurance Act being taken away from us. We have a goods and services tax that it is trying to implement across Canada, against the wishes of over 80 per cent of the people of Canada. Yet it continues to push forward with its agenda. I want to say that the people of Canada do not want that agenda. They want some changes and they want those changes to take place now.
Another concern regarding Bill C-21 is that the federal government will no longer contribute to the unemployment insurance system. Unemployment insurance is no longer a standing basic component of the social welfare system throughout the western world. Bill C-21 has in fact privatized the cornerstone of Canada's social welfare system, a move which has many Canadians asking what next. If the government will no longer contribute to UI, is it not reasonable to wonder if health insurance or pensions are next?
The government is also adding to the costs for businesses. While corporate Canada may be in the position to absorb this direct increase in production costs, the burden on smaller-sized businesses will be relatively greater. Bill C-21 serves as an indirect tax on the average worker who will help pay for the government's former share of the program.
With regard to Bill C-21 and deficit reduction, under Bill C-21 the federal government will no longer contribute to the program, as we have already discussed. This increases the burden on the worker and employer. The worker already faces large tax increases and will lose more purchasing power and this will impact negatively on the local business. For the employer, increases in UI premiums will add to the cost of production, which will in turn add to the price of the goods. This will also have a negative effect on the purchasing power throughout society and with the corresponding impact on local businesses. The point being made is that this cycle is brought on by the reduction. The government's getting out of the program undermines the defaced reduction
objective of the government in the same manner as the high interest rates and taxes.
